To mess about; to fail to get things done.

ety: From Middle English panten, whence also English dialectal pank. Possibly from Old French pantoyer, a byform or of Old French pantoisier (“to be breathless”) (compare modern French panteler (“to gasp for breath”)), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pantasiō (“struggling for breath when having a nightmare”), from Ancient Greek φαντασιόω (phantasióō, “to be subject to hallucinations”), from φαντασία (phantasía, “appearance, image, fantasy”).

s.def: A quick breathing; a catching of the breath; a gasp: the panting of animals such as a dog with their tong hung out- as a form of thermoregulation.
Eager longing.
A violent palpitation of the heart.
To breathe quickly or in a labored manner, as after exertion or from eagerness or excitement; to respire with heaving of the breast; to gasp.
ex: Pluto pants for breath from out his cell.
There is a cavern where my spirit / Was panted forth in anguish.

s.def: To long eagerly; to desire earnestly.
ex: As the hart panteth after the water brooks.

s.def: To long for (something); to be eager for (something).
Of the heart, to beat with unnatural violence or rapidity; to palpitate.
ex: Yet might her piteous heart be seen to pant and quake

s.def: To sigh; to flutter; to languish.
To heave, as the breast.
To bulge and shrink successively, of iron hulls, etc.

ety: From pantal(oon) + -ette + -s.

s.def: A form of long underpants with a frill at the bottom of each leg.
ex: A couple of shifts, some clean pantalettes, stockings, a spare pair of shoes: a suitcase is soon full.

s.def: A removable kind of ruffle worn at the feet of women's drawers.

ety: From Pantechnicon, a 19th-century firm which owned a building with a Greek-style facade of Doric columns in Motcomb Street, Belgrave Square, London, UK, with a picture gallery, a furniture shop, a shop selling carriages, and a warehouse for storing customers’ furniture and other items. The firm used large horse-drawn vans to collect and deliver their customers' property, which came to be known as Pantechnicon vans. The word was coined by the firm from pan- (“all”) (from Ancient Greek πᾶν (pân),…

s.def: A building or place housing shops or stalls where all sorts of (especially exotic) manufactured articles are collected for sale.
Originally pantechnicon van: a van, especially a large moving or removal van.
ex: For we do not employ battleships as convoys, nor even as pantechnica conveying landing parties.
In fact, as they later found, the auxiliary vehicle was a very large removers' van – the kind known as a pantechnicon.

ety: From pan- + theism, in which pan derives from Ancient Greek πᾶν (pân), meaning “all”, and theism from Ancient Greek θεός (theós), meaning “god”. The first known use is from 1702, in an English translation of Joseph Raphson’s 1697 book De Spatio Reali seu Ente Infinito, written in Latin, which coined the Latin term Pantheismus.

s.def: The belief that the Universe is in some sense divine and should be revered. Pantheism identifies the universe with God but denies any personality or transcendence of such a God.
The belief in all gods; omnitheism.

ety: From Pantheon (“a Roman temple to the gods later used as a church”), c. 1300.

s.def: A temple dedicated to all the gods.
All the gods of a particular people or religion, particularly the ancient Greek gods residing on Olympus, considered as a group.
A category or classification denoting the most honored persons of a group.
ex: Usain Bolt seals his place in the pantheon with stunning fifth gold

ety: From Middle English pantere, panter, from Old French pantere, from Latin panthēra, from Ancient Greek πάνθηρ (pánthēr, “panther”).

s.def: Any big cat of the genus Panthera.
big cat with black fur
Any of various big cats with black fur; most especially, the black-coated leopard of Africa and Asia.
A cougar; especially the Florida panther.
A girl, especially a young one, who pursues older men.

A creature resembling a big cat, typically incensed (“emitting fire”), and often having a multicolored hide, found in Ancient Greek mythology and in medieval and later heraldry (in which its depiction sometimes approaches that of a horse).
plural of panty
Underpants for women and girls.

Her housecoat had fallen open. She was wearing only panties and bra, which did nothing to make her scrawny, wrinkled body appealing.

s.def: Alternative form of pantofle.

ety: From French pantographe, from panto- (from Ancient Greek παντός (pantós), genitive singular of πᾶν (pân, “all”)), and -graphe (from γράφειν (gráphein, “to write”)).

s.def: A mechanical linkage based on parallelograms causing two objects to move in parallel; notably as a drawing aid.
ex: A pantograph can be adjusted to make either scaled or exact copies.

s.def: A similarly-formed conductive device, now usually Z-shaped, that collects electric current from overhead lines for trains and trams.
By extension, a structure of crosswise bars linked in such a way that it can extend and compress like an accordion, such as in a pantograph mirror or a scissor lift.
A pattern printed on a document to reduce the ease of photocopying.
ex: I was impressed by the quality of the pantograph; I hadn't noticed it on the original, but the copies were covered in unpleasant lines.

s.def: To engrave by means of a pantograph (parallel linkage) system.

ety: First appears c. 1606, from Latin pantomīmus, from Ancient Greek παντόμιμος (pantómimos), from πᾶς (pâs, “each, all”) + μιμέομαι (miméomai, “to mimic”). The verbal form first appears c. 1768.

s.def: The act of gesturing without speaking; a dumb-show, a mime.
ex: A staid, steadfast man, whose life for the most part was a telling pantomime of action, and not a tame chapter of sounds.
In pantomime, Chief Joyi would fling his spear and creep along the veld as he narrated the victories and defeats.

s.def: A Classical comic actor, especially one who works mainly through gesture and mime.
ex: [He] saw a pantomime perform so well that he could follow the performance from the action alone.

s.def: The drama in ancient Greece and Rome featuring such performers; or (later) any of various kinds of performance modelled on such work.

A traditional theatrical entertainment, originally based on the commedia dell'arte, but later aimed mostly at children and involving physical comedy, topical jokes, call and response, and fairy-tale plots.
To make (a gesture) without speaking.
ex: I pantomimed steering a car; he understood, and tossed the keys to me.

s.def: To entertain others by silent gestures or actions.

ety: From Middle English panetrie, from Old French paneterie, related to Latin panis (“bread”).

ex: Next to the saloon is the pantry, which includes a wine cabinet, J. E. Hall bottle-cooling unit, a Stills Café set and ample cupboard space.

s.def: A break room.

ety: From pantry + -man.

s.def: A person in charge of the pantry, or food store, on a ship, train, or other transport where food is kept for passengers and crew. Also in a hospital, school, or hotel, etc.

A parish priest in the Greek Orthodox Church.

ety: From Middle English papal, from Old French papal and Medieval Latin pāpālis (“papal”).

s.def: Having to do with the pope or the papacy.

tree

ex: Near-synonym: report

Money.
A toy airplane made by folding up a sheet of paper.

a paper cut bug: a bug which causes harm and would be easy to fix.

ex: He was wearing a red paper flower in his lapel.

Having flexible binding.
To issue or publish (a book) in a paperback edition.

ety: From paper + white.

ex: Which by the ancient sages was thus parabled.

s.def: That can easily be prepared or procured; obtainable.
ex: The most parable and easy, and about which many are employed, is to teach a school, turn lecturer or curate […].

Short for hyperbolic paraboloid
A group of South China Sea islands administered under Sansha, Hainan, China, as Xisha (claimed by Taiwan (ROC) and Vietnam).
ex: The Republic of China has reiterated its sovereignty over the Nansha and Hsisha Islands (Spratly and Paracel Islands).

ety: Borrowed from French parachute, from para- (“protection against”) (as in parasol) and chute (“fall”).

s.def: A device, generally constructed from fabric, that is designed to employ air resistance to control the fall of an object or person, causing them to float instead of falling.
A web or fold of skin extending between the legs of gliding mammals, such as the flying squirrel and colugo.
Any of various mushrooms with broad, domed caps.
A small collar which fastens around the scrotum and from which weights can be hung.
ex: Parachutes are usually made of leather and can be purchased through most fetish catalogs or stores catering to the BDSM scene.
A parachute is a small collar, usually made from leather, which fastens around the scrotum, and from which weights can be hung.

s.def: A large sheet of fabric used in children's physical education, often colorful, with handles allowing many people to control its motion.
To jump, fall, descend, etc. using such a device.
To introduce into a place using such a device.
ex: The soldiers were parachuted behind enemy lines.

s.def: To place (somebody) in an organisation in a position of authority without their having previous experience there; used with in or into.
To wrap illicit drugs in a covering before swallowing them, so that they will be released for absorption when the covering dissolves within the body.

ety: From parachute + -ing.

s.def: The sport or activity of jumping with a parachute.

s.def: Someone who jumps from an aircraft using a parachute, especially as a sport.
ex: Some hit the rocky outcrops Some fell into the sea Some even 'Roman Candled' (A parachutist I would never be)

ety: See Paraclete.

s.def: An advocate or helper.
Alternative letter-case form of Paraclete, the Holy Spirit or Holy Ghost.

ety: From French parade (“an ostentatious display, a military display”), from parer (“to beautify, prepare, take pride in”) + -ade probably under influence from earlier Italian parata (“preparation, a military parade, an ostentatious display”) and Latin magnō parātū (“with great preparation”). Various senses similarly influenced by earlier French and Italian uses. Doublet of pare.

s.def: An organized display of a group of people, particularly
ex: See how the Flow’rs, as at Parade, Under their Colours stand displaid: Each Regiment in order grows, That of the Tulip Pinke and Rose.
Verrall... seldom put on his uniform for morning parade, not thinking it necessary with mere Military Policemen.

s.def: Synonym of show: any similarly orderly or ostentatious display, especially of a variety of people or a series of things paraded around.
ex: ...the ravishing assault of a well-disciplined diction, in a parade of curiosly-mustered words in their several ranks and files...
Parade (Fr.), an appearance or shew, a bravado or vaunting offer.
...the most virtuous and laudable deed that his whole Life could make any parade of...

s.def: A place reserved for such displays, particularly
ex: Parade, is a Military word, signifying the Place where Troops usually draw together, in order to mount the Guards, or for any other Service.
When Barracks are occupied by Troops, the Yards and Parades are to be swept, rolled, and kept clean by them.

s.def: The people who make up such a display, particularly
ex: The Commanding Officer is then to direct the Parade to Order Arms.

s.def: Ellipsis of programme parade: a description of the programming schedule formerly announced on the radio and various television channels.
ex: Scottish Programme Parade
Listen to your regional Programme Parade at 8.10 a.m. daily.

s.def: A row of shops beside a street.
ex: Most new shopping centres... have broken away from the old strip parades which usually face each other across heavy inter-town traffic.

s.def: To take part in a parade
ex: ... the other three Companies were ordained by foure a clocke afternoone, to parade in the Market place, and afterwards to march to their Post...
Hooper had been detailed to inspect the lines. The company was parading at 0730 hours with their kit-bags piled before the huts.

s.def: To cause to take part in a parade, particularly
ex: The men were paraded and briefly addressed by the colonel in my presence...

s.def: To furnish with a parade or parades.
ex: The modern part that faces the sea is... paraded, well lighted, well drained.

s.def: Synonym of parry in both its literal and figurative senses.
ex: ...in case the adversary after a finda, going to the parade, discover his brest to caveat...

ety: From Middle English paradygme, from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”), from παραδείκνυμι (paradeíknumi, “I show [beside] or compare”) + -μα (-ma, suffix forming nouns concerning the results of actions). Doublet of paradigma.

s.def: A pattern, a way of doing something; especially a pattern of thought, a system of beliefs, a conceptual framework.
ex: Near-synonyms: style, model, worldview

s.def: An example serving as the model for such a pattern; an exceptionally good or prototypical example of a pattern or group.
ex: Near-synonyms: template, exemplar, archetype, poster child; see also Thesaurus:exemplar, Thesaurus:model
According to the Fourth Circuit, “Coca-Cola” is “the paradigm of a descriptive mark that has acquired secondary meaning”.
DRT is a paradigm example of a dynamic semantic theory, […]

s.def: A set of all forms which contain a common element, especially the set of all inflectional forms of a word or a particular grammatical category.
ex: The paradigm of "to sing" is "sing, sang, sung". The verb "to ring" follows the same paradigm.

ety: From Middle English paradis, paradise, paradys, from Late Old English paradīs, borrowed from Old French paradis, from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. Doublet of parvis. Displaced Old English neorxnawang.

s.def: heaven
The place where sanctified souls are believed to live after death.
ex: Living in paradise comes with a price.
The imagination of the Hindoo paints his Swergas as "profuse of bliss," and all the joys of sense are collected in the Paradise of the Mussulman.
I believe the soul in Paradise must enjoy something nearer to a perpetual adulthood than to any other state we know.

s.def: A very pleasant place, such as a place full of lush vegetation.
ex: Near-synonym: rose garden
an island paradise in the Caribbean
Let me live here ever; So rare a wonder’d father and a wife Makes this place Paradise.

s.def: An ideal place for a specified type of person, activity, etc.
ex: a shoppers’ paradise

s.def: A very pleasant experience.
ex: The weariest and most loathed worldly life That age, ache, penury and imprisonment Can lay on nature is a paradise To what we fear of death.
He poured the last of the wine as Fanny, her face composed as she stroked his leg, after a paradise of expectation touched his aroused organ.

s.def: An open space within a monastery or adjoining a church, such as the space within a cloister, the open court before a basilica, etc.
A churchyard or cemetery.
The upper gallery in a theatre.
A cake, often as a paradise slice.
Alternative letter-case form of Paradise (“Heaven”).

ety: From Middle French paradoxe, from Latin paradoxum, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).

s.def: An apparently self-contradictory statement, which can only be true if it is false, and vice versa.
ex: "This sentence is false" is a paradox.
The active sense of living which we all enjoy, before reflection shatters our instinctive world for us, is self-luminous and suggests no paradoxes.

s.def: apparent contradiction which is nonetheless true
A counterintuitive conclusion or outcome.
ex: It is an interesting paradox that drinking a lot of water can often make you feel thirsty.
The most fundamental paradox is that if we're never to use force, we must be prepared to use it and to use it successfully.

s.def: A claim that two apparently contradictory ideas are true.
ex: Not having a fashion is a fashion; that's a paradox.

s.def: A thing involving contradictory yet interrelated elements that exist simultaneously and persist over time.
A person or thing having contradictory properties.
ex: He is a paradox; you would not expect him in that political party.
You are a paradox of bitch and angel.

s.def: An unanswerable question or difficult puzzle, particularly one which leads to a deeper truth.
ex: And only by dismantling our preconceptions of age can we be free to understand the paradox: How young are the old?

s.def: A statement which is difficult to believe, or which goes against general belief.
ex: they contended to make that Maxim, that there is no faith to be held with Infidels, a meere and absurd Paradox [...].

s.def: The use of counterintuitive or contradictory statements (paradoxes) in speech or writing.
ex: The need for paradox is no doubt rooted deep in the very nature of the use we make of language.

s.def: A state in which one is logically compelled to contradict oneself.
ex: Thus, like modern disputants, they aimed either to confute the respondent or to land him in paradox.

s.def: Having self-contradictory properties.
ex: It sounds paradoxical, but I am inclined to think that the weakness and insanity of the curate warned me, braced me, and kept me a sane man.

ety: So called because it is larger as a tadpole than as an adult frog.

s.def: Pseudis paradoxa, a species of frog unusual because it is larger as a tadpole (up to 25 cm or 10 in. long) than as an adult (about a quarter of that length).

ety: From Latin paraffinum, from parum (too little) + affinis (related, affinity). Therefore low affinity or being chemically neutral.

s.def: A petroleum-based thin and colourless fuel oil.
ex: She poured paraffin on the dry floors and on the pandanus-mats, and then she set fire.

s.def: Any member of the alkane hydrocarbons.
Paraffin wax.
To impregnate or treat with paraffin.
To embed in paraffin wax.
One who paraglides.
A lightweight, free-flying, foot-launched glider aircraft with no rigid primary structure.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French paragon, paragone, from Old Italian paragone, from paragonare (“to test on a touchstone”), perhaps from Ancient Greek παρακονᾶν (parakonân, “to sharpen, whet”), from παρά- (pará-) + ἀκόνη (akónē, “whetstone, sharpening stone”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point, edge”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”)).

s.def: A companion; a match; an equal.
ex: Philoclea, who indeed had no paragon but her sister
Nathlesse proud man himselfe the other deemed, Having so peerlesse paragon ygot

s.def: A person of preeminent qualities, who acts as a pattern or model for others.
ex: In the novel, Constanza is a paragon of virtue who would never compromise her reputation.
Liz Cheney and her father are positioning themselves as protectors of the old order, as paragons of truth and as defenders of our American norms.
A paragon must embody liberal democracy. To get its hands dirty defending it is below-stairs.

s.def: Comparison; competition.
ex: good by paragone / Of euill, may more notably be rad, / As white seemes fairer, macht with blacke attone […].

s.def: The size of type between great primer and double pica, standardized as 20-point.
A flawless diamond of at least 100 carats.
To serve as a model for; to surpass.
To compare; to parallel; to put in rivalry or emulation with.
ex: for want of a bigger , to paragon the little one with Artesia's length

s.def: To compare with; to equal; to rival.
ex: Few or none could for Feature paragon with her, and much less excel her.

s.def: To be equal; to hold comparison.

ety: From Middle English paragraf, from Middle French paragraphe from Latin paragraphus (“sign for start of a new section of discourse”), from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos), from παρά (pará, “beside”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). Doublet of paragraphos.

s.def: A passage in text that starts on a new line, the first line sometimes being indented, and usually marks a change of topic.
ex: opening paragraph
final paragraph
paragraph heading

s.def: A mark or note set in the margin to call attention to something in the text, such as a change of subject.
A brief article, notice, or announcement, as in a newspaper.
An offset of 16 bytes in Intel memory architectures.
To sort text into paragraphs.
To publish a brief article, notice, or announcement, as in a newspaper.

English Paraguay Borrowed from Spanish Paraguay, from Classical Guarani Paraguaĭ (“Paraguay River”), from paraguâ (“feather crown”) + ĭ (“river”).

s.def: A country in South America. Official name: Republic of Paraguay. Capital and largest city: Asunción.
A river in South America that flows into the Paraná, through Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia and Argentina; in full, the Paraguay River.

ety: Etymology tree Classical Guarani paraguâ Proto-Tupian *ʔɨ Proto-Tupi-Guarani *ʔɨ Classical Guarani ĭ Classical Guarani Paraguaĭbor. Spanish Paraguaybor. s.def: A person from Paraguay or of Paraguayan descent.
ex: My mother is a Paraguayan.

ety: From Middle French perroquet, probably a diminutive form of the personal name Pierre; some variant forms perhaps via Italian parrocchetto, Spanish periquito.

s.def: Any of various species of small parrot primarily of tropical regions.
ex: we had loved them for our pastimes, as we do apes, monkies, or perokitoes, and not as man.
According to one legend, the parakeets escaped from the set of The African Queen, John Huston's 1951 film made at Shepperton studios.

ety: From Middle French parallaxe, from Ancient Greek παράλλαξις (parállaxis, “alteration”) from παραλλάσσω (parallássō, “to cause to alternate”) from ἀλλάσσω (allássō, “to alter”) from ἄλλος (állos, “other”). See also para- and allo-.

s.def: An apparent shift in the position of two stationary objects relative to each other as viewed by an observer, due to a change in observer position.
ex: […] Heliocentrick places, to which the Parallaxes being applied, give the Geocentrick.

s.def: The angle of seeing of the astronomical unit.
Any of several methods of determining distance.
To measure (a distance) based on parallax observations.
To produce an illusion of levels of distance by shifting layers at different rates.

ety: From Middle French parallèle and its etymon Latin parallēlus, parallēlos. The verb is from the noun. See also para- and allo-.

s.def: Equally distant from one another at all points.
ex: The horizontal lines on my notebook paper are parallel.
the instrument held with its plane roughly parallel to the equinoctial or celestial equato

s.def: Having the same overall direction; the comparison is indicated with "to".
ex: The two railway lines are parallel.
When honour runs parallel with the laws of God and our country, it cannot be too much cherished.

s.def: Either not intersecting, or coinciding.
Involving the processing of multiple tasks at the same time.
ex: a parallel algorithm

s.def: Analogous, similar, comparable.
ex: the parallel lives of two citizens

s.def: Coexisting but normally not interacting with the regular reality.
ex: parallel universe

s.def: With a parallel relationship.
ex: The road runs parallel to the canal.

s.def: One of a set of parallel lines.
ex: Who made the spider parallels design, / Sure as De Moivre, without rule or line?

s.def: Direction conformable to that of another line.
ex: lines that from their parallel decline

s.def: A line of latitude.
ex: The 31st parallel passes through the center of my town.

s.def: A type of computation in which many calculations or processes are carried out simultaneously.
ex: Some of the most impressive applications of massively parallel computing have been in the context of wide-area distributed platforms.

s.def: A universe that exists separately alongside another universe, as part of a multiverse.
The universe of an alternative history.

ety: From Latin parallēlepipedum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδος (parallēlepípedos, “with parallel surfaces”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + ἐπίπεδος (epípedos, “plane”).

s.def: A solid figure, having six faces, all parallelograms, all opposite faces being similar and parallel.
ex: A cuboid is a rectangular parallelepiped.

ety: From parallel + -ism and from Late Latin parallelismus.

s.def: The state or condition of being parallel; agreement in direction, tendency, or character.
The state of being in agreement or similarity; resemblance, correspondence, analogy.
ex: Plutarch (c. AD 46-120), in his Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans, traced a parallelism between the most eminent men of the two countries.

s.def: A parallel position; the relation of parallels.
The juxtaposition of two or more identical or equivalent syntactic constructions, especially those expressing the same sentiment with slight modifications, introduced for rhetorical effect.
The doctrine that matter and mind do not causally interact but that physiological events in the brain or body nonetheless occur simultaneously with matching events in the mind.
In antitrust law, the practice of competitors of raising prices by roughly the same amount at roughly the same time, without engaging in a formal agreement to do so.
Similarity of features between two species resulting from their having taken similar evolutionary paths following their initial divergence from a common ancestor.
The use of parallel methods in hardware or software, so that several tasks can be performed at the same time.

ety: From Latin parallelogrammum, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + γραμμή (grammḗ, “line”).

s.def: A convex quadrilateral in which each pair of opposite edges are parallel and of equal length.
ex: Meronyms: angle, side; see also Thesaurus:polygon

s.def: either of two rectangular areas (respectively the large parallelogram and the small parallelogram) abutting the goal line in front of the goal. (Since 1986 officially named the large rectangle and small rectangle, though the older names are still occasionally used.)
ex: Goulding was fouled in the small parallelogram and O’Connor nicked the penalty into the net off the post.
There are seven Kilkenny players inside the large parallelogram and only two from Tipperary. Yet Tipp have scored a goal.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French paralogisme, from Late Latin paralogismus, from Ancient Greek παραλογισμός (paralogismós).

s.def: A fallacious argument or illogical conclusion, especially one committed by mistake, or believed by the speaker to be logical.
ex: Which is a Paralogism not admittible; a fallacy that dwels not in a cloud, and needs not the Sun to scatter it.

ety: Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”). By surface analysis, para- + -lysis. Doublet of palsy.

s.def: The complete loss of voluntary control of part of a living body, such as one or more limbs.
A state of being unable to act.
ex: The government has been in a paralysis since it lost its majority in the parliament.

ety: Borrowed from French paralytique, from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (paralutikós, “paralyzed”).

s.def: Someone suffering from paralysis.
A drug that produces paralysis.
ex: For example, use of paralytics in morbidly obese patients or those with spinal instability can precipitate complete upper airway obstruction.

s.def: Very drunk.
ex: He hasn't even been openly accused of anything bar drinking himself paralytic at a time that, in hindsight, was inconvenient.

s.def: Pertaining to paralysis.
Affected by paralysis; paralysed.
ex: the cold, shaking, paralytic hand

ety: From para- + magnetic. Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1850 for Michael Faraday.

s.def: Exhibiting paramagnetism.

ety: So named from Parramatta, in Australia.

s.def: A light fabric of cotton and worsted, resembling bombazine or merino.

ety: From Ancient Greek παραμήκης (paramḗkēs, “oval”), from μῆκος (mêkos, “length”).

s.def: An oval-shaped protozoan organism of the genus Paramecium.
ex: The sun beats on his eyelids; inside them a paramecium revolves. A blink and it changes pattern like a kaleidoscope.

ety: From para- + medic.

s.def: A person trained to medically stabilize people through various interventions for victims of trauma or medical events outside of a hospital setting and prepare them for transport to a medical facility.
A person who is licensed at the state or national level to practice medical interventions in an emergency prehospital setting.

ety: From French paramètre, from New Latin parametrum (“parameter”), from Ancient Greek παρα- (para-, “beside”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).

s.def: A value kept constant during an experiment, equation, calculation, or similar, but varied over other versions of the experiment, equation, calculation, etc.
A variable that describes a property or characteristic of some system (material, object, event, etc.) or some aspect thereof.
ex: Cohesion parameters (solubility parameters) can be used with full theoretical justification to characterize many surfaces ...
To this end, we derive an a posteriori error estimator for the error with respect to the unknown parameter.

s.def: An input variable of a function definition, that gets an actual value (argument) at execution time.
An actual value given to such a formal parameter.
A characteristic or feature that distinguishes something from others.
In the ellipse and hyperbola, a third proportional to any diameter and its conjugate, or in the parabola, to any abscissa and the corresponding ordinate.
ex: The parameter of the principal axis of a conic section is called the latus rectum.

s.def: Clipping of uniformizing parameter.
The ratio of the three crystallographic axes which determines the position of any plane.
The fundamental axial ratio for a given species.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Hellenic *pərai Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ́ (părắ) Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ- (pără-)der. English para- English military English paramilitary From para- + military.

s.def: A group of civilians trained and organized in a military fashion, but which do not represent the formal forces of a sovereign power.
A member of a paramilitary group.
Relating to a paramilitary.

ety: From para- + amnesia.

s.def: An inability to distinguish between real memories and dreams or fantasies
An inability to remember the meaning of common words

ety: PIE word *h₂éd From Anglo-Norman paramont /paramount (“paramount, pre-eminent; above”), from Old French par /per (“by”) + amont /amunt (“upward”). s.def: Highest, supreme; also, chief, leading, pre-eminent.
ex: […]a Traitor Paramount;

s.def: Of the highest importance.
ex: Getting those credit cards paid off is paramount.

s.def: Of a law, right, etc.: having precedence over or superior to another.
A chief or superior; (specifically, chiefly South Africa) an African chief having the highest status in a region; a paramount chief.

A supreme ruler; an overlord; (specifically, historical) in the feudal system, a landowner who did not derive ownership of the land from anyone else, and who was able to grant fees to others; a lord paramount.

ety: The adverb is derived from Middle English par amour, paramore, paramours (“with sexual desire or love, passionately; in a courteous or friendly manner”), from Anglo-Norman par amur (“in a friendly or willing manner”) and Old French par amur, par amour, paramours (“by or through love”) (modern French par amour), from par (“by; through; etc.”) (from Latin per (“by means of, through”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through; etc.”)) + amor, amur (“love”, noun) (from Latin amōrem…

s.def: A person who is the object of one's love, especially in an affair or romance; a lover; also, a sexual partner.
A person (especially someone who is not one's spouse) with whom one has an illicit or secret affair; also (Scotland, US, law), one with whom a married person has an adulterous affair.
ex: to run away with a paramour
[G]ive them / Their dowers, according to what / Is reasonable: they should be chaste, not lustful, nor taking paramours: […]

s.def: A woman who is the object of a knight's love, and who he fights for.
God as the object of a person's devotion or love.
To have an illicit or secret affair with a person, especially someone who is not one's spouse.
ex: [W]ine loued I deeply, dice deerely, and in vvoman out paromord the Turke, […]
[I]ndeed a daughter is better ill married, then vvell Paramour'd.
The paramouring matron left / A babe and husband both bereft; […]

s.def: Of loving, etc.: out of or through romantic feeling or sexual desire; passionately.
ex: Because you love par amours, is it reasonable you should throw away your life and ours?
Wolnoth is bound par-amours, to a certain fair Norman dame; and, I trow well, prefers her charms here to the thought of his return.

s.def: Used chiefly when addressing someone: out of or through devotion or kindness; as a favour or kindness.

ety: From Portuguese and Spanish Paraná, both from Língua Geral Paulista paraná (“river”).

s.def: A state of the South Region, Brazil. Capital: Curitiba.
A river in central and southern South America.
The provincial capital of Entre Ríos, Argentina.
A municipality of Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παράνοια (paránoia, “madness”), from παράνοος (paránoos, “demented”), from παρά (pará, “beyond, beside”) + νόος (nóos, “mind, spirit”). By surface analysis, para- (“abnormal, beyond”) + nous (“mind”) + -ia (“(medical) condition”).

s.def: A psychotic disorder, now called delusional disorder, often (in one of six subtypes) characterized by delusions of persecution and a perceived threat against the individual affected with the disorder, and often associated with false accusations and a general mistrust of others.
Extreme, irrational distrust of others.

ety: Etymology tree English paranoia Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o- Proto-Indo-European *weyd- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *wéydos Proto-Hellenic *wéidos Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos) Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-ēs Proto-Hellenic *-ēs Ancient Greek -ης (-ēs) Ancient Greek -ειδής (-eidḗs) Latin -oīdēslbor. English -oid English paranoid From paranoia + -oid.

s.def: Of, related to, or suffering from clinical paranoia.
Exhibiting excessive fear, suspicion, or distrust.
ex: But can the people on TV see me or am I just paranoid?

s.def: A mental disorder characterized by paranoia and a pervasive, long-standing suspiciousness and generalized mistrust of others.
A form of schizophrenia that is accompanied by delusions, either of persecution, grandeur or jealousy.

ety: From Middle French paranymphe, from Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos, “friend of bridegroom”), from παρα- (para-, “para-”) + νύμφη (númphē, “bride”).

s.def: A friend of the bridegroom; a best man; a bridesmaid.
An ally or spokesman; someone who speaks in support of someone else.
ex: But it is the basest of all when lust is the paranymph, and solicits the suit, and makes the contract, and joins the hands; […]

ety: From Middle French parapet, from Italian parapetto.

s.def: A low protective wall.
ex: Engineers will be closely checking the bridge for damage beyond the obvious smashed parapets.

s.def: Part of a perimeter that extends above the roof.
A fortification consisting of a wall.

der: keep one's head below the parapet
put one's head above the parapet

ety: Inherited from Middle English paraf, from Medieval Latin paraffus or its etymon Middle French paraphe, paraffe, shortening of paragraphe, from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos).

s.def: A flourish made after or below one's signature, originally to prevent forgery.
A mark used by medieval rubricators to indicate textual division.
To add a paraph to; to sign, especially with one's initials.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin paraphernālia (“goods which a wife brings over and above her dowry”), use as noun (short for paraphernālia bona (“paraphernal goods”)) of neuter plural of paraphernālis, from Late Latin parapherna + Latin -ālis (suffix forming adjectives), from Ancient Greek παράφερνα (parápherna), a compound of παρά (pará, “beside”) + φερνή (phernḗ, “dowry”). In the propertied classes, a dowry was placed under the control of the husband, while the paraphernalia which she brought wi…

s.def: Miscellaneous items, especially the set of equipment required for a particular activity.
ex: drug paraphernalia
He has an impressive collection of bicycling paraphernalia, but he doesn't ride very often anymore.

s.def: Objects that a married woman owns, such as clothing and jewellery, apart from her dowry.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Hellenic *pərai Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ́ (părắ) Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ- (pără-)der. English para- Proto-Indo-European *bʰil- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *bʰil-o-s Ancient Greek φῐ́λος (phĭ́los) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-íā Ancient Greek -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā) Ancient Greek φῐλῐ́ᾱ (phĭlĭ́ā)der. English -philia English paraphilia From para- (“abnormal”) + -…

s.def: sexual deviation
An abnormal sexual arousal or attraction, especially to objects or situations that are not of a sexual nature; typically of extreme or pathological nature.
ex: As Stoller says, "perversion is a sturdy word, throbbing with assumptions, while paraphilia is a wet noodle."

s.def: Sexual arousal in response to sexual objects or situations which may interfere with the capacity for reciprocal affectionate sexual activity or lead to clinically significant distress or impairment (e.g. are obligatory, require participation of unconsenting individuals, lead to legal issues).

ety: From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis), equivalent to para- + phrase. Doublet of paraphrasis.

s.def: A restatement of a text in different words, often to clarify meaning or from memory rather than verbatim.
ex: Near-synonym: paraphrasis
close paraphrase
The article included a brief paraphrase of the speech.

s.def: One of a certain number of Scripture passages turned into verse for use in the service of praise.
To restate something as, or to compose a paraphrase. To repeat a written or spoken phrase/quote using different words, often in a simpler and shorter form, or sometimes in a humorous context.
ex: She asked the student to paraphrase the passage.

ety: From New Latin paraplegia, from Ancient Greek παραπληγίη (paraplēgíē), Ionic Greek for παραπληξία (paraplēxía, “paralysis on one side”), from παραπλήσσεσθαι (paraplḗssesthai, “to be stricken on one side”), active παραπλήσσειν (paraplḗssein, “to strike on one side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike”).

s.def: A condition where the lower half of a patient's body is paralyzed and cannot move.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Hellenic *pərai Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ́ (părắ) Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ- (pără-)der. English para- English psychology English parapsychology From para- (“above, beyond; abnormal”) + psychology.

s.def: The study of alleged paranormal phenomena; psychic or occult phenomena, such as telepathy and ghosts.

ety: From Latin parasanga, from Ancient Greek παρασάγγης (parasángēs), from unattested Old Persian *frasanhvah (indigenously attested only in Middle Iranian onwards); compare Middle Persian [script needed] (frasang /⁠plsng⁠/, “frasang (4 Roman miles)”) (whence Persian فرسنگ (farsang)). Doublet of farsang and farsakh.

s.def: A historical Iranian unit of itinerant distance used throughout the Western Mediterranean and the Middle East in antiquity, originally the distance travelled in one hour, and generally assumed to be equivalent to about six kilometres.
ex: To see so much difference betwixt words and deeds, so many parasangs betwixt tongue and heart […].
We were told that we still had to drive six or sixty parasang.

ety: From Ancient Greek παρά (pará, “beside”) + σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”).

s.def: Synonym of moon dog.

ety: From Middle French parasite, from Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos, “person who eats at the table of another”), from noun use of adjective meaning "feeding beside", from παρά (pará, “beside”) + σῖτος (sîtos, “food”).

s.def: (biology) organism that exists by stealing resources from another organism

An organism that lives on or in another organism of a different species, deriving benefit from living on or in that other organism, while not contributing towards that other organism sufficiently to cover the cost to that other organism.
ex: Lice, fleas, ticks, and mites are widely spread parasites.

s.def: A person who lives on other people's efforts or expense and gives little or nothing back.
ex: A royalist who publicly called for a military intervention to protect the parasite monarchy.

s.def: A sycophant or hanger-on.
A climbing plant which is supported by a wall, trellis etc.
ex: Her golden tresses shade / The bosom's stainless pride, / Curling like tendrils of the parasite / Around a marble column.

s.def: A retainer or companion of an ancient Celtic warrior, who praised him in song or poetry at gatherings; a bard.
A component of a composite aircraft which is carried aloft and air-launched by a larger carrier aircraft or mother ship to support the primary mission of the carrier; a parasite aircraft.
An isolated (FSDU) (freestanding display unit )
ex: parasite display
parasite stand
parasite unit

s.def: To parasitize.

ety: From French parasol, from Italian parasole, from para- (“to shield”) + sole (“sun”).

s.def: A small light umbrella used as protection from the sun.
A miniature paper umbrella used as a decoration in tropical-themed cocktails.
A sun umbrella for garden use etc., mounted on a stand; these can be foldable and demountable.
A roof or covering of a structure designed to provide cover from wind, rain, or sun.
Any of various Asian species of libellulid dragonfly of the genus Neurothemis.
A parasol mushroom (Macrolepiota procera)
To protect with, or as if with, a parasol; to shade.
ex: […] the buffaloes in the mire, and rows of trees parasolling houses along the waterways.

ety: From para- (“beside, adjacent to”) + sympathetic, because some of these nerves run alongside sympathetic nerves.

s.def: Of or relating to the part of the autonomic nervous system that inhibits or opposes the effects of the sympathetic nervous system. It consists of nerves arising from the brain and the lower end of the spinal cord and supplying the internal organs, blood vessels, and glands.
A parasympathetic nerve.
Ellipsis of parasympathetic nervous system.

ety: From para- + synonym.

s.def: A term (word or phrase) which is parasynonymous with others, but not necessarily considered a synonym.
ex: Near-synonym: synonym

ety: From para- + syphilis.

s.def: Any form of neurosyphilis that formerly was known to be correlated with late-stage syphilis but was misapprehended to be distinct from it.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παράταξις (parátaxis, “placement side by side”), from παρα- (para-) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”); equivalent to para- + taxis.

s.def: Speech or writing in which clauses or phrases are placed together without being separated by conjunctions, for example "I came; I saw; I conquered".
The juxtaposition of two images or fragments, usually starkly dissimilar, without a clear connection.
A coalition or "partisan camp" in the Ancient Greek political system.
A polypeptide hormone that is released by the chief cells of the parathyroid glands and is involved in raising the levels of calcium ions in the blood.

ety: Blend of parachute + trooper.

s.def: A type of soldier who is trained to enter combat zones by parachuting from aircraft.
infantry soldiers deployed by parachute
third-person singular simple present indicative of paratroop

ety: From para- + typhoid.

s.def: Resembling typhoid.
paratyphoid fever

ety: From para- + vane.

s.def: A device, stabilized with vanes, towed alongside a vessel such that the cable attaching it cuts the moorings of submerged mines.
A towed underwater object with hydrofoils, of diverse uses.

ety: From Middle English parboyle, from Old French parbouillir (“to boil thoroughly”), from Medieval Latin perbulliō, from Latin per (“thoroughly”) + bulliō (“to boil”). Sense “to boil partially” (c.1440), rather than original “to boil thoroughly” is by corruption: associating the prefix with part (from Latin pars (“part”)) rather than per.

s.def: To boil food briefly so that it is partly cooked.

ety: Earliest forms are parbuncle, parbunkel and parbunkle. Of unknown earlier origin. Influenced by buckle and French boucle (“loop”)

s.def: A kind of purchase for hoisting or lowering a cylindrical burden, as a cask. The middle of a long rope is fastened aloft, and both ends of the rope are looped under, then over the cylinder and looped back towards the attachment point. The object rests in the loops, and rolls upward in them as the r…
A double sling made of a single rope, for slinging a cask, gun, etc.
To hoist or lower by means of a parbuckle

ety: From Middle English parcel, from Old French parcelle (“a small piece or part, a parcel, a particle”), from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula (“particle”), diminutive of partem (“part, piece”). Doublet of particle.

s.def: A package wrapped, as for shipment or transport.
ex: I saw a brown paper parcel on my doorstep.

s.def: A division of land bought and sold as a unit.
ex: I own a small parcel of land between the refinery and the fish cannery.

s.def: A group of birds.
An indiscriminate or indefinite number, measure, or quantity; a collection; a group.
ex: […] this youthful parcel / Of noble bachelors stand at my bestowing,

s.def: An individual consignment of cargo for shipment, regardless of size and form.
An individual item appearing on an invoice or receipt (only in the phrase bill of parcels).
A small amount of food that has been wrapped up, for example a pastry.
A portion of anything taken separately; a fragment of a whole; a part.
ex: A certain piece of land is part and parcel of another piece.
The same Experiments succeed on two Parcels of the White of an Egg […]
I don't think we are sitting pretty / So far away from our fair city / But I love you more than any parcel of earth.

s.def: To wrap something up into the form of a package.
To wrap a strip around the end of a rope.
ex: Worm and parcel with the lay; turn and serve the other way.

s.def: A usually removable shelf lying behind the back seats or over the trunk of a car.

ety: From Middle English parchen, paarchen (“to parch; dry; roast”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps a variant of Middle English perchen (“to roast”).

s.def: To roast, as dry grain.
ex: Ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn.

s.def: To dry to extremity; to shrivel with heat.
ex: The patient’s mouth is parched from fever.
The last day's march was very painful, for the north wind, blowing full in their faces, parched and benumbed the men.

s.def: To be very thirsty.
ex: We're parched, hon. Could you send up an ale from the cooler?
In my haste I stumbled , and fell over one of the wounded; he groaned, and prayed me for a cup of water to cool the thirst that parched him.
Serpents bit them, thirst parched them, Amalekites assailed them.

s.def: To burn the surface of, to scorch.
ex: The sun today could parch cement.

s.def: To become superficially burnt; to become sunburned.
ex: The locals watched, amused, as the tourists parched in the sun, having neglected to apply sunscreen or bring water.

s.def: To boil something slowly (Still used in Lancashire in parched peas, a type of mushy peas).
The condition of being parched.
ex: Yet here he is, not at the head, but somewhere toward the rear of the serpentine queue wending its way through all this parch […].

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek Πέργαμον (Pérgamon) Proto-Indo-European *-nós Ancient Greek -νός (-nós) Ancient Greek -ηνός (-ēnós) Ancient Greek Περγαμηνὴ (διφθέρα) (Pergamēnḕ (diphthéra))bor. Vulgar Latin *pergamīnus Old French parcheminbor. Middle English parchemyn English parchment From Middle English parchemyn, parchement, from Old French parchemin, via Latin pergamīna, from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós, “of Pergamon”), which is named for the ancient city of Pergamon (modern Bergama)…

s.def: Material, made from the polished skin of a calf, sheep, goat or other animal, used like paper for writing.
A document made on such material.
A diploma (traditionally written on parchment).
Stiff paper imitating that material.
The creamy to tanned color of parchment.
The envelope of the coffee grains, inside the pulp.
Cellulose-based paper used in baking as a disposable nonstick surface.

ety: Variant pronunciation of partner.

s.def: A friend or companion.
A partner.
A local community banking co-op, often set up as an initiative for a social group unable to get formal credit or bank accounts, notably West Indians in Britain.

ety: From Middle English pardonen, from Old French pardoner (modern French pardonner), from Late Latin perdōnāre, from per- + dōnāre, possibly a calque (if not vice-versa) of a Germanic word represented by Frankish *firgeban (“to forgive, give up completely”), from *fir- + *geban. Akin to Old High German fargeban, firgeban (“to forgive”), Old English forġiefan (“to forgive”). More at forgive.

s.def: Forgiveness for an offence.
ex: […] a step, that could not be taken with the least hope of ever obtaining pardon from or reconciliation with any of my friends; […]

s.def: An order that releases a convicted criminal without further punishment, prevents future punishment, or (in some jurisdictions) removes an offence from a person's criminal record, as if it had never been committed.
ex: The President[…]shall have Power to grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offences against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.

s.def: To forgive (a person).
ex: I hope you will not find he has outstepped the truth more than may be pardoned, in consideration of the motive.
Well! the King of France died pardoning & pitying all those who had tortured his Soul & Body, a great Pattern for us all.

s.def: To refrain from exacting as a penalty.
To grant an official pardon for a crime.
Often used when someone does not understand what another person says.
Forgiven for wrongdoing.

ety: From Middle English paren, from Old French parer (“to arrange, prepare, trim”), from Latin parō (“to prepare, arrange; to provide, furnish; to resolve, purpose”) (related to pariō (“to bear, to give birth to; to spawn, produce, beget; to procure, acquire”)), from a Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bring forward, bring forth”).

s.def: To remove the outer covering or skin of something with a cutting device, typically a knife.
ex: Victor pared some apples in preparation to make a tart.

s.def: To reduce, diminish or trim gradually something as if by cutting off.
ex: Albert had to pare his options down by disregarding anything beyond his meager budget.

s.def: To trim the hoof of a horse.
To sharpen a pencil.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek παρηγορικός (parēgorikós, “soothing”), from παρηγορέω (parēgoréō, “to console, comfort”).

s.def: A painkiller; a medicine which soothes or relieves pain; specifically the traditional patent medicine consisting of camphorated tincture of opium.
Assuaging or soothing pain.
ex: paregoric elixir

ety: Borrowed from German Pareidolie, constructed from Ancient Greek παρα- (para-, “alongside”) + εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image”) + -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, par- + eidolia.

s.def: The tendency to interpret a vague stimulus as something known to the observer, such as interpreting marks on Mars as canals, seeing shapes in clouds, or hearing hidden messages in music.
ex: This last is called by Dr. Kahlbaum, changing hallucination, partial hallucination, perception of secondary images, or pareidolia.
Pareidolia underlies several forms of divination.

ety: From Ancient Greek παρέγχῠμα (parénkhŭma, “anything poured in beside”), from πᾰρᾰ- (pără-, “beside”) + ἔγχῠμα (énkhŭma, “instillation, content of a vessel”), given by the Greek anatomist Erasistratus to the peculiar substance of the lungs, liver, kidneys, and spleen, as if formed separately by the veins that run into them. By surface analysis, para- + -enchyma.

s.def: The functional tissue of an organ as distinguished from the connective and supporting tissue.
The cellular tissue, typically soft and succulent, found chiefly in the softer parts of leaves, pulp of fruits, bark and pith of stems, etc.
Cellular tissue lying between the body wall and the organs of invertebrate animals lacking a coelom, such as flatworms.
ex: [I]n a Sponge, the Parenchyma, it seems, is but a kind of mucous gelly, which is very easily and cleerly wash'd away.

ety: From Middle English parent, borrowed from Anglo-Norman parent, Middle French parent, from Latin parentem, accusative of parēns (“parent”), present participle of pariō (“to breed, bring forth”).

s.def: An organism from which a plant or animal is immediately biologically descended.
person from whom one is descended
person who acts as a parent in rearing a child — see also guardian
A person who raises a child (which they have made, adopted, fostered, taken as their own, etc.).
ex: After both her parents were killed in a forest fire, Sonia was adopted by her aunt and uncle.
The NHS is naturally pro-immunisation, reassuring parents that their babies can easily cope with these jabs.

s.def: A person who has had a baby; this person in relation to their child or children.
A surrogate parent.
A third person who has provided DNA samples in an IVF procedure in order to alter faulty genetic material.
A relative.
The source or origin of something.
ex: Misery is often the parent of the most affecting touches in poetry.
Indolence and unalimentary food are the parents of this disease; but to neither are Indians accustomed.

s.def: Sponsor, supporter, owner, protector.

ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis, “insertion”). By surface analysis, par- + en- + thesis.

s.def: Either of a pair of brackets, especially (mainly US) round brackets, ( and ) (used to enclose parenthetical material in a text).
Such brackets as used to clarify expressions by grouping those terms affected by a common operator, or to enclose the components of a vector or the elements of a matrix.
A clause, phrase or word which is inserted (usually for explanation or amplification) into a passage which is already grammatically complete, and usually marked off with brackets, commas or dashes.
ex: How expressive this little parenthesis: "Sakuntalâ makes a chiding gesture with her finger"!

s.def: A digression; the use of such digressions.

ety: Etymology tree English parent Proto-Indo-European *keyt-der. Proto-Germanic *haiduzder. Proto-West Germanic *-haiduder. Old English -hād Middle English -hede English -hood English parenthood From parent + -hood.

s.def: The state of being a parent

ety: Borrowed from Tahitian pāreu.

s.def: A wraparound garment, worn by men or women, similar to a Malaysian sarong.

ety: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πάρεσις (páresis, “letting go, paralysis”), from παρίημι (paríēmi, “relax”), from παρα- (para-) + ἵημι (híēmi, “let go”).

s.def: A paralysis which is incomplete or which occurs in isolated areas.
Inflammation of the brain as a cause of dementia or paralysis.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French parfait (“perfect”). Doublet of parfit, perfect, perfecto, and perfectus.

s.def: A French parfait (parfait glacé), an iced dessert made with egg yolks, sugar, cream, and flavouring (usually fruit), sometimes with the addition of a liqueur.
ex: Brad hesitated, peering at the grid of spun sugar that jutted from his loganberry parfait.

s.def: An American parfait, a layered dessert often consisting of fruit, ice cream, pastries, whipped topping, etc. and served in a glass, often a parfait glass.
A smooth pâté, usually made from liver and flavoured with liqueurs.

ety: From Middle English pargetten, from Old French pargeter, parjeter (“to throw about”), from par- (intensive prefix) (from Latin per-) + jeter (“to throw”) (from Latin iactō, frequentative of iaciō). The noun is derived from the verb.

s.def: To coat with gypsum; to plaster, for example walls, or the interior of flues.
ex: parget the outside of their houses.
the pargeted ceiling with pendants
Sapper insisted that the chimney was to be pargeted so he sent Jack out into the yard to meet the incoming milking cows.

s.def: To paint; to cover over.
Gypsum.
ex: Blind parget cherubs watched from the high corners.

s.def: Plaster, as for lining the interior of flues, or for stuccowork.
ex: The surface of the parget might be finished either smooth, with a coat of whitewash, or as rough-cast with sand or small stones.

s.def: Paint, especially for the face.

ety: From Latin parelion, from Ancient Greek παρήλιον (parḗlion), from παρά (pará) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).

s.def: Synonym of sun dog (“a bright spot in the sky, usually one of two on the parhelic circle on both sides of the sun (or occasionally above and below it), caused by the refraction of the sun's image through ice crystals”).
An image or reflection.
ex: The short (166 lines) Canto One, with all those amusing birds and parhelia, occupies thirteen cards.

ety: From Tamil பறையர் (paṟaiyar), from பறையன் (paṟaiyaṉ, “drummer”), from பறை (paṟai, “drum”) or from Malayalam പറയർ (paṟayaṟ), from പറയൻ (paṟayaṉ, “drummer”), from പറ (paṟa, “drum”). Parai in Tamil or Para in Malayalam refers to a type of large drum designed to announce the king’s notices to the public. The people who made a living using the parai were called paraiyar; in the caste-based society, they were in the lower strata, hence the derisive paraiah and pariah. Alternatively, derived from Sans…

s.def: Synonym of outcast: A person despised and excluded by their family, community, or society, especially a member of the untouchable castes in Indian society.
ex: I’m a pariah, outlawed from Time Lord society.

s.def: A similarly despised group of people or species of animal.
Ellipsis of pariah dog (“an Indian breed, any stray dog in Indian contexts”).
Alternative form of Parian.

ety: Borrowed from Latin pariēs (“wall of a house or room”). Compare French paroi (“wall”), Italian parete (“wall”), Portuguese parede (“wall”) Spanish pared (“wall”) and Romanian perete (“wall”).

s.def: The wall of any cavity or organ.
The triangular middle part of each segment of the shell of a barnacle.

ety: From Latin parietālis, from pariēs (“wall”).

s.def: Of or relating to the wall of a body part, organ or cavity.
ex: Hydrochloric acid is secreted by the parietal cells of the gastric glands, located on the wall of the fundus of the stomach.

s.def: Of or relating to the parietal bones.
Of or relating to college living and, especially, its regulation.
ex: At Harvard College, the officers resident within the college walls constitute a permanent standing committee, called the Parietal Committee.

s.def: Attached to the main wall of the ovary, and not to the axis; said of a placenta.
Either of the two parietal bones, on the top and side of the skull.
Any of the scales of a snake that are located on the head and connected to the frontals towards the posterior.
A flat Roman wall tile with roughened surface, used as a base for plasterwork.
Dormitory rules governing visits from members of the opposite sex.
present participle and gerund of pare
A fragment or shaving that has been pared.
The cutting off of the surface of grassland for tillage.
A thin-bladed knife intended for coring and paring (peeling) fruit such as apples as well as slicing small ingredients, especially used for precise and controlled cutting.
plural of pari.

ety: From Middle English Parys, Paris, from Old French Paris, from the Late Latin name of an earlier settlement, Lutetia Parisiorum (“Lutetia of the Parisii”), from Latin Parīsiī, a Gaulish tribe, from Transalpine Gaulish *parios (“cauldron”), from Proto-Celtic *kʷaryos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer-. Doublet of Parizh.

s.def: capital of France
A Trojan prince who eloped with Helen.
The capital and largest city of France.
A department of Île-de-France, France.
The government of France.
A locale named after the French city.
A community in Ontario; named for nearby gypsum deposits, used to make plaster of Paris (itself named for the city).
An English habitational surname from Old French for someone from Paris.
A male given name from place name.
A female given name transferred from the place name, of modern usage, usually from the French city.

ety: From Middle English parisshe, from Old French paroisse (compare the obsolete variant paroch, from Anglo-Norman paroche, parosse), from Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”).

s.def: An administrative part of a diocese that has its own church.
ex: Near-synonym: vicarate

s.def: The community attending that church; the members of the parish.

An ecclesiastical society, usually not bounded by territorial limits, but composed of those persons who choose to unite under the charge of a particular priest, clergyman, or minister; also, loosely, the territory in which the members of a congregation live.
In any of various countries, an administrative subdivision of an area, often of a county.
To place (an area, or rarely a person) into one or more parishes.
To visit residents of a parish.
ex: "Are you going ‘parishing’ this morning?" inquired Diana, as she watched him fill and light his pipe.

s.def: Pronunciation spelling of perish, representing Mary–marry–merry merger English.

der: a dumb priest never got a parish

ety: From Middle English Parisien, perisien, from Middle French parisien, from Medieval Latin parisiānus. By surface analysis, Paris + -ian.

s.def: A native, citizen and/or inhabitant of Paris, France
ex: Not all of France was inundated by the nationalist wave – it was predominantly young, intelligent Parisians who embraced the new bellicism […].

s.def: Of, relating, or pertaining to Paris, France.
ex: He lived in Paris for ten years, and became more Parisian than the natives.

ety: From Middle French parité, from Late Latin paritās, from Latin pār (“equal”). Equivalent to pari- + -ty.

s.def: Equality; comparability of strength or intensity.
ex: Altogether, Microsoft claims a 99% feature parity between 32-bit and 64-bit editions.

s.def: Senses related to classification into two sets.
ex: Parity is always preserved in such operations.

s.def: In reversi, the last move within a given sector of the board.
Resemblance; analogy.
The number of delivered pregnancies reaching viable gestational age, usually between 20-28 weeks.
The number of times a sow has farrowed.

ety: From Middle English park, from Old French parc (“livestock pen”), from Medieval Latin parcus, parricus, from Frankish *parrik (“enclosure, pen, fence”). Cognate with Dutch perk (“enclosure; flowerbed”), Old High German pfarrih, pferrih (“enclosure, pen”), Old English pearroc (“enclosure”) (whence modern English paddock), Old Norse parrak, parak (“enclosure, pen; distress, anxiety”), Icelandic parraka (“to keep pent in under restraint and coercion”). More at parrock, paddock.

s.def: ground for recreation
To bring (something such as a vehicle) to a halt or store in a specified place.
ex: You can park the car in front of the house.
I parked the drive heads of my hard disk before travelling with my laptop.
Parking is by app, which (when it works) is good. But £7.70 to park is extortionate, so GTR needs to look at reducing that.

s.def: An area of land set aside for environment preservation or recreation.
ex: She went to the park for a jog with him.
17th century, Edmund Waller, At Penshurst While in the park I sing, the listening deer / Attend my passion, and forget to fear.

s.def: A wide, flat-bottomed valley in a mountainous region.
An area used for specific purposes.
ex: a wagon park; an artillery park

s.def: An inventory of matériel.
ex: A country's tank park or artillery park.

s.def: A space in which to leave a car; a parking space.
ex: We finally found a park and walked a few blocks to the building.

s.def: The gear into which one shifts an automatic transmission when one is parking a car or truck. (Denoted with symbol P on a shifter's labeling.)
To defer (a matter) until a later date.
ex: Let's park that until next week's meeting.
The Harry Potter spin-off prequel series Fantastic Beasts has been “parked” by Warner Bros, according to its director David Yates.

s.def: To bring together in a park, or compact body.
ex: to park artillery, wagons, automobiles, etc.

ety: 1780, ultimately from Tundra Nenets парка (parka), via Aleut parka and Russian па́рка (párka). Perhaps from Proto-Uralic; see dialectal Finnish parka (“rag, swaddling clothes”), which may be a cognate from Proto-Uralic, or an early borrowing from another Uralic language.

s.def: A long jacket with a hood which protects the wearer against rain and wind.
ex: Basir tended to wear a beige suede parka over his shalwar kameez.

s.def: A designated area, usually outdoors and divided into marked spaces, intended for the temporary parking of motor vehicles.
ex: Meronyms: parking space, parking spot, parking place
Should we park in that parking lot, or in the garage up the street?
They paved paradise and put up a parking lot.

s.def: A road blocked by stop-start traffic.
ex: The 101 was a parking lot again today.

s.def: A holding area in which to set aside some question or concern for likely future consideration.
ex: Let's put this question in the parking lot for now, and we'll follow up on it later this week.

s.def: A place in a state of complete destruction, especially one achieved through military means.
ex: I was one of the people understanding the need to turn Afghanistan into a parking lot on the way to finding Bin Laden and bringing him to justice.

ety: Named after English physician James Parkinson (1755-1824).

s.def: A chronic neurological disorder affecting movement, characterized by tremors, slowness of movement (bradykinesia), cogwheel or lead-pipe rigidity, and postural instability.

ety: Borrowed from French parkour, altered spelling of parcours (“course, route”).

s.def: An athletic discipline, in which practitioners traverse any environment in the most efficient way possible using their physical abilities, and which commonly involves running, jumping, vaulting, rolling, flipping, and other similar physical movements.
ex: On Astypalea, the possibilities for parkour routines are endless, as illustrated by the variety of tricks each athlete unveiled at Art of Motion.

ety: From park + way.

s.def: A path, carriage-way, or road through a park or a landscaped right of way.
ex: A parkway is a combined park and road. Strictly speaking, it is a road through a park and is indistinguishable from the park areas which it traverses.
Natchez Trace is a parkway. It is not a freeway nor a throughway nor a speedway

s.def: A scenic freeway.
A divided highway with a landscaped median.
ex: As they cruised, she remembered the old saw: Why do we drive on a parkway and park in a driveway?

s.def: A tree lawn.
A railway station built on the edge of a town, typically with a large car park to function as a park and ride interchange.

ety: From Middle English *parlaunce, from Anglo-Norman parlance, parlaunce, from parler (“to talk”) + -ance.

s.def: A certain way of speaking, of using words; especially that associated with a particular job or interest.
ex: To my childish fancy, it had seemed an imaginary flag-staff, or, in rustic parlance, the "liberty pole" of some former generation […]
We approach the contest, still known in the common parlance of the country, as "the first Pennimite War."

s.def: Of a word, the quality of being lexicalized; especially as jargon or slang.
Speech, discussion or debate.
ex: And without further parlance they fought, […]

ety: The verb is derived from paroli (“cumulative bet in card games”), possibly modified under the influence of French parler (“to speak, talk”). Paroli is derived from French paroli (“double stake”), from Italian paroli, plural of parolo (first-person singular present indicative of parare (“to protect or shield (from); to prepare”), from Latin parāre, present active infinitive of parō (“to arrange, prepare; to furnish, provide”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through; to carry forth, fare”…

s.def: To carry forward the stake and winnings from a bet on to a subsequent wager or series of wagers.
To increase (an asset, money, etc.) by gambling or investing in a daring manner.
ex: Shall we parlay the value of our products?

s.def: To convert (a situation, thing, etc.) into something better.
Alternative spelling of parley (“to have a discussion, especially one between enemies”).
ex: Jack "parlayed" with them until he had completed his task, and then he closed the gate in their faces.

s.def: A bet or series of bets where the stake and winnings are cumulatively carried forward; an accumulator.

ety: From Middle English parlai (“speech, parley”), from Old French parler (“to talk; to speak”), from Late Latin parabolō, from Latin parabola (“comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παρά (pará, “beside”) with βολή (bolḗ, “throwing”). Doublet of palaver.

s.def: A conference, especially one between enemies.
ex: We yield on parley, but are stormed in vain.
Without further parley Garland rode off up the hog's-back and the sheriff rode off down it [...]

s.def: To have a discussion, especially one between enemies.
ex: Jack "parlayed" with them until he had completed his task, and then he closed the gate in their faces.

s.def: In many countries, the legislative branch of government, a deliberative assembly or set of assemblies whose elected or appointed members meet to debate the major political issues of the day, make, amend, and repeal laws, authorize the executive branch of government to collect and spend money, and i…
ex: The row started over who will run for parliament in a wealthy rightwing constituency on the left bank in Paris, a safe seat for Sarkozy's ruling UMP.

s.def: A formal council summoned (especially by a monarch) to discuss important issues.
ex: By the 13th Century, a parliament was when kings met up with English barons to raise cash for fighting wars - mostly against Scotland.

s.def: A particular assembly of the members of such a legislature, as convened for a specific purpose or period of time (commonly designated with an ordinal number – for example, first parliament or 12th parliament – or a descriptive adjective – for example, Long Parliament, Short Parliament and Rump Parl…
ex: Following the general election, Jane Doe took her oath of office as a member of the nation's fifth parliament.

s.def: A gathering of birds, especially rooks or owls.
ex: A group of owls is called a parliament.

s.def: Parliament cake, a type of gingerbread.
a length of time for which a parliament is summoned, in modern times therefore the period between two consecutive elections.
ex: This parliament has been more scandal-filled than any other in history.

ety: Inherited from Middle English parlour, from Old French parleor, parloir, parleoir, from the verb parler (“to speak”); compare Medieval Latin parlātōrium. Doublet of parloir. Displaced native Old English sprǣchūs.

s.def: The living room of a house, or a room for entertaining guests; a room for talking; a sitting-room or drawing room.
The apartment in a monastery or nunnery where the residents are permitted to meet and converse with each other or with visitors from the outside.
A comfortable room in a public house.
A covered open-air patio.
A shop or other business selling goods or services specified by context.
ex: tattoo parlor pizza parlor ice cream parlor

s.def: A shed used for milking cattle; a milking parlor.

ety: From Middle English parles, parlous, perlous, [and other forms], a contraction of perilous (“dangerous; dreadful, terrible; morally corrupt, sinful, wicked; inauspicious, unlucky”) (and thus a doublet of perilous), from Old French perilleus, perillos, perillous, perilluse, perilleuse, perilleux (“very dangerous, perilous”) (modern French périlleux), from Latin perīculōsus (“dangerous, hazardous, perilous”), from perīculum (“danger, hazard, peril, risk”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per…

s.def: Attended with peril; dangerous, risky.
ex: The situation became parlous when the weather made resupply impossible.
The safest way in such a parlous doubt, / Is steady watch and keep a sharp look out.

s.def: Appalling, dire, terrible.
ex: in a parlous state
Isa. Y'are a parlous Fool. Ant. No danger in me: I bring nought but Love
During these suppers McCluskey's conversation centred almost exclusively around the parlous moral, cultural and environmental state of the planet.

s.def: Dangerously clever or cunning; also, remarkably good or unusual.
Extremely, very.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French parmesan, from an earlier Vulgar Latin *parmēsānus, restructuring of Latin parmēnsis (from Latin Parma). Compare Italian parmigiano, Catalan parmesà, Portuguese parmesão, Sicilian parmisanu, Spanish parmesano

s.def: A hard, full-fat Italian cheese from Parma or its neighboring province Reggio Emilia.
A similar cheese produced elsewhere.
ex: Most of the parmesan in our grocery store comes from Wisconsin.

s.def: Money.
ex: Finesse a nigga with some counterfeits, but now I'm countin' this / Parmesan where my accountant lives, in fact I'm downin' this

ety: From Anglo-Norman parochial and its source Late Latin parochialis, an alteration of paroecialis (“of a church province”), from paroecia, from Hellenistic Greek παροικία (paroikía, “stay in a foreign land”), later “community, diocese”, from Ancient Greek πάροικος (pároikos, “neighbouring, neighbour”), from παρα- (para-) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

s.def: Pertaining to a parish.
ex: The parish council handles parochial affairs. [civil context]
The rector and vestry handle parochial affairs. [church context]

s.def: Characterized by an unsophisticated focus on local concerns to the exclusion of wider contexts; elementary in scope or outlook.
ex: The use of simple, primary colors in the painting gave it a parochial feel.
Some people in the United States have been accused of taking a parochial view, of not being interested in international matters.
Its atmosphere might have been provincial, but it was never merely parochial.

s.def: A parochial individual.
ex: Australia is divided between cosmopolitans and parochials.

ety: From Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía, “parody”), from παρά (pará, “besides”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

s.def: A work or performance that imitates another work or performance with ridicule or irony.
ex: The lively parody which he wrote […] was received with great applause.

s.def: A popular maxim, adage, or proverb.
To make a parody of something.
ex: The comedy movie parodied the entire Western genre.

ety: from Middle French parole, from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parable.

s.def: Word of mouth.
Verbal, oral, informal.
ex: Parol, or extrinsic evidence should only be used where it may clarify ambiguous terms of a contract.

s.def: A word; an oral utterance.
Oral declaration; word of mouth.
A writing not under seal.
ex: Leases , like other conveyances , were good at common law If by deed , by parol

s.def: An ornamental star-like Christmas lantern from the Philippines.
