s.def: Conditional release of a prisoner (now especially before the end of a custodial sentence), or the term or state of such release; the system governing such releases.
ex: A Minnesota woman who killed her 6-year-old son will now spend the rest of her life in prison without the possibility of parole.

s.def: Originally, one's oath or word of honour, given as a condition of release from custody; now specifically, describing the release of a former prisoner under certain conditions, especially the promise of good behaviour.
ex: He will be on parole for nearly two more years.
He was released on parole.

s.def: A word of honor, especially given by a prisoner of war, to not engage in combat if released.
ex: This man had forfeited his military parole.
In hospital he gave his parole, and was enlarged after paying for the torn blanket.

s.def: A watchword or code phrase; (military) a password given only to officers, distinguished from the countersign, which is given to all guards.
ex: ‘Classical quotation is the parole of literary men all over the world.’
[…] their parole or watchword, which is orange, distinguishes them from the rebels in any action, to prevent disagreeable mistakes.

s.def: Language in use, as opposed to language as a system.
The permission for a foreigner who does not meet the technical requirements for a visa to be allowed to enter the U.S. on humanitarian grounds.
Alternative form of parol.
To release (a prisoner) on the understanding that s/he checks in regularly and obeys the law.
To be released on parole.
ex: I am a gay guy that likes S&M, and am looking for a master out on the streets to write me in here. I would like to parole to NYC some day if I can.

ety: From Latin paronomasia, from Ancient Greek παρονομασία (paronomasía, “play upon words which sound alike”), from παρα- (para-) + ὀνομασία (onomasía, “naming”).

s.def: A pun or play on words.
ex: Ev’rywhere but at Norfolk, where talk of Passion far outweighs its Enactment,– indeed, the Sailors’ paronomasia for that wretched Place, is ‘No-Fuck’.

s.def: The use of puns.
ex: Paronomasia to the sense alludes, When words but little varied it includes.

ety: Coined around 1846 from Ancient Greek παρώνυμος (parṓnumos, “derivative”), equivalent to para- + -onym.

s.def: A word derived from the same root or stem as another word; classes include cognates and naturalizations of foreign words.
A near-homophone, a word that sounds like another word (some example pairs are cognate).

ety: By surface analysis, para- + ot- + -id, literally “near the ear”.

s.def: Relating to the parotid gland.
The parotid gland.

ety: From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”), from Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, and Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”) (modern French paroxysme), and from their etymon Late Latin paroxismus, paroxysmus (“a fit; onset of a disease; violent impulse or sadness”), from Ancient Greek πᾰροξῠσμός (păroxŭsmós, “exasperation, irritation; severe fit of a disease”), from πᾰροξῡ́νω (p…

s.def: A period (especially one of several recurring periods) during the course of an illness when symptoms worsen; a sudden attack of a disease symptom, such as a bout of coughing or a seizure.
Chiefly followed by of: a sudden outburst of violent activity or feeling; also, the most severe part of an activity or incident; the climax.
ex: If prevented by force, the screams she sometimes uttered in her paroxysms of rage were fearful, and must inevitably be heard.
Unable to turn his back on the fanged danger and go on, the bull would be driven into paroxysms of rage.
The Russian soldier left a trail of blood and devastated lives in a last paroxysm of violence only hours before Russian troops began withdrawing.

s.def: An outburst of a violent argument or disagreement.
ex: [A]n election was at hand, which, it was expected, would throw the whole country into a paroxysm.
The passions which inflame us, the sophisms which delude us, will not last for ever. The paroxysms of faction have their appointed season.

s.def: A violent occurrence of a natural phenomenon, such as an earthquake, thunderstorm, or volcanic eruption; specifically (volcanology), the most explosive event during a series of volcanic eruptions.
Disastrous or sudden change.

ety: Etymology tree Early Medieval Latin par(ri)cus Old French parc Middle French parc French parc Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Italic *-tosder.? Late Latin -ittus Old French -et Middle French -et French -et French parquetbor. English parquet Borrowed from French parquet.

s.def: A wooden floor made of wooden tiles or veneers arranged in a decorative geometrical pattern.
In some European countries, the branch of the administrative government that handles prosecutions; a procuratorate.
The part of a theatre between the orchestra and the parquet circle.

In some European bourses or stock exchanges, the railed-in space within which the agents de change, or privileged brokers, conduct business; also, the business conducted by them, distinguished from the coulisse, or outside market.
To lay or fit such a floor.

ety: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīda, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

s.def: Someone who kills a relative, especially a parent.
ex: I told him the reuenging Gods, / ’Gainst Paricides did all the thunder bend […]

s.def: Someone who commits treason.
The killing of a relative, especially a parent.
The killing of a ruler, or other authority figure; treason.

ety: First attested in 1525. From Middle French perrot, either a diminutive of Pierre or a shortened form of perroquet (whence also parakeet). Compare French pierrot and Occitan parrat. A number of origins have been suggested for perroquet, such as Spanish periquito and Italian parrocchetto. The relationship between these various words is disputed. Replaced earlier popinjay.

s.def: A kind of bird, many species of which are colorful and able to mimic human speech, of the order Psittaciformes or (narrowly) of the family Psittacidae.
ex: I bought a wonderful parrot at the pet store.

s.def: A parroter; a person who repeats the words or ideas of others.
ex: What kind of a parrot are you? He just said that.

s.def: A puffin.
channel coal.
A transponder.
To repeat (exactly what has just been said) without necessarily showing understanding, in the manner of a parrot.
ex: The interviewee merely parroted the views of her tabloid.

s.def: An infectious disease caused by the bacterium Chlamydophila psittaci and contracted from many species of bird.

ety: From earlier parree, from Middle English *parree, *paree, from Old French paree (“preparation, ceremony, parade”), from Medieval Latin parāta (“preparation, parade”), from parāre (“to ward off, guard, defend, prepare, get ready”). More at pare. The English verb is taken from the noun. Doublet of parade. Alternative etymology derives the verb parry from French parez, the imperative form of parer (“to fend off”), ultimately from the Medieval Latin parāre. See above.

s.def: To avoid, deflect, or ward off (an attack, a blow, an argument, etc.).
A defensive or deflective action; an act of parrying.
A simple defensive action designed to deflect an attack, performed with the forte of the blade.

A defensive move intended to change the direction of an incoming strike to make it miss its intended target, rather than block and absorb it; and typically performed with an open hand in a downward or sideways slapping motion.

ety: Borrowed from Classical Persian پَارْس (pārs), from Middle Persian 𐭯𐭠𐭫𐭮𐭩 (Pārs), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠pārsa⁠/).

s.def: A province and historical region in southwestern Iran, homeland of the Persians; known to the ancient Greeks as Περσίς (Persís) or Περσική (Persikḗ), to the Romans as Persis or Persia, and to the Arabs as فَارِس (fāris).
ex: PARS, Fars or Farsistan, is a province of the kingdom of Persia which gives its name to the country.
Yet the Bundehesh locates it in Pars.
[…] of Pars or Persia.

ety: Possibly from Middle English pars (“parts, shares; parts of speech, grammar”), from Old French pars (plural of part (“part, portion, share”)), from Latin pars (“part, piece, share”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to carry forth; to sell”).

s.def: To resolve (a sentence, etc.) into its elements, pointing out the several parts of speech, and their relation to each other by agreement or government; to analyze and describe grammatically.
To examine closely; to scrutinize.
To split (a file or other input) into pieces of data that can be easily manipulated or stored.
To resolve (a string of code or text) into its elements to determine if it conforms to a particular grammar.
Of a string of code or text, sentence, etc.: to conform to rules of grammar, to be syntactically valid.
ex: This sentence doesn't parse.

s.def: An act of parsing; a parsing.
ex: The parse will fail if the program contains an unrecognised keyword.

s.def: The result of such an act; a parsing.
ex: This parse is incorrect and indicates a fault in the parser.

ety: Contraction of parallax second.

s.def: Syllabic abbreviation of parallax second.

ety: From parse + -er.

s.def: A computer program that parses.
One who parses.

ety: Etymology tree Middle English parcimonie English parsimony Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Old French -usbor. Middle English -ous English -ous English parsimonious From parsimony + -ous.

s.def: Exhibiting parsimony; sparing in the expenditure of money; frugal, possibly to excess.
ex: The first three college-savings plans stand out for their parsimonious expenses […]

s.def: Using a minimal number of assumptions, steps, or conjectures.
ex: Statistical methods offer the ability to enforce parsimonious selection of the most influential potential predictors of each gene's state.

s.def: Not conceding many goals.

ety: From Late Middle English parcimonie, parcimony (“economy, frugality, thrift”), borrowed from Latin parcimōnia, parsimōnia (“frugality, thrift, parsimony; moderation, restraint; stinginess”), from pars- (the past participial stem of parcō (“to economize, save up; etc.”)) + -mōnia (suffix forming abstract nouns). The further etymology of parcō is uncertain; it is possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“away; off”) + *h₂erk- (“to hold; to guard, protect; to lock”).

s.def: With a negative connotation: great reluctance to spend money or other resources; miserliness, stinginess; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: If mere parsimony could have made a man rich, Sir Pitt Crawley might have become very wealthy […]
William and Lavinia were furtively avaricious; they couldn't help being stingy, since parsimony ran in their blood— […]

s.def: With a positive connotation: careful spending of money or other resources; frugality, thrift; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: They accuse the divine providence of a certain parsimony.
No poet is so splendidly superfluous as he; none knows so well that in poetry enough is not only not so good as a feast, but is a beggarly parsimony.

ety: From Middle English persely, from Old French peresil, from Latin petroselīnum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon, “parsley”), from πέτρος (pétros, “rock, stone”) + σέλῑνον (sélīnon, “celery”). Displaced Old English petersiliġe, which goes back to the same root.

s.def: A bright green, biennial herb, Petroselinum crispum, having many cultivars.
ex: Though the parsley seemed to have died, outside it started to regenerate. New crimped leaves came free from the sprigs and spread.

s.def: The leaves of this plant used in Middle Eastern, European, and American cooking.
Any herb resembling parsley, such as cilantro (Chinese parsley) or chervil (French parsley).
To add parsley to.
ex: Put a layer of mashed potato on one side and also on the other after peppering, salting and finely-chopped parsleying it to taste.

ety: From 16th-century parsnepe, from Middle English passenep, a modification of Old French pasnaie by influence of Middle English nepe (“turnip”), from Latin pastināca (“parsnip, carrot”), from pastinum (“two-pronged fork”) as in pastināre (“to dig up the ground”).. The irregular intrusive r may be due to influence from parsley.

s.def: A biennial plant, Pastinaca sativa, related to the carrot.
The root of the parsnip, when used as a vegetable.

ety: Etymology tree English parson Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos Latin -ātus Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icus Latin -āticus Latin -āticum Old French -agebor. Middle English -age English -age English parsonage From parson + -age.

s.def: The third most populated Greek city (after Athens and Thessaloniki), the most populated city in the Peloponnese and the capital of Western Greece (administrative region of Greece).

ety: From Middle English patriark, patriarche, from Late Latin patriarcha; later reinforced by Old French patriarche, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -ᾰ́ρχης (-ắrkhēs, “-arch”), with some senses likely influenced directly by Latin pāter (“father”) or Ancient Greek πᾰτήρ (pătḗr, “father”). Compare matriarch. By surface analysis, patri- + -arch.

s.def: The highest form of bishop, in the ancient world having authority over other bishops in the province but now generally as an honorary title; in Roman Catholicism, considered a bishop second only to the Pope in rank.
A male leader of a family, tribe or ethnic group, especially one of the twelve sons of Jacob (considered to have created the twelve tribes of Israel) or (in plural) Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
A founder of a political or religious movement, an organization or an enterprise.
An old leader of a village or community.
The male progenitor of a genetic or tribal line, or of a clan or extended family.
The male head of a household or nuclear family.
A shade of purple

ety: From Latin patriarchia, from Byzantine Greek πατριαρχία (patriarkhía), from Koine Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “patriarch”), from πατρία (patría) and ἄρχω (árkhō). By surface analysis, patri- + -archy.

s.def: A social system in which the father is head of the household, having authority over women and children, and in which lineage is traced through the male line.
A power structure in which men are dominant.
ex: England is under the rule of a patriarchy.

s.def: The office of a patriarch; a patriarchate.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French patricien, from Latin patricius, derived from patrēs cōnscrīptī (“Roman senators”). May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian

s.def: A member of any of the families constituting the populus Romanus, or body of Roman citizens, before the development of the plebeian order; later, one who, by right of birth or by special privilege conferred, belonged to the senior class of Romans, who, with certain property, had by right a seat in…
A person of high birth; a nobleman.
ex: The emperor elevated several loyal families to the status of patricians.

s.def: One familiar with the works of the Christian Fathers; one versed in patristic lore or life.
Of or pertaining to the Roman patres (“fathers”) or senators, or patricians.
ex: The cognomen was first used in patrician families, who were distinguished from the plebeians by their three names.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a person of high birth; noble; not plebeian; aristocratic.
ex: born in the patrician file of society

s.def: Characteristic of or appropriate to a person of high birth; classy.
Politically active to help people in lower classes, especially in a patronizing or condescending way.
ex: It will speed the shrivelling of the patrician “one nation” Tories, who tried to curb the extremes of Thatcherism and ended by providing its veils.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French patricide or Latin patricīdium. Equivalent to patri- + -cide.

s.def: The murder of one's father.
One who has murdered their father.

ety: From earlier patrimoyne, from patremoyne, from Middle French patrimoine/patremoine, semilearned borrowing from Latin patrimōnium, from pater (“father”) + -mōnium (“state, condition”). First attested in 1513. By surface analysis, patri- + -mony. Compare matrimony. Displaced native Old English fæderġestrēon.

s.def: A right or estate inherited from one's father; or, in a larger sense, from any male ancestor.
Formerly, a church estate or endowment.

ety: From Middle French patriote, from Late Latin patriōta (“fellow countryman”) from the Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “of the same country”), from πατρίς (patrís, “father land", "country”), from πατήρ (patḗr, “father”).

s.def: A person who loves and zealously supports and defends their country.
A fellow countryman, a compatriot.
ex: The aim of patriots, therefore, was to set limits to the power which the ruler should be allowed to exercise over the community.

ety: From French patriotique, from Late Latin patriōticus, from Ancient Greek πατριωτικός (patriōtikós), from πατριώτης (patriṓtēs), equivalent to patriot + -ic.

s.def: Inspired by or showing patriotism; done out of love of one's country; zealously and unselfishly devoted to the service of one's country
ex: a patriotic statesman
a patriotic song

ety: Etymology tree English patriot Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English patriotism From patriot + -ism.

s.def: Love of one's country; devotion to the welfare of one's compatriots; passion which inspires one to serve one's country.
ex: "I have the intense patriotism of an immigrant," says Ferguson

s.def: The actions of a patriot.
The desire to compete sharply with, and perhaps also dominate, other nations; nationalism.
ex: Near-synonyms: chauvinism, superpatriotism

der: patriotism is the last refuge of a scou…

ety: From French patrouille, from Old French patrouille, patouille (“a night-watch”, literally “a tramping about”), from patrouiller, patouiller, patoiller (“to paddle or pudder in water, dabble with the feet, begrime, besmear”), from patte, pate (“paw, foot of an animal”), from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”), from Frankish *patta (“paw, sole of the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *paþjaną, *paþōną (“to walk, tread, go, step, pace”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pent-, *(s)pat- (“path; to wa…

s.def: A going of the rounds along the chain of sentinels and between the posts, by a guard, usually consisting of three or four men, to insure greater security from attacks on the outposts.
ex: Four members of the squadron were on patrol.

s.def: A movement, by a small body of troops beyond the line of outposts, to explore the country and gain intelligence of the enemy's whereabouts.
The guards who go the rounds for observation; a detachment whose duty it is to patrol.
The largest division of officers within a police department or sheriff's office, whose assignment is to patrol and respond to calls for service.
Any perambulation of a particular line or district to guard it; also, the people thus guarding.
ex: a customs patrol
a fire patrol
1787-1788, Alexander Hamilton, The Federalist Papers In France there is an army of patrols […] to secure her fiscal regulations.

s.def: A unit of a troop, usually defined by certain ranks or age groups within the troop, and ideally comprised of six to eight members.
To go the rounds along a chain of sentinels; to traverse a police district or beat.
To go the rounds of, as a sentry, guard, or policeman
ex: to patrol a frontier
to patrol a beat
Watchmen are stationed continuously at each end of the bridge, and the main spans are patrolled twice during the night.

ety: From Middle English patroun, patrone, from Old French patron, from Latin patrōnus, derived from pater (“father”). Doublet of padrone, Patronus, patroon, and pattern.

s.def: An influential, wealthy person who supported an artist, craftsman, a scholar or a noble.
One who protects or supports; a defender or advocate.
ex: patron of my life and liberty
the patron of true holiness
Let him who works the client wrong beware the patron’s ire!

s.def: A customer, as of a certain store or restaurant.
ex: This car park is for patrons only.
In our trial of the AOT, a transect was used to collect data about the languages being spoken by patrons of the NIE cafeteria during lunchtimes.

s.def: A protector of a dependent, especially a master who had freed a slave but still retained some paternal rights.
One who has gift and disposition of a benefice.
A padrone.
A property owner, a landlord, a master. (Compare patroon.)
To be a patron of; to patronize; to favour.
ex: a good cause needs not to be patroned by passion

s.def: To treat as a patron.

ety: From patron + -ize (verb ending); or from Old French patroniser, from Medieval Latin patronizāre (“to lead a galley as patron”). Piecewise doublet of patternize.

s.def: To treat condescendingly; to talk down to.
ex: Near-synonyms: condescend, infantilize, denigrate

s.def: To act as a patron of; to defend, protect, or support.
To be a customer of (an establishment), especially a regular customer.
To blame, to reproach.

ety: From Ancient Greek πατήρ (patḗr, “father”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”) (a variant form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”)). Also patronym + -ic, from patro- + -onym.

s.def: Derived from one's father.
Derived from one's ancestors.
ex: a patronymic denomination
I proposed to her that we give our first-born baby a patronymic name.

s.def: A name acquired from one's father.

A name acquired from the first name of one's father, grandfather or earlier (male) ancestor. Some cultures use a patronymic where other cultures use a surname or family name; other cultures (like Russia) use both a patronymic and a surname.

ety: The term dates back at least to the 1870s in the United States, close to the peak of Irish migration. The OED's recent revisions link Patsy with Pat and Paddy, the stereotype of the bogtrotter just off the boat. The American Heritage Dictionary and Online Etymology Dictionary quotes the OED it may derive from the Italian pazzo (“madman”), and souther Italian dialect paccio (“fool”). Another possibility is the term derives from Patsy Bolivar, a character in an 1880s minstrel skit who was blamed…

s.def: A person who is easily manipulated, victimized, or made to take the blame for something.
A conspirator, secretly designated by co-conspirators to take full blame and punishment for a wrongdoing, particularly an assassination; a fall guy.
To treat (a person) as a patsy or sucker; to pin the blame on.
To mess around; to waste time.
ex: I was in no mood for patsying around, and I let him have it with both barrels.

ety: From Middle English patyn, patin, pateyn, from Old French patin, from patte (“paw, hoof”), from Latin patta, of imitative origin.

s.def: Any of various types of footwear with thick soles, often used to elevate the foot, especially wooden clogs.
One of various wooden attachments used to lift a shoe above wet or muddy ground.
A circular wooden plank attached to a horse's foot to prevent it from sinking into a bog while plowing.
ex: Some trials have been made in Ireland to put pattens on bullocks instead of horses, for ploughing on bog.

s.def: An ice skate.
An iron hoop attached to a person's boot in cases of hip-joint disease.
The base of a pillar.
To go about wearing pattens.
Obsolete form of paten.

ety: 1610s, pat + -er (“frequentative (indicating repeated action)”), of (onomatopoeia) origin.

s.def: A soft repeated sound, as of rain falling, or feet walking on a hard surface.
ex: I could hear the patter of mice running about in the dark.

s.def: To make irregularly repeated sounds of low-to-moderate magnitude and lower-than-average pitch.
ex: The bullets pattered into the log-cabin walls.
The stealing shower […] 'Tis scarce to patter heard.

s.def: To spatter; to sprinkle.
ex: 1819 (published in 1835) Joseph Rodman Drake, The Culprit Fay Patter the water about the boat.

s.def: Glib and rapid speech, such as from an auctioneer, a stage magician, a sports commentator, or a salesperson with a slick style of selling.
ex: sales patter
This particularly rapid, unintelligible patter isn't generally heard, and if it is it doesn't matter.
Dad, I want to be a jock. All a jock needs is some hep patter and a real gone image. Now, they just don't teach that jazz in college.

s.def: To speak glibly and rapidly, as does an auctioneer or a sports commentator.
To repeat the Lord's Prayer.
To pray.
To repeat hurriedly; to mutter.
One who pats.
ex: I used to hate head patters, and I have realized that all children dislike being patted on the head.

ety: From earlier patten, paterne, from Middle English patron (“patron; example”), from Old French patron, from Medieval Latin patrōnus (“patron”). Doublet of padrone, patron, Patronus, and patroon.

s.def: Model, example.
ex: The wallpaper had a floral pattern.
There is no reason why all colleges and universities should be cut to the same pattern.

s.def: Coherent or decorative arrangement.
ex: follow a pattern
There’s a clear pattern of behavior emerging.
pattern of growth

s.def: intelligible arrangement which has a mathematical, geometric, statistical etc. relationship
A wont or habit to cause an annoyance or bother; to stir up trouble
ex: This guy always chut pattern like badminton.

s.def: The devotions that take place within a parish on the feast day of the patron saint of that parish.
To apply a pattern.
To make or design (anything) by, from, or after, something that serves as a pattern; to copy; to model; to imitate.
ex: [A temple] patterned […] from that which Adam reared in Paradise.

s.def: To arrange, to organise, to fix.
ex: MALACHI: Are you two fucking mad? Listen, you need to pattern up, you know?

s.def: To follow an example.
ex: Under his system, patterned after the French, the army corps became a more mobile, flexible command.

s.def: To fit into a pattern.
A structured method of describing good design practices within a field of expertise.

ety: From earlier meaning "small pie" from pattipan (“something baked in a small pan”), from French pâté (“liver paste, pâté”), from pâte (“pastry, dough, paste, batter”) + -é. Doublet of pastie /pasty (“meat pie”), pate (“cheese portion”), and pâté (“finely-ground paste”) and related to pasta and paste.

s.def: A pastry with various fillings and spices baked inside a flaky shell, often tinted golden yellow with an egg yolk mixture or turmeric.
A foolish or stupid person.
A flattened portion of ground meat or a vegetarian equivalent, usually round but sometimes square in shape.
ex: The cook fried the hamburger patty, then put it in a bun.

s.def: Alternative form of patté.
ex: a cross patty

ety: From Latin patulus.

s.def: Open; spread; exposed
ex: The foramen ovale was patulous — the opening about four lines in diameter.

ety: From Middle English paucete, paucite, paucyte, partly from Middle French paucité and partly from its etymon, Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”). Related to few.

s.def: Fewness in number; too few.
ex: But when I had crossed the threshold, I was astonished at the paucity of facts to be gleaned from the inmates themselves.
This paucity of trains helps to explain why electrification is not planned between Paris and Belfort.
Your tax refund might be late, owing to a paucity of number crunchers.

s.def: A smallness in size or amount that is insufficient; meagerness, dearth.
ex: Now came shipwrecks and life in open boats, with the usual paucity of food.
Here is where the paucity of our language is made manifest.
Genteel America was handicapped by meagerness of soul, thinness of temper, paucity of talent.

ety: Learned borrowing from New Latin paulownia, from German Pawlowna, transliterating Russian Па́вловна (Pávlovna), the patronymic of Anna Pavlovna.

s.def: Any member of the genus Paulownia, comprising deciduous flowering trees native to Asia.
ex: “This is a nice dry piece of paulownia wood,” she said, “for drawing my eyebrows.”

ety: From Middle English paunche, from Old Northern French panche, Old French pance (French panse), from Latin pantex.

s.def: The first compartment of the stomach of a ruminant, the rumen.
The contents of this stomach in a slaughtered animal, viewed as food or a byproduct.
The belly of a human, especially a large, fat protruding one.
ex: See also: pooch
Since retiring from athletics, he has developed a paunch.
“And another sort of weak, flailing blow to the paunch. Neither of these two are in any condition to be fighting.”

s.def: A paunch mat.
The thickened rim of a bell, struck by the clapper.
To remove the internal organs of a ruminant, prior to eating.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin pauper (“poor”). Originally a legal term. Doublet of poor.

s.def: One who is extremely poor.
ex: He has hundreds of thousands of dollars in the bank, and he lives like a pauper!

s.def: One living on or eligible for public charity.
To make a pauper of; to drive into poverty.
ex: “There’s no sense in you paupering yourself because you’re too stubborn to take my money.” ¶ “I’m not paupering myself.”

ety: From Middle French pause, from Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis), from Ancient Greek παύω (paúō, “stop”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of pausa.

s.def: To take a temporary rest, take a break for a short period after an effort.
To interrupt an activity and wait.
ex: When telling the scary story, he paused for effect.
Tarry, pause a day or two.
pausing a while thus to herself she mused

s.def: To halt the play or playback of, temporarily, so that it can be resumed from the same point.
ex: to pause a song, a video, or a computer game
Press Start at any time to pause the game.

s.def: A temporary stop or rest; an intermission of action; interruption; suspension; cessation.
To stop (an activity) for a while.
To hesitate; to hold back; to delay.
To consider; to reflect.
ex: Take time to pause.

s.def: A short time for relaxing and doing something else.
Hesitation; suspense; doubt.
ex: to take pause
to give pause

s.def: In writing and printing, a mark indicating the place and nature of an arrest of voice in reading; a punctuation mark.
ex: Teach the pupil to mind the pauses.

ety: From French pavane, from dialectal Italian pavana, contraction of the older padovana, feminine of padovano, meaning from the city of Padua (Italian Padova, dialectal form Pava).

s.def: A musical style characteristic of the 16th and 17th centuries.
ex: And he tasted in the language of memory ambered wines, dying fallings of sweet airs, the proud pavan […]

s.def: A moderately slow, courtly processional dance in duple time/meter.
ex: Why then be merry; be merry, or I’le be Out of humour, and then who shall dance the Pavan With Ossorio?
From the wings I heard and watched the pavane of tragedy move steadily toward its climax.

s.def: To dance the pavane.

ety: From Old French paver (“to pave, to cover”), from Vulgar Latin *pavāre (“to beat down, to smash”), from Latin pavīre (“to beat, strike, ram, tread down”).

s.def: To cover something with paving slabs.
To cover with stone, concrete, blacktop or other solid covering, especially to aid travel.
ex: They paved Paradise and put up a parking lot.

s.def: To pave the way for; to make easy and smooth.

ety: From the idea that once a paved path has been laid, travel on the route is easier and smoother for others.

s.def: To make future progress or development easier.
ex: Germany's development of rocket weapons paved the way for human controlled spaceflight.
Prince Louis Napoleon was president of France, and his dictatorial behaviour was paving the way for his assumption of the imperial crown.

ety: From Middle English pament, from Anglo-Norman pavement and reinforced by Middle French pavement; both from Latin pavīmentum (“paved surface or floor”), from pavīre (“to beat, to ram, to tread down”). Morphologically pave + -ment.

s.def: A paving (paved part) of a road or other thoroughfare; the roadway or road surface.
ex: The antirunway munitions are specifically designed to cause maximum destruction to airfield pavements.
89.2 million tons of RAP are used annually in new asphalt pavement construction in the United States.

s.def: A paved surface; a hard covering on the ground.
ex: The riches of heaven's pavement, trodden gold.

s.def: A paved path, for the use of pedestrians, located at the side of a road.
The paved part of an area other than a road or sidewalk, such as a cobblestone plaza, asphalt schoolyard or playground, or parking lot.
Interior flooring, especially when of stone, of large buildings.

ety: From Middle English pavilloun, from Anglo-Norman pavilloun, from Latin pāpiliōnem, form of pāpiliō (“butterfly, moth”) (due to resemblance of tent to a butterfly’s wings), of unknown origin. Doublet of papilio and papillon. Cognate to French pavillon (“pavilion”) and papillon (“butterfly”), and similar terms in other Romance languages.

s.def: An ornate tent.
A structure, sometimes temporary, erected to house exhibits at a fair, etc.
A light roofed structure used as a shelter in a public place.
The building where the players change clothes, wait to bat, and eat their meals.
ex: Only one player has hit a six over the Lord's pavillion.

s.def: A detached or semi-detached building at a hospital or other building complex.
The lower surface of a brilliant-cut gemstone, lying between the girdle and collet.
The cartiliginous part of the outer ear; auricle.
The fimbriated extremity of the Fallopian tube.
A flag, ensign, or banner.
An ornate tent, used either as a charge or bearing, or surrounding a shield as or atop the mantling.
present participle and gerund of pave
The hard durable surface placed directly atop the ground, as on a street or sidewalk.
Interior pavement, as in a cathedral.
Pertaining to the material used for pavement, or to the surface itself.
One of many flat stones used to pave an outdoor area.

ety: From oblique stem of Latin pāvō, pāvōnis (“peacock, peafowl”) + -ine, ultimately from Latin pāvōnīnus, from pāvō + -īnus.

s.def: Of or pertaining to the genus Pavo or its family Pavonidae, including the peafowl.
Possessing the coloring or iridescence of a peacock feather.
Showy, like a peacock's tail; exhibiting vanity.
Tarnish found on some ores and metals which resembles the tail feathers of a peacock.
Any bird from the family Pavonidae.

ety: From Middle English pawe, from Old French poue, poe, from Vulgar Latin *pauta. Further origin unknown, perhaps from Frankish *pōta, from Frankish *pōtōn (“to put, stick, plant”), from Proto-Germanic *putōną, whence also Old English potian (“to push”), pȳtan (“to put out, poke out”). See more at put. Doublet of pote, put, and putt. Cognate with Dutch poot, poten (“to plant”), Low German Pote, German Pfote, Icelandic pota (“to stick”).

s.def: The soft foot of a mammal or other animal, generally a quadruped, that has claws or nails; comparable to a human hand or foot.
A hand.
ex: Get your grubby paws off my things!
Abel smiled broadly and proffered his hamlike paw to the chief […]

s.def: Of an animal, to touch (something) with a paw.
ex: He paweth in the valley, and rejoiceth in his strength: he goeth on to meet the armed men.

s.def: To touch (someone) in a sexual way.
To clumsily dig (through something).
To flatter.
Alternative form of pa (“father”).

ety: 17th c., perhaps from Low German or Dutch pal (“catch (mechanism)”), or from either French pal (“stake”) or épaule (“shoulder”).

s.def: A pivoted catch designed to fall into a notch on a ratchet wheel so as to allow movement in only one direction (e.g. on a windlass or in a clock mechanism), or alternatively to move the wheel in one direction.
A similar device to prevent motion in other mechanisms besides ratchets.
To stop with a pawl.
Alternative form of paul (“kind of tent”).

ety: From Middle English paun, pawyn, pawnd, from Old French pan, pant (“pledge for a payment”), from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *pand (“deposit, security, pledge”), further origin uncertain. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Pound (“deposit, pledge, pawn”), West Frisian pân (“pawn”), Dutch pand (“pledge, pawn”), German Low German Pand (“deposit, pledge, pawn”), German Pfand (“deposit, pledge, pawn”), Swedish pant (“pledge, pawn”), Faroese pantur (“security, lien”), Icelandic pantur (“pledge…

s.def: A person being manipulated by another, being used to some end.
ex: Near-synonym: chess piece
Though a pawn of the gods, her departure is the precipitating cause of the Trojan War.

s.def: chess piece
An instance of pawning something.
ex: Redeem from broking pawn the blemish'd crown.

s.def: An item given as security on a loan, or as a pledge.
ex: Brokers, takers of pawns, biting userers, I will not admit; yet […] I will tolerate some kind of usery.
As for mortgaging or pawning,[…]men will not take pawns without use [i.e. interest].

s.def: The state of being held as security for a loan, or as a pledge.
ex: All our jewellery was in pawn by this stage.

s.def: A pawnshop; pawnbroker.
To pledge; to stake or wager.
To give as security on a loan of money; especially, to deposit (something) at a pawn shop.
ex: But you'd better take your diamond ring, you'd better pawn it, babe.

s.def: The most numerous chess piece, or a similar piece in a similar game. In chess, each side starts with eight; moves are only forward, and attacks are only diagonally or en passant.
Alternative form of paan.
ex: A tray filled with pawns, prepared with the usual ingredients, as lime cuttie (a bitter gum), betel-nut, tobacco, spices, &c.

ety: From pawn + shop.

s.def: The business premises of a pawnbroker; where loans are made, with personal property as security

ety: From Middle English payen, from Old French paiier (“pay”), from Medieval Latin pācāre (“to settle, satisfy”) from Latin pācāre (“to pacify”). In this sense, displaced native Old English ġield (“pay”) and ġieldan (“to pay”), whence Modern English yield.

s.def: To give money or other compensation to in exchange for goods or services.
ex: pay cash or pay in cash, pay by credit/debit card
pay in dollars/euros, etc.
How much will the job pay?

s.def: To deposit into an account.
ex: I pay a portion of each paycheck into a savings account.

s.def: To discharge, as a debt or other obligation, by giving or doing what is due or required.
ex: to pay compensation, to pay a fine
She offered to pay the bill.
He is paying his debt to society.

s.def: To be profitable; to be worth it.
ex: It didn't pay him to keep the store open any more.
Crime doesn’t pay.
It will pay to wait.

s.def: To cover, as a cost.
ex: Those investments paid for her college education.

s.def: To yield as a benefit.
ex: to pay dividends; to pay interest
You will get paid from this investment yearly.

s.def: To give (something else than money).
ex: to pay attention, to pay tribute, to pay a visit
not paying me a welcome

s.def: To suffer consequences, especially justly.
ex: He paid for his fun in the sun with a terrible sunburn.

s.def: To admit that a joke, punchline, etc., was funny.
ex: Sutho took a pull at his Johnny Walker and Coke and laughed that trademark laugh of his and said: `Okay. I'll pay that all right.'

s.def: Money given in return for work; salary or wages.
ex: Many employers have rules designed to keep employees from comparing their pays.

der: borrow from Peter to pay Paul

s.def: To attend; to be attentive; to focus one's attention.
ex: Please pay attention to the danger signs.
I was on my way to the door, but all at once, through the fog in my head, I began to sight one reef that I hadn't paid any attention to afore.

ety: From pay + day.

s.def: The day of the week or month, or the specific day, on which an employee's wages or salary is paid.

ety: From pay + -ee.

s.def: one to whom money is paid.

ety: Etymology tree English pay Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English payer From pay + -er (“subject of action”).

s.def: One who pays; specifically, the person by whom a bill or note has been, or should be, paid.
ex: The company is the largest tax payer in the region.
Health insurance depends on both the payer and the provider.

s.def: A swaption which gives its holder the option to enter into a swap in which they pay the fixed leg and receive the floating leg.

ety: From pay + load. From the early 20th century.

s.def: That part of a cargo that produces revenue.
The total weight of passengers, crew, equipment, and cargo carried by an aircraft or spacecraft.
That part of a rocket, missile, propelled stinger, or torpedo that is not concerned with propulsion or guidance, such as a warhead or satellite.
The actual data in a data stream.
The functional part of a computer virus or another type of malware program, rather than the part that spreads it.

I could care less how she perform when she in the bed

s.def: To act in a way set forth in a contract.
ex: Failure to perform a contract on time may constitute a breach of contract.

s.def: To do (something) in front of an audience, such as acting or music, often in order to entertain.
ex: She will perform in the play.
The magician performed badly—none of his tricks worked.
The string quartet performed three pieces by Haydn.

s.def: To behave theatrically so as to give the impression of (a quality, character trait, etc.); to feign.
ex: The accused only performed remorse.
As things now stand, Brexit is a pointless gesture, a politics of headlines in which sovereignty is performed by bleating world-beating absurdities.

s.def: Of a social actor, to behave in certain ways.
ex: perform masculinity
perform authority
Even before her seven decades as monarch began, she performed Britishness more intuitively than anyone ever had, or likely ever will again.

ety: From Middle English parfourmaunce; equivalent to perform + -ance.

s.def: The act of performing; carrying into execution or action; execution; achievement; accomplishment; representation by action.
ex: the performance of an undertaking or a duty
Though the result wasn't what we were hoping for, I have to commend the performance of the team, never giving up until the end.

s.def: A live show or concert.
ex: The band played a mix of old and new songs during their 90-minute performance.
We saw the whole ballet performance from the front row.

s.def: That which is performed or accomplished; a thing done or carried through; an achievement; a deed; an act; a feat; especially, an action of an elaborate or public character.
The amount of useful work accomplished estimated in terms of time needed, resources used, etc.
ex: Better performance means more work accomplished in shorter time and/or using fewer resources.

s.def: The actual use of language in concrete situations by native speakers of a language, as opposed to the system of linguistic knowledge they possess (competence), cf. linguistic performance.

ety: Etymology tree English perform Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English performer From perform + -er.

s.def: One who performs for, or entertains, an audience.
One who performs or does anything.
ex: the performer of an action
It is imperative that these forms are completed accurately for work performed by you bearing your unique performer number, […]

ety: Borrowed from Middle French parfum, perfum. Doublet of parfum.

s.def: A pleasant smell; the scent, odor, or odoriferous particles emitted from a sweet-smelling substance; a pleasant odor.
A substance created to provide a pleasant smell or one which emits an agreeable odor.
ex: She bought a perfume at the airport.

s.def: To apply perfume to; to fill or impregnate with a perfume; to scent.

ety: From perfume (noun and verb) + -ed.

s.def: Scented, having been given a pleasant smell.
ex: The perfumed pages of the letter contrasted with its doleful writing.

ety: From perfume (noun and verb) + -er, perhaps modelled on Middle French parfumeur.

s.def: A person who makes or sells perfume.
One who perfumes something.

ety: Etymology tree English perfume Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -ārius Old French -ier Latin -ia Old French -ie Old French -eriebor. Middle English -erie English -ery English perfumery From perfume + -ery.

s.def: A shop selling perfumes.
ex: These perfumeries were also used as places of assignation and sexual rendezvous.

s.def: A factory where perfume is made.
The manufacture of perfume.

ety: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.

s.def: Done only or merely to conform to a minimal standard or to fulfill a protocol or presumptive duty.
ex: a perfunctory kiss
He then poured some wine for me to taste, and harassed me with perfunctory courtesies that had to be acknowledged.

s.def: Performed in a careless or indifferent manner as a thing of rote.
ex: He did a perfunctory job cleaning his dad's car, finishing quickly but leaving a few spots still dirty.
Alternatively it may mean that a perfunctory search is enough to ensure that a purchase is acceptable, so less search is carried out.

s.def: To permeate or suffuse something, especially with a liquid or with light.
ex: As a patient has decreased ability to perfuse tissue, conversion of glucose into carbon dioxide and energy in the cellular level is also decreased.

s.def: To force a fluid to flow over or through something, especially through an organ of the body.
ex: When AVP was perfused into punctate regions in the brain of the sheep or rabbit, the pyrogen-induced fever was suppressed.

ety: From Latin Pergamum, from Ancient Greek Πέργαμον (Pérgamon).

s.def: An ancient Greek city, in western Anatolia, near modern Bergama.

ety: Borrowed from Italian pergola, from Latin pergula.

s.def: Such a framework employed to provide shade, especially over a patio.
A framework in the form of a passageway of columns that supports a trelliswork roof; used to support and train climbing plants.
ex: While both pergolas and arbors are most dramatic cloaked in climbing, flowing plants, only a pergola will stand naked as a piece of architecture.

s.def: indicating a lack of certainty
Possibly.
ex: Perhaps John will come over for dinner.
There was a perhaps credible witness.
He was seriously wounded, perhaps fatally.

s.def: By chance.
ex: […] will live until he dies perhaps, and then lie down in clover.

s.def: An uncertainty.

ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پری (peri), from Persian پری (pari).

s.def: A sprite or supernatural being.
ex: The Padishah's son was also there, and he realized that the peri looked very familiar.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per-der. Ancient Greek περῐ́ (perĭ́)der. English peri- From Ancient Greek περί (perí, “about, around”). Cognate to for via Proto-Indo-European.

s.def: surrounding
ex: peri- + meter → perimeter

s.def: near
ex: peri- + helion → perihelion

s.def: during
ex: peri- + natal → perinatal

ety: From French périanthe, from New Latin perianthium.

s.def: The sterile parts of a flower; collectively, the sepals and petals (or tepals).
The sterile, tubelike tissue that surrounds the female reproductive structure in a leafy liverwort.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek περικάρδιον (perikárdion)lbor. English pericard(ium) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis)lbor. New Latin -itisder. English -itis English pericarditis From pericard(ium) + -itis.

s.def: Inflammation of the pericardium, the membrane that surrounds the heart.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περικάρδιον (perikárdion).

s.def: A serous membrane that surrounds the heart allowing it to contract.
ex: The Pericardium is sometimes swelled, as overcharged with too great a quantity of Serous Liquor, making a kind of Dropsie […]

ety: From French péricarpe, from New Latin pericarpium, from Ancient Greek περικάρπιον (perikárpion, “pod, husk, shell”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + καρπός (karpós, “fruit”). By surface analysis, peri- + -carp.

s.def: The outermost layer, or skin, of a ripe fruit or ovary.
The outer layer of anything.
ex: He learned, afternoon after afternoon, how to edge her into delicious frenzies, how to tremble the clitoris, pericarp, and tip.

ety: peri- + chondro- + -ium

s.def: a dense layer of fibrous connective tissue surrounding the cartilage of developing bone

ety: From Late Latin pericope, from Ancient Greek περικοπή (perikopḗ, “section”), from περι- (peri-, “across”) + κοπή (kopḗ, “cutting”), from κόπτω (kóptō, “I cut”).

s.def: A section of text forming a coherent thought, suitable for use in a speech.
A passage of Scripture to be read in public worship or a book containing such passages.
ex: The reader looked up the Sunday morning pericope.
The oldest known system of pericopes in the Western Church is ascribed to Jerome.

ety: From late Latin pericranium, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek περικράνιον (perikránion), noun use of the neuter form of περικράνιος (perikránios, “around the skull”), from περί (perí, “around”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”).

s.def: The membrane (or periosteum) which covers the outer surface of the skull.
The head, skull; one's mind.

ety: From Middle English peritot, from Anglo-Norman peridou, peridout, Middle French perido, peridon, of uncertain origin; later reborrowed from modern French péridot.

s.def: A transparent olive green form of olivine, used as a gem.
ex: Gem-quality olivine is known as peridot, which has a subtle green light all its own.

s.def: A yellow-green color, like that of the peridot.

ety: From French périgée via Latin perigeum, perigaeum, ultimately from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “near”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

s.def: The point, in an orbit about the Earth, that is closest to the Earth: the periapsis of an Earth orbiter.
The point, in an orbit about any planet, that is closest to the planet: the periapsis of any satellite.
ex: [Nereid’s] apogee—farthest point from Neptune—is five times the distance of its perigee—its closest point.

s.def: The point, in any trajectory of an object in space, where it is closest to the Earth.

ety: PIE word *sóh₂wl̥ From perihelium (“perihelion”) (obsolete) + -ion (suffix used for other names of apsides). Perihelium is borrowed from Late Latin perihelium, from Ancient Greek περι- (peri-, “around; surrounding”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”)), which was modelled after perigeum (“point in an orbit about the Earth that is closest to the Earth, perigee”).

s.def: The point in the elliptical orbit of a comet, planet, etc., where it is nearest to the Sun.
The highest point or state; the peak, zenith.

ety: From Middle English peril, from Old French peril, from Latin perīculum. Doublet of periculum.

s.def: A situation of serious and immediate danger.
ex: Your life is in peril.

s.def: Something that causes, contains, or presents danger.
ex: the perils of the jungle (animals and insects, weather, etc.)

s.def: An event which causes a loss, or the risk of a specific such event.
To cause to be in danger; to imperil; to risk.
ex: "I will have nothing to do with this matter, whatever it is. Do you think I am going to peril my reputation for you?"

ety: From Middle English perilous, from Old French perilleus, equivalent to peril + -ous, from the noun peril, or from Latin perīculōsus. Doublet of periculous.

s.def: Dangerous, full of peril.

ety: From Latin perimetros, Ancient Greek περίμετρος (perímetros). Equivalent to peri- + meter.

s.def: The sum of the distance of all the lengths of the sides of an object.
The length of such a boundary.
The outer limits of an area.
A fortified strip or boundary usually protecting a military position.
An instrument for determining the extent and shape of the field of vision.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin perinaeum, from Ancient Greek περίναιον (perínaion, “space between the anus and scrotum”), from Ancient Greek περίνεος, περίνεοι (períneos, períneoi, “male genitals”), itself from earlier Ancient Greek περίς (perís, “penis”) through influence from Ancient Greek πηρίς (pērís, “scrotum”).

s.def: The region between the genitalia and anus.
ex: The prostate is surrounded by venous plexi and the perineum has a rich blood supply.
The perineum is diamond shaped and stretches from the pubic symphysis to the coccyx.

s.def: Inflammation of the perineurium.
The sheath of connective tissue that surrounds a fascicle of nerve fibres

s.def: The punctuation mark “.” (indicating the ending of a sentence or marking an abbreviation).
ex: ‘You know, a period? The black spot at the end of a sentence — what do you call them over there?’

s.def: interval of time
history: period of time seen as coherent entity
A length of time.
ex: There was a period of confusion following the announcement.
You'll be on probation for a six-month period.
Philip Miles, defending, said: "This was a single instance, there was no allegation of continuing behaviour over a long period of time."

s.def: A length of time in history seen as a single coherent entity; an epoch, era.
ex: Food rationing continued in the post-war period.
Sung Yung-hsi of Ch’u-hsiung was a government student during the Chia-ch’ing period.

s.def: A decisive end to something; a stop.
The length of time during which the same characteristics of a periodic phenomenon recur, such as the repetition of a wave or the rotation of a planet.
Female menstruation; an episode of this.
ex: When she is on her period, she prefers not to go swimming.

s.def: A section of an artist's, writer's (etc.) career distinguished by a given quality, preoccupation etc.
ex: This is one of the last paintings Picasso created during his Blue Period.

s.def: Each of the divisions into which a school day is split, allocated to a given subject or activity.
ex: I have math class in second period.

ety: From French périodique, from Medieval Latin periodicus (“cyclical”), from Latin periodus (“complete sentence, period, circuit”), from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “cycle, period of time”). By surface analysis, period + -ic.

s.def: Having repeated cycles.
Occurring at regular intervals.
Periodical.
Pertaining to the revolution of a celestial object in its orbit.
For which any return to it must occur in multiples of k time steps, for some k>1.
Having a structure characterized by periodic sentences.
Relative to a period or periods.
Relating to the highest oxidation state of iodine; of or derived from a periodic acid.

ety: The table is termed “periodic” because it follows the periodic law – when chemical elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, elements with similar properties recur at intervals.

s.def: A tabular chart of the chemical elements according to their atomic numbers so that elements with similar properties are in the same group (column).

Periodic.
ex: The periodical times of all the satellites.

s.def: Published at regular intervals of more than one day, especially weekly, monthly, or quarterly.
ex: influence opinion through the periodical press.

s.def: Of, or relating to such a publication.

ex: Put two encasings on a mattress if one must be removed periodically for cleaning.

s.def: A membrane surrounding a bone.

s.def: Inflammation of a periosteum

ety: From French péripatétique, from Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περιπατητικός (peripatētikós, “given to walking around”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) (English peri-)+ πατέω (patéō, “to walk”).

s.def: Tending to walk about.
Constantly travelling.
ex: Near-synonyms: itinerant, nomadic

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Peripatetic.
ex: The true peripatetic school.

s.def: One who walks about; a pedestrian; an itinerant.
Alternative letter-case form of Peripatetic (“Aristotelian”).
ex: He who would think clearly must think like a peripatetic even if he is unwilling to walk like one.

Beside the point.
Unimportant.

Related to or located in the peripheral nervous system.

s.def: A peripheral device.
ex: Check your peripheral's manual for the information you'll need.
Turn on the Mac, and check your peripheral. Since you've already installed your device driver, it should be available where you need it....

s.def: Peripheral vision.
ex: As I sat by the window and read, I caught sight of the mailman in my peripheral.

s.def: The part of the nervous system which is not the central nervous system.

s.def: The outside boundary, parts or surface of something.
ex: The suburbs are a city's periphery.
Tumor location was concentrated in the macula and superonasal periphery in patients 13.2 months.

s.def: A first-rank administrative division of Greece, subdivided into provinces.
The more anomalous and infrequent aspects of a language, as opposed to the frequent and regular core aspects.

ety: Formed in English from peri- + -scope.

s.def: A form of viewing device that allows the viewer to see things at a different height level and usually with minimal visibility.
A general or comprehensive view.
To rise and peer around, in the manner of a periscope.
ex: Thousands of ungainly black-beaked heads would periscope and freeze in the direction of the approaching intruder.
Her black and white head suddenly popped out from under the covers and periscoped around.

ety: From Middle English perishen, borrowed from Old French perir (via the stem periss- used in various conjugations), from Latin perīre (“pass away, perish”), from per (“through”) + īre (“pass, go”).

s.def: To decay and disappear; to waste away to nothing.
To decay in such a way that it cannot be used for its original purpose
ex: The difficulty is that fresh foods perish due to the multiplication in them of harmful bacteria.

s.def: To die; to cease to live.
ex: When it goeth well with the righteous, the citie reioyceth: and when the wicked perish, there is shouting.

s.def: To cause to perish.
ex: that closeness did impair and a little perish his understanding

ety: From Middle English *persishable, perysabyl, equivalent to perish + -able. Compare Old French perissable (and modern French périssable).

s.def: Liable to perish, especially naturally subject to quick decomposition or decay.
ex: perishable goods
perishable foodstuffs

s.def: That which perishes or is short-lived.
Food that does not keep for long.

ety: From French périsperme. See peri- and sperm.

s.def: The layer of nutritive tissue, derived from the nucellus, that surrounds the embryo of a seed in some angiosperms.

ety: From Ancient Greek δύναμις περισταλτική (dúnamis peristaltikḗ, “the action of the bowels by which their contents are propelled”), from περιστέλλω (peristéllō, “to wrap around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to make ready, to prepare”).

s.def: The coordinated, rhythmic, wavelike contraction and relaxation of smooth muscle that propels contents through a hollow organ, particularly food through the gastrointestinal tract.

ety: Etymology tree English peristalsis Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English peristaltic From peristalsis + -ic.

s.def: of or pertaining to peristalsis

ety: From French péristyle, from Classical Latin peristȳlum, from Ancient Greek περίστυλον (perístulon), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”), equivalent to peri- + -style.

s.def: A colonnade surrounding a courtyard, temple, etc., or the yard enclosed by such columns.
A porch surrounded by columns.
A sacred roofed courtyard with a central pillar (the potomitan), used as a space for voodoo ceremonies, either alone or as an adjunct to an enclosed temple or altar-room.
ex: The peristyle is a roofed structure, open at the sides, in which most of the ceremonials and dances take place.
Most peristyles in Haiti have hard-packed dirt floors that can soak up libations when they're poured on the ground in honor of the spirits.

ety: From Latin peritonaeum, from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion), from περιτόναιος (peritónaios, “stretched or strained over”).

s.def: In mammals, the serous membrane lining the cavity of the abdomen and that is folded over the viscera.
In animals, the membrane lining the coelom cavity.

ety: Etymology tree English peritoneum Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis)lbor. New Latin -itisder. English -itis English peritonitis From peritoneum + -itis.

s.def: Inflammation of the peritoneum, especially when caused by an infectious organism introduced into the abdominal cavity.
ex: Oh, a very well-known man. He has a great reputation as an operator for peritonitis.

ety: Alteration of Middle French perruque. Doublet of peruke.

s.def: A wig, especially any kind of stylised wig as formerly worn by men and women.
ex: Methinks she makes almost as fair a sign / As some old gentlewoman in a periwig.
The floods in icie fetters bound. Crusted earth. Every honey-headed twig Wears his snowie Periwig, And every bough his snowy beard.
From her own Head, Megwra takes A Perriwig of twisted Snakes; Which in the nicest Fashion curl'd, Like Toupets of this upper World […]

s.def: To dress with a periwig, or with false hair; to bewig.
ex: Discord periwigg'd with snakes

ety: Diminutive of Middle English perwinke, from Old English perfince, perwince (compare Middle High German berwinke), from Latin pervinca (compare French pervenche, Italian pervinca).

s.def: Similar plants of genus Catharanthus.
Any of several evergreen plants of the genus Vinca with blue or white flowers.
ex: The Periwinkle is a great binder, staying bleeding both at mouth and nose if some of the leaves be chewed.

s.def: A color with bluish and purplish hues, somewhat light.
Of pale bluish purple colour.
A mollusk of family Littorinidae.
ex: He was working a pin into a periwinkle shell, turning it to extract the toothsome morsel of meat.

s.def: A caddisfly larva.

ety: From Old French parjurer, from Latin periūrō.

s.def: To knowingly and willfully make a false statement of witness while in court.
ex: He perjured himself.

s.def: To cause to violate an oath or a vow; to cause to make oath knowingly to what is untrue; to make guilty of perjury; to forswear; to corrupt.
ex: Want will perjure the ne'er-touched vestal.

s.def: To make a false oath to; to deceive by oaths and protestations.
ex: And with a virgin innocence did pray / For me, that perjured her.

s.def: A perjured person.
ex: He comes in like a perjure, wearing papers

ety: From perjure + -er.

s.def: someone who has committed perjury by lying under oath
ex: Come in, you false witness, you perjurer, you suborner of evidence, come in!

ety: From Anglo-Norman perjurie, from Latin perjūrāre (“swear falsely”), from per- + jūrāre. Displaced native Old English mānāþ (literally “false oath”).

s.def: The deliberate giving of false or misleading testimony under oath.
ex: We declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct.

ety: Clipping of perquisite.

s.def: Perquisite.
ex: Free coffee is one of the perks of the job.

s.def: A bonus ability that a player character can acquire; a permanent power-up.
To make (coffee) in a percolator or a drip coffeemaker.
ex: I’ll perk some coffee.

s.def: Of coffee: to be produced by heated water seeping (“percolating”) through coffee grounds.
ex: The coffee is perking.

ety: Originally northern dialectal, from Scots pet (“an animal that has been tamed and is kept as a pet; a darling or favourite; a petted or spoiled child”), probably from Scottish Gaelic peata (“pet, tamed animal, spoiled child”), from Middle Irish petta, peta (“pet, lap-dog”), of uncertain origin, possibly from a pre-Indo-European substrate. s.def: Appearance; a perceptible aspect of something that is mutable.
A fact or event considered very unusual, curious, or astonishing by those who witness it.
A wonderful or very remarkable person or thing.
ex: "This, sir," said Mr Vincent Crummles, bringing the maiden forward, "this is the infant phenomenon—Miss Ninetta Crummles."
But, all the same, you're a phenomenon, and as queer a phenomenon as you are a blackguard.

s.def: An experienced object whose constitution reflects the order and conceptual structure imposed upon it by the human mind (especially by the powers of perception and understanding).
ex: Every "phenomenon" must be, at any rate, partly subjective or dependent on the subject.
The Kantian phenomenon is the real as we are compelled to think it.

ety: From pheno- + -type, from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, to show, to appear”) + τύπος (túpos, “mark, type”).

s.def: The appearance of an organism based on a multifactorial combination of genetic traits and environmental factors, especially used in pedigrees.
Any observable characteristic of an organism, such as its morphological, developmental, biochemical or physiological properties, or its behavior.

ety: Etymology tree English phenylketone Proto-Indo-European *h₁wers-der. Ancient Greek οὐρέω (ouréō) Ancient Greek οὖρον (oûron) Ancient Greek -ουρία (-ouría)bor. New Latin -ūriabor. English -uria English phenylketonuria From phenylketone + -uria.

s.def: A metabolic disorder in which individuals lack the liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) which is needed to metabolize the amino acid phenylalanine.

ety: From φέρω (phérō, “I bring, bear, carry”) and hormone.

s.def: A chemical secreted by an animal, especially an insect, that affects the development or behavior of other members of the same species, functioning often as a means of attracting a member of the opposite sex.

ety: Attested since the early 17th century. An onomatopoeia for rapid exhalation, as one may make when a trying situation is over, or in order to get rid of an unpleasant odour. Compare Scots feuch, Spanish fu, Czech fuj, and many more such forms.

s.def: Used to express relief of tension, fatigue, or surprise.
ex: Phew, that took a long time to cook!

s.def: Used to show disgust.
ex: Phew, it stinks in here!

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek Φιλάδελφος (Philádelphos) Ancient Greek Φιλαδέλφεια (Philadélpheia)bor. Latin Philadelphiabor. English Philadelphia From Latin Philadelphia, from Ancient Greek Φιλαδέλφεια (Philadélpheia), from φιλάδελφος (philádelphos, “brother/sibling-loving”) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming placenames”), from the combining form of φῐλέειν (phĭléein, “to love”) + ἀδελφός (adelphós, “brother, sibling”). In reference to the city in Turkey, named for the loyal Attalus II Philadelphus of…

s.def: The largest city in Pennsylvania, United States, and the county seat of coterminous Philadelphia County; the former capital of the United States.
ex: Philadelphia police said they were investigating. No charges were immediately filed.

s.def: Former name of Amman: the capital of Jordan.
Former name of Alaşehir: a city, municipality, and district of Manisa Province, Turkey.
A locale in the United States; named for the city in Pennsylvania.
A village in Brandenburg, Germany; named for the city in Pennsylvania.
A village in Sunderland, Tyne and Wear, England; named for the city in Pennsylvania (OS grid ref NZ3352).
A suburb of Cape Town, South Africa.

ety: As a verb, first seen in the 1824 play Philandering: Or, The Rose Queen, by Samuel Beazley. From the given name Philander, used for love interest or suitor stock characters in several 18th century stories and poems, from Ancient Greek Φίλανδρος (Phílandros), name of the mythological son of the nymph Acacallis and the god Apollo. Semantically disconnected from the adjective φίλανδρος (phílandros, “loving one’s husband; excessively attracted to males, slutty, boy crazy”).

s.def: A lover.
ex: Yes, I'll baste you together, you and your Philander!

s.def: A South American opossum, bare-tailed woolly opossum, of species Caluromys philander (syn. Didelphis philander).
A greater bilby, an Australian marsupial of species Macrotis lagotis (syn. Perameles lagotis).
To woo women; to play the male flirt.
ex: You can't be philandering after her again.

ety: From philander (“lover”) + -er, from Ancient Greek φίλανδρος (phílandros), from φίλος (phílos, “love”) + ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”).

s.def: One who plays at courtship; a fickle lover; a flirt (usually applies only to men).
Someone who engages in casual sex, usually frequently.
ex: A philanderer's tie, a murderer's shoe Life's rich demand creates supply in the hand of the powers—the only vote that matters

ety: Etymology tree English philanthropy Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-tās Ancient Greek -τής (-tḗs) Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. s.def: A person who loves humankind in general.
A person or institution who seeks to improve the world, especially by monetary gifts.
ex: […]and with a passing vague wonder as to what manner of man the ‘philanthropist’ might be who had more money than he knew what to do with,[…]
He was a noted philanthropist, and played a public-spirited part in the support of the Army during the Crimean War.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía). By surface analysis, phil- + -anthropy.

s.def: Benevolent altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of humankind.
Charitable giving, charity.
ex: As public funding is reduced, we depend increasingly on private philanthropy.

s.def: A philanthropic act.
ex: His tombstone lists his various philanthropies.

s.def: A charitable foundation.
ex: the Rockefeller philanthropies

s.def: A person who collects and studies postage stamps.

ety: First use appears c. 1865. Borrowed from French philatélie, coined by French stamp collector Georges Herpin in 1864 (in Le Collectionneur de Timbres-poste, Nov. 15, 1864), from Ancient Greek φιλέω (philéō, “I love”) + ἀτέλεια (atéleia), the closest word he could find in Ancient Greek to the concept of "postage stamp", from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + τέλος (télos, “tax”). This word serves as a reminder of the original function of postage stamps, now often forgotten: the cost of letter-carrying formerl…

s.def: Stamp collecting.
The study of postage stamps, postal routes, postal history, etc.

ety: Clipping of pedophile.

s.def: A pedophile.
ex: Release the files, not the philes!

s.def: A lover (of something).
ex: This is a list of over 15 different types of philes.

ety: From French philharmonique; from Italian filarmonico. By surface analysis, phil- + harmonic.

s.def: Appreciative of music, but especially to its performance; devoted to music.
A full-size symphony orchestra.

ety: From Latin philippicus, from Ancient Greek φιλιππικός (philippikós), from Φίλιππος (Phílippos, “lover of horses”), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).

s.def: Any of the discourses of Demosthenes against Philip II of Macedon, defending the liberty of Athens.
Any tirade or declamation full of bitter condemnation.
ex: "Sir Robert Akhurst is a good man, a very good man, notwithstanding his philippic; but he is an old one, which makes all the difference."

s.def: A marginal sea in the Pacific Ocean to the north and east of the Philippines.

ety: See Name of the Philippines in Wikipedia for a complete etymology. Borrowed from French Philippines, originally from Spanish Filipinas, which was from Felipe (the name of a king of Spain). By surface analysis, Philip + -ine + -s.

s.def: A country in Southeast Asia. Official name: Republic of the Philippines. Capital: Manila.
ex: The rolling Chocolate Hills of Bohol in the Philippines could easily be mistaken for a child’s landscape drawing.

s.def: An archipelago of Southeast Asia.

ety: The noun is derived from Philistine, influenced by philister, Philister (“(historical) in German universities: person not associated with the university; person who lacks appreciation of or is antagonistic towards art or culture”), from German Philister (“person from ancient Philistia; (figurative, dated) person not associated with a university; (figurative) person who lacks appreciation of or is antagonistic towards art or culture”), from Late Latin Philistaeus, Philisteus (compare Philistinus…

s.def: A person who is ignorant or uneducated; specifically, a person who lacks appreciation of or is antagonistic towards art or culture, and who has pedestrian tastes.
ex: "Oh, the Philistine! The boorish Philistine!" he murmured; [...]
War was looked upon as inherently monstrous, and those who waged it – namely, military officers – were looked upon as brutes and philistines.
They all want to know how you get to me, let them feel how they feel and be philistines because this type of love's the epitome said.

s.def: Ignorant or uneducated; specifically, lacking appreciation for or antagonistic towards art or culture, and having pedestrian tastes.
ex: [Robert] Walpole, moreover, left England not only more corrupt than he found it, but crasser and more Philistine.
Miles was taken seriously by the great dames of Manhattan society and was not scorned by even the most Philistine of their husbands.

ety: From New Latin philodendron, from Ancient Greek φῐλόδενδρον (phĭlódendron), neuter of φῐλόδενδρος (phĭlódendros, “loving trees”). First known use: 1877.

s.def: Any of several climbing plants, of the genus Philodendron, native to America and the West Indies that are often grown as house plants.

s.def: Of or pertaining to the history of literature and words.
Pertaining to historical linguistics.

ety: Inherited from Middle English Philologie, from Latin philologia, from Ancient Greek φιλολογίᾱ (philologíā, “love of argument or reasoning, love of learning and literature”).

s.def: philology
The humanistic study of texts and their languages, especially ancient or classical languages.
Historical or comparative linguistics.
Love and study of learning and literature, broadly speaking.

ety: From philo- + mel(os).

s.def: The nightingale.
ex: And lonely Philomel, still waking, sings.
And Philomel becometh dumb.

s.def: A musical instrument similar to the violin, but having four steel-wire strings.

ety: The origin of philopena is unclear. Despite its appearance, it is not formed from classical roots. The traditional game seems to have originated in Germany, and to have included a formulaic greeting, guten Morgen Vielliebchen (“Good morning, sweetheart”), with Vielliebchen being accepted into French as a proper name, and the game's tag becoming Bonjour Philippine. A different account suggests that the word began as the French Valentin(e), with the nut exchanged considered as a St. Valentine's D…

s.def: A game in which a person, on finding a double-kernelled almond or nut, may offer the second kernel to another person and demand a playful forfeit from that person to be paid on their next meeting. The forfeit may simply be to exchange the greeting "Good-day, Philopena" or it may be more elaborate.…
The occasion on which a philopena is forfeited; the forfeit paid.
A nut or almond with a double kernel, as used to set a philopena.

ety: From philoprogenitive + -ness.

s.def: The state or condition of being philoprogenitive.

ety: From Middle English philosophre, from Anglo-Norman or Middle French philosophe, from Latin philosophus, from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos, literally “lover of wisdom”) + -er. Credited as having been coined by Pythagoras to describe himself. Displaced native Old English ūþwita.

s.def: person devoted to studying philosophy
A lover of wisdom.
A student of philosophy.
A scholar or expert engaged in or contributing to philosophical inquiry.
A person who applies the principles of philosophy to the conduct of their life, as by acting calmly and rationally in the face of inevitable change.
ex: Then certaine Philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoikes, encountred him

s.def: A student, scholar, or expert in any branch of knowledge, especially those branches studied prior to being considered part of pure science.
An alchemist.

ety: A misconstruction of philosophers' stone, from Middle English philosophres ston, a calque of Latin lapis philosophōrum.

s.def: A supposed substance able to turn base metals, such as lead or mercury, into gold or silver, also sometimes claimed to cure any illness (as panacea) or confer immortality (as elixir of life), among other functions.
ex: […] I entered with the greatest diligence into the search of the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life.

s.def: A piece of such a substance.

ety: From philosophy + -ical, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía, “love of knowledge, scientific learning”). Displaced native Old English ūþwitlīċ.

s.def: Of, or pertaining to, philosophy.
Rational; analytic or critically minded; thoughtful.
ex: His richly philosophical intellect was not at any time affected by unrealities.

s.def: Detached, calm, stoic.
ex: She bore the desertion with philosophical indifference.
