s.def: To ponder or reason out philosophically.

ety: From Middle English philosophie, Old French philosophie, and their source, Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”). By surface analysis, philo- + -sophy. Displaced Old English ūþwitegung.

s.def: An academic discipline that seeks truth through reasoning rather than empiricism, often attempting to provide explanations relating to general concepts such as existence and rationality.
ex: Philosophy is often divided into five major branches: logic, metaphysics, epistemology, ethics and aesthetics.

s.def: A view or outlook regarding fundamental principles underlying some domain.
ex: a philosophy of government; a philosophy of education

s.def: A general principle (usually moral).
A comprehensive system of belief.
The love of wisdom.
A calm and thoughtful demeanor; calmness of temper.
Synonym of small pica (especially in French printing).
A broader branch of (non-applied) science.
ex: natural philosophy

s.def: To philosophize.

The study of the assumptions, foundations, and implications of science, including such questions as what distinguishes science from non-science, what are the aims of science, or what is a successful scientific explanation of a phenomenon.
A particular theory within the former.

ety: From phleb(o)- + -itis.

s.def: Inflammation of a vein, usually in the legs.

ety: From Old French flebothomie (French phlébotomie), from Late Latin phlebotomia, from Ancient Greek φλεβοτόμος (phlebotómos, “that opens a vein”), from φλέψ (phléps, “vein”). By surface analysis, phlebo- + -tomy.

s.def: The opening of a vein, either to withdraw blood or for letting blood; venesection.
ex: Now butter with a leafe of Sage is good to Parge the bloud, Fly Venus and Phlebotomy for they are neither good.
Phlebotomy is promiscuously used before and after physick, commonly before and upon occasion is often reiterated, if there be any need at least of it.
Of course, members of the family were foremost in spilling loyal blood on Marston Moor, that great field of plebotomy to so may Cavaliers.

ety: From Middle English flewme, fleume, fleme, from Old French fleume, Middle French flemme (French flegme), and their source, Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame; inflammation; clammy humor in the body”), from φλέγειν (phlégein, “to burn”). Possible burning sensation when coughing up phlegm. Compare phlox, flagrant, flame, bleak (adjective), fulminate. Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and Greek roots. The regularly developed form /fliːm/ has been displaced…

s.def: Viscid mucus produced by the body, later especially mucus expelled from the bronchial passages by coughing.
One of the four humors making up the body in ancient and mediaeval medicine; said to be cold and moist, and often identified with mucus.
A watery distillation, especially one obtained from plant matter; an aqueous solution.
Calmness of temperament, composure; also seen negatively, sluggishness, indifference.
ex: Orloff's phlegm broke completely, and he snatched at the monocle as it dropped[.]

ety: From Middle English fleumatik, flewmatik, flematik, fleumatyke, flewmatyk, from Old French fleumatique, from Latin phlegmaticus, from Ancient Greek φλεγματικός (phlegmatikós), from φλέγμα (phlégma), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with mildness, coldness, sluggishness, and indifference. Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and Greek roots, with modern pronunciation following this new spelling.

s.def: Generating, causing, or full of phlegm.
ex: cold and phlegmatic bodies
Near-synonyms: phlegmish, phlegmy
phlegmatic humors

s.def: Not easily excited to action or passion; calm; sluggish.

ety: From phlegm + -y.

s.def: Charged with phlegm.
ex: His phlegmy cough disgusted everybody on the train.
Pockmarks rise with hair all along his arm, and he reaches for a bottle and hacks up a big phlegmy gob of spit.

ety: From Khmer ភ្នំពេញ (phnum pɨñ, literally “Penh’s hill”).

s.def: The capital city of Cambodia.
The Cambodian government.

ety: Borrowed from Vietnamese phở.

s.def: A Vietnamese soup with a beef base, typically served with rice noodles and optionally beef or chicken.

ety: First attested in c. 1790, from words ending in -phobia, ultimately from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”). Compare ism, from -ism, itis, from -itis, and ana, from -ana.

s.def: An irrational, abnormal, or obsessive fear (of something).
ex: I know someone with a strange phobia of ladders.

s.def: An aversion or dislike (of something).

ety: From Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos) + -phobia, equivalent to phobo- + -phobia.

s.def: The fear of fear; the fear of developing a phobia.
ex: When Franklin Delano Roosevelt said, "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself," he was describing phobophobia -- the fear of being afraid.

ety: From Ancient Greek Φόβος (Phóbos, “Fear”).

s.def: A son of Ares (Mars). Also the Greek god of fear.
The innermost natural satellite of Mars.

ety: From early 18th c. Imitative, influenced by the name Phoebe.

s.def: Any of several birds of the genus Sayornis.

ety: Borrowed from Latin Phoenicia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Φοινίκη (Phoiníkē). The word is already found in the Mycenaean Greek ethnonym 𐀡𐀛𐀑𐀍 (po-ni-ki-jo). Ultimately from Egyptian fnḫw, f:n:x-w-V12:Z2 ‘Canaanites, Syrians’.

s.def: land of the Phoenicians
The land of city states of the Phoenicians which around 1000 BC was situated on the coast of present day Syria and Lebanon, and included the cities of Tyre and Sidon.
The trading empire of the Phoenicians which spread across most of the eastern Mediterranean Sea as far west as Sicily.

ety: Attested as a noun in Middle English as phenicienes (only plural); from Ancient Greek Φοῖνιξ (Phoînix, “Phoenician”).

s.def: Of, from, or related to the country or civilisation of Phoenicia.
ex: The term phallus is reputedly of Phoenician origin.

s.def: An inhabitant of Phoenicia (a country located on the shores of North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean Sea around the year 1000 BCE).
An inhabitant of Phoenix, Arizona.
The now extinct Semitic language spoken by the inhabitants of Phoenicia.

ety: From Old English and Old French fenix, from Medieval Latin phenix, from Latin phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix), from Egyptian b-n:nw*w-G31 (bnw, “grey heron”). Doublet of Bennu. The grey heron was venerated at Heliopolis and associated in Egypt with the cyclical renewal of life because the bird rises in flight at dawn and migrates back every year in the flood season to inhabit the Nile waters.

s.def: A mythological bird, said to be the only one of its kind, which lives for 500 years and then dies by burning to ashes on a pyre of its own making, ignited by the sun. It then arises anew from the ashes.
ex: burn the long-lived phoenix in her blood

s.def: Anything that is reborn after apparently being destroyed.
ex: Astronomers believe planets might form in this dead star's disk, like the mythical Phoenix rising up out of the ashes.
Lord Allerton was that modern phœnix, a young man, without a single objection.
Many of the legitimate nightclubs of today sprang like legalized phoenixes from the still-hot ashes of the speakeasies of prohibition days.

s.def: A mythological Chinese chimerical bird whose physical body symbolizes the six celestial bodies; a fenghuang.
A Greek silver coin used briefly from 1828 to 1832, divided into 100 lepta.
ex: The national currency, the phoenix, which had been established by Kapodistrias, was renamed after an ancient Greek coin, the drachma.

s.def: A marvelous person or thing.
A geometer moth of species Eulithis prunata.
To transfer assets from one company to another to dodge liability
ex: Australian Restructuring Insolvency and Turnaround Association CEO John Winter said phoenixing has been "endemic" for decades.

der: like a phoenix from the ashes

ety: From Latin phoenīx, Phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνῐξ (phoînĭx), Φοῖνῐξ (Phoînĭx).

s.def: A geometer moth of species Eulithis prunata.
A German breed of long-tailed chicken.
A white variety of grape of German origin used for winemaking.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁-der. Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle)lbor. French télé- Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂-der. Proto-Hellenic *pʰōnā́ Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ)der. s.def: A device for transmitting conversations and other sounds in real time across distances, now often a small portable unit also capable of running software etc.
ex: Daragh's on the phone at the moment. He'll call you when he's finished.
My phone ran out of battery.
There's an old-fashioned phone in the doctor's waiting room - it doesn't work anymore, of course.

s.def: A person's telephone number (as a means of contact); digits.
To call (someone) using a telephone.
ex: Phone me as soon as you land at the airport.
Her father told her to phone him to pick her up in case it started raining heavily.
"You bloody fools!" shrieked Nickle, stung by a sudden dreadful inspiration, "we've let him phone. He has got through!"

s.def: To say via telephone.
ex: Well, the first I knew, Mr. Cooney phoned he had a buyer for my farm, and wanted to know if he could come down.
After I wrote the 23ⁿᵈ bout midnite Charles phoned he got my note + could I come over then?

A protective covering designed to fit around a mobile phone.

ety: From Ancient Greek φώνημα (phṓnēma, “sound”), from φωνέω (phōnéō, “to sound”), from φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). By surface analysis, phone (“speech sound”) + -eme (“unit”).

s.def: An indivisible unit of sound in a given language. A phoneme is an abstraction of the physical speech sounds (phones) and may encompass several different phones.

ety: Etymology tree English phoneme Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic Old English -as Middle English -es English -s English -ics English phonemics From phoneme + -ics.

s.def: The study of phonemes and their written representations.

ety: Borrowed from Latin phōnēticus, from Ancient Greek φωνητῐκός (phōnētĭkós). By surface analysis, phone + -etic.

s.def: Relating to the sounds of spoken language.
Relating to phones (as opposed to phonemes).
Relating to the spoken rather than written form of a word or name, as opposed to orthographic.
ex: All unfamiliar names have been transcribed in phonetic spelling.

s.def: In such writing systems as the Chinese writing system, the portion of a phono-semantic character that provides an indication of its pronunciation; contrasted with semantic (which is usually the radical).
ex: I suspect that 田 dien is the original character and true phonetic of the whole group.
In the first case the character is pronounced identically, even as to tone, as the phonetic.
Or, the semantic may wrap around the phonetic, or position within the phonetic.

s.def: A writing system used to unambiguously transcribe the sounds of human speech.
ex: International Phonetic Alphabet

s.def: A spelling alphabet: a set of code words used to substitute the names of the letters of the alphabet, usually for clarity of communication when spelling out words.
ex: NATO phonetic alphabet

ex: The hard words in the passage have been spelled phonetically.
Equipment on a warship set to be upgraded or disposed of was given the code AT-6, or phonetically “eighty-six”.

ety: Etymology tree English phonetic Old English -as Middle English -es English -s English phonetics From phonetic + -s.

s.def: The study of the physical sounds of human speech, concerned with the physical properties of speech sounds (phones), and the processes of their physiological production, auditory reception, and neurophysiological perception, and their representation by written symbols.
ex: This dictionary shows the phonetics of the words.

ety: From Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”) + -ic.

s.def: Of or pertaining to sound; of the nature of sound; acoustic.

ety: From phono- + -gram.

s.def: A character or symbol (grapheme) that represents a sound, as opposed to logograms and determinatives.
An audio recording, regardless of physical format.

ety: From phono- + -graph.

s.def: A device that captures sound waves onto an engraved archive; a lathe.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).

s.def: A short written or spoken expression.
ex: I've made progress, but this is still, in Churchill's phrase, just "the end of the beginning."

s.def: A word or, more commonly, a group of words that functions as a single unit in the syntax of a sentence, always containing an expressed or implied head (the principal word or subgroup, with core importance) and often consisting of a head plus some other elaborating words.
ex: Holonyms: clause, sentence; phrasing, phraseology, turn of phrase; phrase-book; document, message; language; communication
Meronyms: head, complement, adjunct, supplement, modifier; term, word

s.def: A small section of music in a larger piece.
A mode or form of speech; diction; expression.
ex: […] From out a common vein of memory / Sweet household talk, and phrases of the hearth, […]

s.def: A short individual motion forming part of a choreographed dance.
To express (an action, thought or idea) by means of particular words.

These suns — for so they phrase 'em.

To divide into melodic phrases.

ety: From phrase + book.

s.def: Of one's fluency of a language, limited or deficient.
Of or pertaining to a phrasebook.

ety: From phraseology + -ical.

ety: From Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “speech”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation”).

A group of specialized words and expressions used by a particular group.
A collection of phrases; a phrasebook.
present participle and gerund of phrase
The way a statement is put together, particularly in matters of style and word choice.
The way the musical phrases are put together in a composition or in its interpretation, with changes in tempo, volume, or emphasizing one or more instruments over others.

Relating to the mind or mental activity

ety: From Latin phrenītis, from Ancient Greek φρενῖτις (phrenîtis), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).

s.def: Madness, especially as caused by inflammation of the brain; encephalitis, encephalomeningitis, or meningitis.
ex: Phrenitis, which the Greeks derive from the word φρήν, is a disease of the mind, with a continual madness or dotage […].

ety: From Latin Phrygia, from Ancient Greek Φρυγία (Phrugía).

ety: From Phrygian (“of or relating to Phrygia, its people or their culture”) + cap. Sense 2 (“congenital abnormality of the gall bladder”) is a calque of German phrygische Mütze, coined by J. Bartel in 1916 and popularized by Edward A. Boyden.

s.def: A soft, close-fitting conical cap with the top bent forward, represented in Greek and Roman art as worn by ancient Phrygians, and later associated with the Roman liberty cap.

ety: From Middle English tisike, from Anglo-Norman, from Latin phthisicus (“suffering from tuberculosis”), from Ancient Greek φθισικός (phthisikós, “consumptive”), from φθίσις (phthísis, “tuberculosis, consumption”).

s.def: Either of two small leather cases containing scrolls with passages from the Torah, traditionally worn by a Jewish man (one on the arm (usually the left) and one on the forehead) and now sometimes by a woman at certain morning prayers as a reminder to obey the law as set out in the Bible; a tefilla.
A fringe which an Israelite was required to wear as a reminder to obey the law as set out in the Bible; (by extension) any fringe or border.
ex: [S]uddenly now, / Full-statured, with uplifted head she walks, / And drops her loosed phylacteries in the dust.

s.def: Synonym of amulet (“a protective charm or ornament”).
A scroll with words on it depicted as emerging from a person's mouth or held in their hands, indicating what they are singing or speaking; a banderole, a speech scroll.

ety: From the masculine Ancient Greek Φύλλις (Phúllis) or from the feminine Φυλλίς (Phullís).

s.def: A girl who killed herself for love and was turned into an almond tree.

ety: From Greek φύλλο (fýllo, “leaf”). Doublet of phyllon, distantly also with foil, folio, and folium.

ety: From phyllo- + -ome.

s.def: A leaf, leaflike part of a plant, or part derived from a leaf, such as a petal.

ety: From phyllo- + -pod.

ety: Borrowed from German Phylogenie, coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866, a neologism created as if borrowed from a Classic Greek word φυλογένεια (phulogéneia), composed from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, genus, species”) + -γένεια (-géneia, “-geny (generation, production)”), equivalent to phylo- + -geny.

s.def: A phylogenetic diagram.
ex: Holonym: tree of life

s.def: The historical development of a human social or racial group.
ex: Understanding the phylogeny of this musical group helps us understand its music.

s.def: The historical development of any thing, idea, etc.

ety: From Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, race”).

s.def: A large division of possibly related languages, or a major language family which is not subordinate to another.

ety: From Middle English phisik, from Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).

The art or profession of healing disease; medicine.

A room, allocated as a children's play area, in which noisy or boisterous activities are tolerated.

ety: From play + station; coined by Sony Computer Entertainment.

s.def: A video game console of the PlayStation brand.
ex: His dad bought him a Playstation 5 yesterday.
Back then, kids didn't have TV or video games, so I guess slaughtering your mom and dad was a bit like the Playstation^([sic]) of its day.
The Everlasting Treat Ball landed like the PlayStation of the pet products world back in 2004.

s.def: The original PlayStation.

ety: From play + thing.

s.def: A thing or person intended for playing with.
A person at the mercy of fate.
ex: We talk of our energies and of our will—we are the mere playthings of subtle and malignant chances.

s.def: Used for the purpose of play or amusement.
ex: Like the cards which form a child's plaything palace, our pleasures are nicely balanced one upon the other.

ety: From play + time.

s.def: Time for play or diversion.
A time when children can play outside during the school day.
ex: The school bell rings to mark the end of playtime.

s.def: A duration of time when one is not as serious or committed as one could be, especially in a conflict of sorts.
ex: I thought I could go easy on you and win, but I suppose playtime is over.

s.def: The duration of a recording.
ex: The longest track on the album has a playtime of eight minutes.

ety: From play + wright (“builder, craftsman”).

s.def: A writer and creator of theatrical plays.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- Proto-Indo-European *-us Proto-Indo-European *pléth₂us Proto-Hellenic *plətús Ancient Greek πλᾰτῠ́ς (plătŭ́s) Ancient Greek πλᾰτεῖᾰ (plăteîă)bor. Latin plateaslbor. Spanish plazabor. English plaza Borrowed from Spanish plaza (“town-square or central place of gathering”), from Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), clipping of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Doublet of piatza, piazza, place, and platz.

s.def: A town's public square.
ex: Tourists gathered in the central plaza.
It's one of only three street plazas in the country, a new generation of parks for streetstyle skateboarding.
Someone set themself on fire Friday at the plaza in front of the US Supreme Court building, a court spokesperson said.

s.def: An open area used for gathering in a city, often having small trees and sitting benches.
A strip mall.
A shopping mall.
ex: The hotel overlooks a busy shopping plaza.

s.def: Initialism of programmable logic controller.
Initialism of public limited company.
Initialism of packet loss concealment.
Abbreviation of placebo.
Initialism of phospholipase C.
Initialism of prefecture-level city.
Initialism of power line communication.
Initialism of program-length commercial.

ety: From Middle English ple, from Old French plait, plaid, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc., Latin an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of placitus, past participle of placere (“to please”). Cognate with Spanish pleito (“lawsuit, suit”). Doublet of placit. See also please, pleasure.

s.def: An excuse; an apology.
ex: Necessity, the tyrant’s plea.
No Plea must serve; ’tis cruelty to spare.

s.def: An appeal, petition, urgent prayer or entreaty.
ex: Even if only one person answers my plea for someone to correspond with it will be a blessing.
a plea for mercy

s.def: That which is alleged or pleaded, in defense or in justification.
That which is alleged by a party in support of his cause.
An allegation of fact in a cause, as distinguished from a demurrer.
The defendant’s answer to the plaintiff’s declaration and demand.
A cause in court; a lawsuit; as, the Court of Common Pleas.
ex: they or any three of them shall be a Court and have cognizance of pleas real, personal, and mixed.

s.def: To plead; to argue.

ety: The verb is from Late Middle English pleshe, Middle English plechen, pleche (“to layer; to propagate (a plant) by layering, to pleach”), possibly from Anglo-Norman and Middle French plesser, plessier, Middle French plescer, variants of Middle French, Old French plaissier, plessier (“to plash”), from Late Latin *plaxus, from Latin plexus (“braided, plaited, woven; bent, twisted”), perfect passive participle of plectō (“to braid, plait, weave; to bend, turn, twist”). The noun is derived from the…

s.def: To unite by interweaving, as (horticulture) branches of shrubs, trees, etc., to create a hedge; to interlock, to plash.
ex: [I]n Messina, he pleaches Leonato's bower with honeysuckle; [...]

s.def: An act or result of interweaving; specifically, (horticulture) a hedge or lattice created by interweaving the branches of shrubs, trees, etc.
ex: Not a dryad of the beeches, / Through the filmy forest-reaches, / That a tress of summer pleaches, / But had owned her queen; [...]

s.def: A branch of a shrub, tree, etc., used for pleaching; a pleacher.
A notch cut into a branch so that it can be bent when pleaching is carried out.
ex: When laying hedges, notches (pleaches) are cut in branches that are to be bent (the bent bits must go upwards, otherwise the sap will not run).

ety: From Middle English pleden, plaiden, from Old French plaider (“to plead, offer a plea”), from plait, from Medieval Latin placitum (“a decree, sentence, suit, plea, etc.", in Classical Latin, "an opinion, determination, prescription, order; literally, that which is pleasing, pleasure”), neuter of placitus, past participle of placeō (“to please”). Cognate with Spanish pleitear (“to litigate, take to court”).

s.def: To present (an argument or a plea), especially in a legal case.
ex: The defendant has decided to plead not guilty.
O that one might plead for a man with God, as a man pleadeth for his neighbour!

s.def: To beg, beseech, or implore, especially emotionally.
ex: He pleaded with me not to leave the house.
He was pleading for mercy.

s.def: To offer by way of excuse.
ex: Not wishing to attend the banquet, I pleaded illness.
It is no defence to plead that you were only obeying orders.

s.def: To discuss by arguments.

ety: From Middle English plesaunte, from Old French plaisant. By surface analysis, please + -ant. Related to Dutch plezant (“full of fun or pleasure”). Partly displaced Old English wynsum, which became Modern English winsome.

s.def: Giving pleasure; pleasing in manner.
ex: We had a pleasant walk around the town.
It wasn't so hot outside, but pleasant enough to have lunch in the garden.
Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!

s.def: Facetious, joking.
A wit; a humorist; a buffoon.
ex: […] Galba was no better than one of the buffons or pleasants that professe to make folke merry and to laugh.

ety: From pleasant + -ry, probably modelled on Middle French plaisanterie.

s.def: A casual, courteous remark.
A playful remark; a jest.
Anything that promotes pleasure or merriment.

ety: From Middle English plesen, plaisen, borrowed from Old French plaise, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleHk- (“pleasingness, permission”). In this sense, displaced native Old English līcian, whence Modern English like.

s.def: To make happy or satisfy; to give pleasure to.
ex: Her presentation pleased the executives.
I'm pleased to see you've been behaving yourself.
Our new range of organic foods is sure to please.

s.def: To desire; to will; to be pleased by.
ex: Just do as you please.
He doesn't think, he just says whatever he pleases.
Whatsoeuer the Lord pleased, that did he in heauen and in earth: in the Seas, and all deepe places.

s.def: Used to make a polite request.
ex: Please, pass the bread.
Would you please sign this form?
Could you tell me the time, please?

s.def: interjection to make a polite request
Used as an affirmative to an offer.
ex: Near-synonym: thank you
May I help you? —(Yes,) please.
D'you mind if I open the window? —Please do.

s.def: An expression of annoyance, impatience, or exasperation.
ex: Oh, please, do we have to hear that again?
So it's safe to let a 10-year-old use a gun? Please.
So now I have to go back there a third time? Please!

s.def: Said as a request to repeat information.
ex: Customer while ordering: Can I get a [unintelligible]? Restaurant employee: Please?
Fellow: May I have a few days off to get married? Reply, in the Cincinnati idiom by a boss who had heard the sound but not the sense: Boss: Please?

s.def: A request for help.
A request for the interlocutor to repeat what the speaker says next. Often used in language training.
Used as request for the interlocutor to repeat what he or she said previously.
Offering a seat to somebody.
Used to ask the interlocutor to speak more slowly.
When giving directions to a person (for example, a taxi driver), indicates that he or she should turn left.
When giving directions to a person (for example, a taxi driver), indicates that he or she should turn right.

ety: From Middle English plesed, iplesed (past participle) and Middle English plesede (preterit), both equivalent to please + -ed.

s.def: Happy, content.
ex: She was pleased about her exam results.
I’m pleased to meet you at last.
They seemed pleased by the unexpected gift.

s.def: Agreeable, consenting (when referring to a monarch or other powerful person).
ex: The queen was pleased to accept the countess into her household as a lady-in-waiting.

der: is that a gun in your pocket or are you…

s.def: A polite formula used when being introduced to somebody.

ety: From Middle English plesynge, pleizinge, plesende (present participle), equivalent to please + -ing.

s.def: Agreeable; giving pleasure, cheer, enjoyment or gratification.
ex: These two designs were neat and handsome, by modern standards, and very pleasing in appearance.

s.def: present participle and gerund of please.
pleasure or satisfaction, as in the phrase "to someone's pleasing."

ety: Etymology tree English pleasure Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English pleasurable From pleasure + -able.

s.def: That gives pleasure
ex: The massage was a pleasurable experience.
c. 1620, Francis Bacon, letter of advice to Sir George Villiers Planting of orchards is very […] pleasurable.
At Rome every Pleasurable Female pays a Julio per Week to the Church […]

ety: From Early Modern English pleasur, plesur, alteration (with ending accommodated to -ure) of Middle English plaisir (“pleasure”), from Old French plesir, plaisir (“to please”), infinitive used as a noun, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-k- (“wide and flat”). Related to Dutch plezier (“pleasure, fun”). More at please.

s.def: A state of being pleased or contented; gratification.
ex: He remembered with pleasure his home and family.
I get a lot of pleasure from watching others work hard while I relax.
Maximize all the pleasure / Even with all this weather / Nothing can make it better / Maximize all the pleasure

s.def: Sexual enjoyment.
A person, thing or action that causes enjoyment.
ex: It was a pleasure to meet you.
Having a good night's sleep is one of life's little pleasures.
Festus, willing to do the Jews a pleasure

s.def: One's preference.
ex: What is your pleasure: coffee or tea?

s.def: The will or desire of someone or some agency in power.
ex: to hold an office at pleasure: to hold it indefinitely until it is revoked
to be imprisoned at Her Majesty's pleasure: to be imprisoned indefinitely
at Congress's pleasure: whenever or as long as Congress desires

s.def: pleased to meet you, "It's my pleasure"
To give or afford pleasure to.
ex: [H]e / [...] / Had tost his ball and flown his kite, and roll'd / His hoop to pleasure Edith, [...]

s.def: To give sexual pleasure to.
ex: Johnny pleasured Jackie with his mouth last night.

s.def: To take pleasure; to seek or pursue pleasure.
ex: to go pleasuring

s.def: The principle that human decisions and behavior are strongly motivated by the instinctual desire of the id, arising in infancy, to experience pleasure and avoid pain.
ex: They can’t seem to decide if the moral imperative is more crucial than the pleasure principle, or the other way around.
The pleasure principle is, on the whole, a sound one, then: having what you like is fine so long as you don't have too much of it in one go.

ety: From Middle English, from a variant of plait, from Old French pleit. Doublet of plait.

s.def: A fold in the fabric of a garment, usually a skirt, as a part of the design of the garment, with the purpose of adding controlled fullness and freedom of movement, or taking up excess fabric. There are many types of pleats, differing in their construction and appearance.
A similar fold in a filter, lampshade, or various other products.
A fold in an organ, usually a longitudinal fold in a long leaf such as that of palmetto, lending it stiffness.
A plait.
To form one or more pleats in a piece of fabric or a garment.
To plait.
ex: pleat my hair

ety: A clipping of plebeian and plebe, sometimes also understood as a back-formation from plebs.

s.def: A commoner; a member of the lower class of a society.
A common person; an unsophisticated or cultureless person.
ex: You're under my roof, you pleb.

s.def: A freshman cadet at a military academy.
ex: I found some of the novices, plebs they are called, home-sick, and weary with their discipline.
At Annapolis, the natives are crabs, the freshmen plebs, the sophomores youngsters.

s.def: Of or concerning the lower class of a society.
Undistinguished, commonplace, unsophisticated, vulgar, coarse.

ety: From Latin plēbs (“the plebeian class”), probably via Middle French plebe (“plebeians, commoners, the rabble”) and possibly later understood as a clipping of plebeian. Cognate with Italian plebe, Spanish plebe, Portuguese plebe.

s.def: A plebeian, a member of the lower class of Roman citizens.
The plebs, the plebeian class.
ex: All other roomes were free for the plebe or multitude.

s.def: The similar lower class of any area.
A freshman cadet at a military academy.
ex: My drill master, a young stripling, told me I was not so ‘gross’ as most other pleibs, the name of all new cadets.
Plebes spend their first summer at Cadet Basic Training — Beast Barracks — where they get soldierized.

ety: From Latin plēbēius (“a commoner; common”) + -an (adjective-forming suffix), from Latin plēbēs + -ius (adjective-forming suffix), possibly under the influence of Middle French plebeyen, plebein, plebien (“a commoner”) and plebeien (“concerning the common people”). Cf. Medieval Latin plēbēiānus (“a commoner”), from plēbēius + -ānus.

s.def: A member of the plebs, the common citizens of ancient Rome.
ex: Na plebeane will tak þe dochter of ane patriciane but hir consent. [No plebeian will take the daughter of any patrician but her consent]
The cognomen was first used in patrician families, who were distinguished from the plebeians by their three names.

s.def: A commoner, particularly (derogatory) a low, vulgar person.
Of or concerning the plebs, the common citizens of ancient Rome.
ex: To what purpose be the plebeian Magistrates ordeined?

s.def: Of or concerning the common people.
ex: ...priuate person or plebian multitude...

s.def: Common, particularly (derogatory) vulgar, crude, coarse, uncultured.
ex: For to plebeyan wits, it is as good, As to be silent, as not vnderstood.
[…] told me love was too plebeian / told me you were through with me

ety: Sense 1 (“referendum”) is borrowed from French plébiscite, from Latin plēbiscītum, plēbis scītum, plēbī scītum (“law of the common people or plebs”), from plēbis (the genitive singular of plēbs (“common people, plebeians”)) + scītum (“decree, ordinance, statute”). Sense 3 (“law enacted by the common people”) is a learned borrowing from Latin plēbiscītum: see above. It is attested earlier than English plebiscitum. Cognates * Italian plebiscito * Middle French plebiscite (modern French plébiscite…

s.def: A direct popular vote on an issue of public importance, such as an amendment to the constitution, a change in the sovereignty of the nation, or some government policy.
An expression of the public's views on an issue, whether legally binding or not.
Synonym of plebiscitum (“a law enacted by the common people, under the superintendence of a tribune or some subordinate plebeian magistrate, without the intervention of the senate”).

ety: From Latin plēbs (“the plebeian class”), variant of earlier plēbēs. Later also understood as the plural of pleb.

s.def: plural of pleb
The plebeian class of Ancient Rome or its equivalent in other ancient societies.
ex: Why I am going with my pidgeons to the tribunall Plebs.

s.def: The common people, especially (derogatory) the mob.
ex: For 'tis an Easier Thing To make Trees Leape, and Stones selfe-burthens bring (As once Amphion to the walls of Thæbes,)
1993, Max Cavalera, "Refuse/Resist", Sepultura, Chaos A.D. Chaos A.D. / Tanks On The Streets / Confronting Police / Bleeding The Plebs
The lesser plebs are not unscrupulous troublemakers.

ety: Borrowed from Latin plēctrum, from Ancient Greek πλῆκτρον (plêktron, “anything to strike with, an instrument for striking the lyre, a spear point”), from πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike, to smite, to sting”). Displaced native Old English sleġel.

s.def: A small piece of plastic, metal, ivory, etc., for plucking the strings of a guitar, lyre, mandolin, etc.
anatomical part
A projection of bone or other stiff tissue, such as the ridges in some insects' stridulatory organs.

ety: From Middle English plege, from Anglo-Norman plege, from Old French plege (Modern French pleige) from Medieval Latin plevium, plebium, from plebiō (“to pledge”), from Frankish *plehan (“to pledge; to support; to guarantee”). Akin to Old High German pflegan (“to take care of, be accustomed to”), Old Saxon plegan (“to vouch for”), Old English plēon (“to risk, endanger”). More at plight.

s.def: To make a solemn promise (to do something).
ex: pledge allegiance to the flag

s.def: To deposit something as a security; to pawn.
To give assurance of friendship by the act of drinking; to drink to one's health.
A solemn promise to do something.
An asset or person temporarily handed over to guarantee the fulfilment of something promised, under threat of permanent loss of the thing handed over; surety, security, hostage.
A bailment of personal property to secure payment of a debt without transfer of title.
A person who has taken a pledge of allegiance to a college fraternity, but is not yet formally approved.
A drinking toast.

ety: English dialect word for a small plug, using -et (“diminutive suffix”).

s.def: A small flat absorbent pad of cotton or wool, used to medicate, drain, or protect a wound or sore.
A string of oakum used in calking.
To apply a pledget to.

ety: From Latin Pleiades, from Ancient Greek Πλειάδες (Pleiádes). In the astronomical sense, displaced Old English seofonstierre (literally “the seven stars”).

s.def: The "seven sisters", companions of Artemis and daughters of the Titan Atlas and the sea-nymph Pleione.
An open cluster of hot blue stars in the constellation Taurus, and the most easily visible such cluster from Earth.
ex: The Pleiades and Hyades are sometimes spoken of as constellations, but this is a mistake; they are integral parts of Taurus.

ety: From Middle English plenarie, plenarye, from Late Latin plēnārius, from Latin plēnus (“full”).

s.def: Fully attended by a plenum; for everyone's attendance.
Complete; full; entire; absolute.
ex: The method of treating a subject should be plenary or full.

s.def: A plenary session.
ex: After lunch, we will all be in the main auditorium listening to the plenary.

s.def: Part of a lesson, usually at or towards the end, designed to review or evaluate the learning that has taken place.

ety: From Latin plēnilūnium (“full moon”).

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the full moon.
ex: He went ahead, his plenilunar buttocks tight in the very short shorts.

ety: From Medieval Latin plēnipotentiārius (“having full power”), Late Latin plēnipotēns, from plēnus (“full”) + potēns (“mighty, powerful”).

s.def: A person invested with full powers, especially as the diplomatic agent of a sovereign state, (originally) charged with handling a certain matter.
ex: None but the like-minded can come plenipotentiary to our court.
Two of them are hanging up there on Golgotha, and that ought to be enough to show the authority of Rome’s ah plenipotentiary.

s.def: Invested with full power.
ex: Near-synonyms: omnicompetent; omnipotent, almighty, all-powerful

s.def: Of or relating to a plenipotentiary agent

ety: From Middle English plenitude, that borrowed from Anglo-Norman plenitude, Middle French plenitude, and their source, Latin plēnitūdō.

s.def: Fullness; completeness.
ex: The idea that the love of Philimore had abated, when hers for him seemed in its plenitude, was a most severe aggravation of her misfortune.
Louis ignored him, recalling the parlements to the plenitude of their powers on 23 September.

s.def: Fullness (of the moon).
An abundance; a full supply.
ex: Mankind's old greatness was created in scarcity. But what may we expect from plenitude?

s.def: The metaphysical idea that the universe contains everything that is possible.

ety: From Middle English plentewos, plentevous, et al., circa 1300, from Old French plentiveus (“fertile, rich”) (early 13th century), from plentif (“abundant”), from plenté (“abundance”) (Modern French pleinté, English plenty), from Latin plenitatem, accusative of plenitas (“fullness”), from plenus (“complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

s.def: In plenty; abundant.
ex: His farm, though small, nevertheless allowed him a plenteous supply of healthy food.
Reaping plenteous crop.

s.def: Having plenty; abounding; rich.

ety: From Middle English plentiful, plentyfull, plentefull, equivalent to plenty + -ful.

s.def: Existing in large number or ample amount.
ex: a plentiful harvest
a plentiful supply of water
She accumulated a plentiful collection of books.

s.def: Yielding abundance; fruitful.
ex: Some years, the tree is a plentiful source of apples.
If it be a long winter, it is commonly a more plentiful year.

s.def: Lavish; profuse; prodigal.
ex: He that is plentiful in expenses will hardly be preserved from decay.

ety: From Anglo-Norman plent(é) + -y, from Middle English plentie, plentee, plente, from Anglo-Norman plenté, from Old French plenté, from Latin plēnitātem, accusative of plēnitās (“fullness”), from plenus (“complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”), from which English full also comes, via Proto-Germanic. Related to the Latin derivatives replenish, plenary, complete, deplete, replete.

s.def: A more-than-adequate amount; plenitude; a great deal.
ex: We are lucky to live in a land of peace and plenty.

s.def: More than enough.
ex: Acquire one of these and you'll have plenty of car for your money.

s.def: More than sufficiently.
ex: This office is plenty big enough for our needs.
For the likes of her, the down-at-heels support of Hoboken pier was plenty good enough.

s.def: Used as an intensifier, very.
ex: She was plenty mad at him.
Seeing clichés mimicked this skillfully is plenty hilarious.

s.def: much, enough
ex: There'll be plenty time later for that

s.def: many
ex: Get a manicure. Plenty men do it.

s.def: Plentiful.
ex: if reasons were as plenty as blackberries
Radishes are very plenty. Of cabbages a few heads of this year's crop have come to hand this week, and sold readily at quotations; […]

ety: From Latin plēnum n (“space filled with matter”), from plēnus (“full”). The sense of "legislative meeting" is a semantic loan from Russian пле́нум (plénum, “plenary session”), from the same Latin source.

s.def: A space that is completely filled with matter.
ex: The idea was that a thing could only move into an empty place, and that, in a plenum, there are no empty places.

s.def: A state of fullness, a great quantity (of something).
A legislative meeting (especially of the Communist Party) in which all members are present.
An enclosed space having greater than atmospheric pressure.
The space above a false ceiling used for cables, ducts etc.
A type of network cabling which satisfies a given plenum rating for the purpose of fire safety.

ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).

s.def: Redundancy in wording.
ex: St. Jerome and St. Augustine are both sparing in the employment of the device of pleonasm.
My salvation is in my Saviour who saveth me hence the redundancy and pleonasm of my asseveration.

s.def: A phrase involving pleonasm; a phrase containing one or more words which are redundant because their meaning is expressed elsewhere in the phrase.

ety: From pleonasm + -astic.

s.def: Of, or relating to pleonasm.
Redundant.
Characterised by the use of redundant words or an excessive number of words.
Any of the genus †Plesiosaurus of extinct long-necked marine reptiles from the Early Jurassic.
ex: "Plesiosaurus! A fresh-water plesiosaurus!" cried Summerlee.

ety: Borrowed from Late Latin plēthōra, from Ancient Greek πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “fullness, satiety”), from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to be full”) + -η (-ē, nominal suffix).

s.def: An excessive amount or number; an abundance.
ex: The menu offers a plethora of cuisines from around the world.
1817, Francis Jeffrey, review of Lalla Rookh, in the Edinburgh Review He labours under a plethora of wit and imagination.
The story of the woodhen is one outstanding conservation triumph in a plethora of tragedy.

s.def: Excess of blood in the skin, especially in the face and especially chronically.
ex: [Y]our Character at Present is like a Person in a Plethora, absolutely dying of too much Health—

ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Medieval Latin pleura.

s.def: Each of a pair of smooth serous membranes which line the thorax and envelop the lungs in humans and other mammals.
ex: The lungs […] may be said to be inclosed in separate bags, or to have distinct pleuras.

s.def: A lateral part in an animal body or structure.
plural of pleuron
The part of the thoracic cavity that surrounds the lungs and is enclosed by the pleurae.

ety: From Middle English pleuresi, pleresye, that borrowed from Old French pleuresie (French pleurésie), from Late Latin pleurisis, alteration of Latin pleuritis. By surface analysis, pleur- + -isy.

s.def: Inflammation of lung pleura.
ex: And the dope often gave him a painful case of pleurisy if he smoked it for more than two straight days of heavy continuous smoking[…]
Pleurisy usually causes pain, which is made worse by deep breathing, since the two inflamed layers of the pleura rub against each other.

ety: From pleuro- + pneumonia.

s.def: inflammation of the pleura and lungs; a combination of pleurisy and pneumonia, especially a kind of contagious and fatal lung disease of cattle and pigs, caused by infection by Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae
A city in northern Bulgaria.

ety: From Ancient Greek πλῆξις (plêxis, “stroke, percussion”) + -meter.

s.def: Something used to absorb the energy generated by the strike from a percussion hammer, during medical percussion. Usually this is simply the doctor's hand.

ety: From Hellenistic Ancient Greek πλῆξις (plêxis, “stroke”) + -or, after flexor etc.

s.def: A hammer (or other instrument) used to test a person's reflexes.
ex: Crowded in amongst his pocket's pens was the rubber head of a diagnostic plexor.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pel- Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ-der. Proto-Italic *plektōder. Latin plectō Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Italic *-tus Latin -tus Latin plexusbor. English plexus Borrowed from Latin plexus (“a twining, plaiting, braid”).

s.def: A network of anastomosing or interwoven nerves, blood vessels, or lymphatic vessels.
An interwoven combination of parts or elements in a structure or system.

s.def: To make plump; to fill (out) or support; often with up.
ex: to plump oysters or scallops by placing them in fresh or brackish water
to plump up the hollowness of their history with improbable miracles

s.def: To give a plumper (kind of vote).
To give (a vote), as a plumper.
To favor or decide in favor of.
To cast or let drop (something) all at once, suddenly and heavily.
ex: to plump a stone into water

s.def: To drop or fall suddenly or heavily, all at once.
ex: September 24, 1712, The Spectator No. 492, letter from a prude Dulcissa plumps into a chair.

ety: From Latin plūmula, diminutive of plūma (“feather”); compare French plumule. By surface analysis, plume + -ule.

s.def: The first bud, or growing point, of a plant embryo, situated above the cotyledons.
A down feather.
The aftershaft of a feather.
One of the featherlike scales of certain male butterflies.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *plew- Proto-Indo-European *plewk-der. Proto-Indo-European *plewk-smeh₂ Proto-Italic *plouksmā Latin plūma Anglo-Norman plumebor. Middle English plume English plume English -y English plumy From plume + -y.

s.def: Covered or adorned with plumes, or as with plumes; feathery.

ety: Recorded since 1632 during the Thirty Years War, native British use since the Cromwellian Civil War. Borrowed from German plündern (“to loot”), from Middle High German, from Middle Low German plunderen, from a noun originally meaning "household goods, bedding, clothing," of obscure ultimate origin. This is first attested in medieval records, and according to Gijsseling, is therefore attested too late to be considered a substrate word. Due to the lack of obvious cognates in other languages from…

s.def: To pillage, take or destroy all the goods of, by force (as in war); to raid, sack.
ex: The mercenaries plundered the small town.
The shopkeeper was plundered of his possessions by the burglar.

s.def: To take by force or wrongfully; to commit robbery or looting, to raid.
ex: “Now to plunder, mateys!” screamed a buccaneer, to cries of “Arrgh!” and “Aye!” all around.

s.def: To take (goods) by pillage.
ex: The mercenaries plundered all the goods they found.

s.def: To make extensive (over)use of, as if by plundering; to use or use up wrongfully.
ex: The miners plundered the jungle for its diamonds till it became a muddy waste.

s.def: To take unexpectedly.
ex: The Serb teed up Steve Davis, who crossed low for Graziano Pellè to plunder his fifth league goal of the campaign.

s.def: To amass ill-gotten wealth (by public officials) through a combination or series of overt criminal acts.
The loot attained by plundering.
ex: The Hessian kept his choicest plunder in a sack that never left his person, for fear that his comrades would steal it.

s.def: An instance of plundering.
Baggage; luggage.
The commission of plunder (verb definition 6).

ety: From Middle English plungen, ploungen, Anglo-Norman plungier, from Old French plongier, (Modern French plonger), from unattested Late Latin frequentative *plumbicō (“to throw a leaded line”), from plumbum (“lead”). Compare plumb, plounce.

s.def: To dive, leap or rush (into water or some liquid); to submerge oneself.
ex: he plunged into the river

s.def: To thrust into liquid, or into any penetrable substance; to immerse.
ex: to plunge the body into water
"Most of them don't wash. Those who do usually plunge their head into some brook or rill, if there happens to be one about."

s.def: To cast, stab or throw deep and fast into some thing, state, condition or action.
ex: to plunge a dagger into the breast
He flicked a switch and the room was plunged into darkness.
to plunge a nation into war

s.def: To baptize by immersion.
To fall or rush headlong into some thing, action, state or condition.
ex: to plunge into debt
to plunge into controversy
profits plunge 90%

s.def: To pitch or throw oneself headlong or violently forward, as a horse does.
To bet heavily and recklessly; to risk large sums in gambling.
To entangle or embarrass (mostly used in past participle).
ex: Plunged and gravelled with three lines of Seneca.

s.def: To overwhelm, overpower.
The act of plunging or submerging.

ety: Etymology tree English plunge Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English plunger From plunge + -er.

s.def: A device that is used to remove blockages from the drain of a basin or tub, by suction.
The internal piece of a syringe that pushes out or pulls in any contents.
The sliding activator of an exploder, an electrical generator used to trigger electrical detonators such as blasting caps.
Certain equipment for brewing coffee.
One who plunges; a diver.
A horse that plunges, or throws itself suddenly forward.
A cavalryman.
A device similar to a piston but without a mechanism; a long solid cylinder used, instead of a piston or bucket, as a forcer in pumps.
The moving portion of a solenoid.
The spring-loaded assembly that propels the ball onto the table.

ety: Onomatopoeic; the noun is attested earlier than the verb. Noun etymology 1, noun sense 3 (“dollar; large sum of money”) may refer to the sound of a coin hitting a surface. Compare plonk, plink. As regards verb etymology 1, verb sense 1.4 (“(transitive) to drop, set, or throw (something, or oneself) abruptly and/or heavily”) and etymology 1, verb sense 2.4 (“(intransitive) to drop, land, or set abruptly and/or heavily”), compare French plonquer (Picardy), a variant of plonger (“to plunge”).

s.def: A (heavy) blow or hit.
A large sum of money.
A brief, dull sound, such as the sound of a string of a stringed instrument being plucked, or the thud of something landing on a surface.
ex: They listened and could hear the steady plunk, plunk of an axe somewhere far above them.

s.def: A dollar.
ex: Den I gives him a five-plunk piece, and he gins me the shange.
Dere's a loidy here […] dat's got a necklace of jools what's wort' a hundred t'ousand plunks. Honest, boss. A hundred t'ousand plunks.

s.def: With a brief, dull sound, such as the thud of something landing on a surface.
Directly, exactly, precisely.
Often reduplicated: used to represent a brief, dull sound, such as the sound of a string of a stringed instrument being plucked, or the thud of something landing on a surface.
ex: Look at me; is my eye dilated? do you notice a quiver anywhere? Feel my pulse: plunk—plunk—plunk—same as if I were asleep.
John, swinging the axe, plunk, plunk, plunk, was chopping the thinner branches all to the same length.

s.def: To pluck and quickly release (a string of a stringed instrument); also, to play (a stringed instrument) by plucking strings; to play (a piano, etc.) by striking keys; or, to play (a note or tune) on such an instrument.
ex: Her friends were boggled by how long it took her to plunk out simple texts, but Kate says she learned skills her peers have never had to master.

s.def: Often followed by down: to drop, set, or throw (something, or oneself) abruptly and/or heavily into or on to a surface or some other thing, making a dull sound; to plump.
ex: Enrique plunked his money down on the counter with a sigh and bellied up to the bar.
Exhausted, she plunked herself on the sofa.

s.def: To hit or injure (someone or something); also, to shoot (someone or something) with a firearm.
ex: Say, I jes' jumped d' bar, an' d' way I plunked [hit] dat bloke was outa sight. See? Dat's right! In d' jaw!

ety: From Middle English plurelle, from Old French plurel (“plural”), Borrowed from Latin plūrālis (“of or belonging to more than one, belonging to many”, adjective), from plūs, plūris (“more”) + -ālis.

s.def: Consisting of or containing more than one of something.
ex: The notion of culture is one whose meanings are plural and shifting.

s.def: In systems of number, not singular or not singular or dual.
ex: English nouns usually have singular and plural forms.

s.def: Pluralistic.
ex: Although the nation was far more plural than Canada in the number of its Christian groups
The Hong Kong and Singapore markets are way more "plural" than most Western economies, but they have not led to pluralistic politics.
History is perhaps more plural than traditionally imagined, leaving room for more groups to express their story.

s.def: Having some form of multiplicity, especially dissociative identity disorder.
A word in the form in which it potentially refers to something other than one person or thing; and other than two things if the language has a dual form.
ex: The plural of 'cat' is 'cats', but the plural of 'child' is 'children'.

s.def: The plural number. In English, referring to more or less than one of something.
A person with some form of multiplicity, particularly dissociative identity disorder.

ety: From Latin plūrāle tantum (“plural as such; plural only”), from plūrāle + tantum.

s.def: A noun (either in certain of its senses or in all its senses) that does not generally have a singular form.

ety: Etymology tree English plural Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English pluralism From plural + -ism.

s.def: The quality or state of being plural, or in the plural number.
The state of a pluralist; the holding of more than one ecclesiastical living at a time.
A social system that permits smaller groups within a society to maintain their individual cultural identities.
ex: Instead, it is more probable that globalization is leading to a plurality of pluralisms.

s.def: The belief that there should be diverse and competing centers of power in society.
The acknowledgement of a diversity of political systems.
The existence of differing legal systems in a population or area.
The belief that values can be simultaneously antagonistic and incommensurable.
ex: Pluralism is a creative force because it admits of multiple ways to see a thing, multiple valuable paths to choose from.

s.def: The belief that a plural predicate refers to its individuals rather than to a collective.

ety: From plural + -ity, from Middle English pluralite, from Old French pluralité (“multitude, state of being plural”), from Latin plūrālitās.

s.def: The state of being plural.
ex: Nominal plurality in Basque is originally exclusively marked on definite determiners and not on nouns.

s.def: The holding of multiple benefices.
A state of being numerous.
A number or part of a whole which is greater than any other number or part, but not necessarily a majority.

A number of votes for a single candidate or position which is greater than the number of votes gained by any other single candidate or position voted for, but which is less than a majority of valid votes cast.
A margin by which a number exceeds another number, especially of votes.
A group of many entities: a large number.
ex: A plurality of ideas were put forth at the meeting, most of which were rejected out of hand.

s.def: A group composed of more than one entity.
ex: The array is organized into a plurality of vertical (column) blocks.

s.def: Polygamy.
Synonym of multiplicity (“the condition whereby a person displays or experiences multiple distinct personalities or selves in one body”).
ex: In this paper I argue that hearing voices experiences and plurality are part of a broad, rich, and complex spectrum of human experience, […]
People often find it easiest to recognise plurality in themselves when they reflect on how they behave in different relationships or situations.

ety: Etymology tree English plural Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English pluralize From plural + -ize.

s.def: To make plural.
ex: The word "orange" can be pluralized into "oranges".

s.def: To take a plural; to assume a plural form.
ex: Nouns pluralize in English, but verbs do not.

s.def: To multiply; to make manifold.
To hold more than one ecclesiastical benefice at the same time.
Official name of Bolivia: a country in South America.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-yōs Proto-Indo-European *pléh₁yōs Proto-Italic *plēōs Old Latin plousder. Latin plūsbor. English plus Borrowed from Latin plūs (“more”).

s.def: And; sum of the previous one and the following one.
ex: Two plus two equals four.
A water molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms plus one of oxygen.

s.def: With; having in addition.
ex: I've won a holiday to France plus five hundred euros in spending money!

s.def: Being positive rather than negative or zero.
ex: −2 * −2 = +4 ("minus 2 times minus 2 equals plus four")

s.def: And also; in addition; besides (which).
ex: Let's go home now. It's late, plus I'm not feeling too well.

s.def: A positive quantity.
ex: The figures show a plus.
But the pluses far outweigh the criticisms.

s.def: An asset or useful addition.
ex: He is a real plus to the team.
Look at Trife. He's got two felonies. That means he's finished in society. But he can rap. His two felonies, in rap, man, that's a plus.

s.def: A plus sign: +.
Abbreviation of LGBT+
Positive, or involving advantage.
ex: He is a plus factor.

s.def: Electrically positive.
ex: A battery has both a plus pole and a minus pole.

s.def: The symbol + used to denote the operation of addition, to indicate that a number is positive, and so on.

ety: From French peluche (“fluff, plush”). The fact that historically (in past centuries) plush upholstery was so expensive as to be socially exclusive undoubtedly connects the senses of "luxurious" and "soft".

s.def: Very extravagant.
Very expensive, or appearing expensive; opulent, luxurious.
ex: They lived in a plush apartment complex.

s.def: Having a soft, fluffy exterior (of a man-made object, especially stuffed animals or upholstery).
ex: This plush toy is so cute and soft — I want it!

s.def: A textile fabric with a nap or shag on one side, longer and softer than the nap of velvet.
A plush toy.
ex: […] L.A. Prop Cinema Storage, full of kids' clothing (mostly for girls), PJs, and lots of toys and plushes (there's also a substantial infant area).

s.def: To give a soft, fluffy surface to.
ex: Green moss plushed the boulders that were stewn ^([sic]) about, reaching up to splash the cliffs with a velvet mantle.

s.def: A soft toy with a soft, plush covering.

ety: Originally coined in 2006 by the American Dialect Society, in reference to Pluto's demotion from planet status, defeating climate canary for Word of the Year.

s.def: To demote or devalue something.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploûtos) Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Ancient Greek -ων (-ōn) Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn)bor. Latin Plūtōbor. Middle English Pluto English Pluto From Middle English Pluto, Pluton, from Latin Plūtō, from Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn, “god of the underworld”). Doublet of Plouton. Venetia Burney is often credited as having suggested the name for the celestial body.

s.def: The Greco-Roman god of the underworld.
The largest dwarf planet and formerly the ninth planet, represented by the symbol ♇ or ⯓, both now used mostly in astrology.
The American cartoon character created by Walt Disney and Norm Ferguson.

ety: From Ancient Greek πλουτοκρατία (ploutokratía, “rule of the wealthy”), from πλουτοκρατέω (ploutokratéō, “I rule through wealth”), from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth”) + κρατέω (kratéō, “I rule”) (from κράτος (krátos, “power”, “might”)).

s.def: Government by the wealthy.
A controlling class of the wealthy.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn)bor. Latin Plūtōbor. Middle English Pluto English Pluto English -oid English plutoid From Pluto + -oid.

s.def: A trans-Neptunian dwarf planet.

ety: Back-formation from Plutonic.

s.def: A body of igneous rock formed beneath the surface of the earth by consolidation of magma

ety: See Plutonic.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Plutonic.
Containing plutonium in a higher oxidation state.

ety: From Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn, “Pluto, Greek and Roman god of the underworld”) (from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “riches, wealth”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to fly; to flow; to run”)) + -ων (-ōn)) + -ic (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). The English word is cognate with Middle French plutonique (modern French plutonique (“of or pertaining to Pluto, the underworld, or the interior of the Earth”)).

s.def: Of or pertaining to rocks formed deep in the Earth's crust, rather than by volcanoes at the surface of the Earth.
ex: These cliffs, I may remark, are basaltic, and therefore plutonic.

s.def: Synonym of Plutonian (“of or relating to Pluto, the Greek and Roman god of the underworld; demonic, infernal”).
Synonym of Plutonian (“of, relating to, or having characteristics associated with the underworld; dark, gloomy; mournful”).
ex: a dark, handsome lady, of no little majesty, and rather like a plutonic Madonna

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or supporting plutonism (“the theory that the rocks of the Earth were formed in fire by volcanic activity, with a continuing gradual process of weathering and erosion, then deposited on the sea bed, re-formed into layers of sedimentary rock by heat and pressure, and raised again”…

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploûtos) Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Ancient Greek -ων (-ōn) Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn)bor. Latin Plūtōbor. Middle English Pluto English Pluto English -n- Proto-Indo-European *-om Proto-Italic *-om Latin -umder. English -ium English plutonium After Pluto (dwarf planet) + -n- + -ium. More in Wikipedia at plutonium § History.

s.def: The transuranic chemical element with atomic number 94 and symbol Pu: a silvery-gray fissile radioactive actinide metal that tarnishes when exposed to air.
ex: Plutonium? You mean this sucker's nuclear?

s.def: Alternative form of ploutonion.

ety: Borrowed from French pluvial, from Middle French pluvial, borrowed from Latin pluviālis (“pertaining to rain”).

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or produced by rain.
Occurring through the action of rain.
a rainy period

ety: From Latin pluvius (“rain”) + -meter.

s.def: A scientific instrument for measuring the amount of rainfall.

ety: From Middle English pleit, plit, plite (“a fold, pleat, wrinkle; braid, strand in a braided cord, ply”), from Anglo-Norman pli, plei, pleit, and Middle French pli, ploy, ply (“a fold, pleat; joint in armour; situation, state”) (modern French pli (“a fold, pleat”)), from plier, ployer (“to bend, fold”), from Latin plicāre (“to bend, fold, roll up”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to fold, plait, weave”).

s.def: A layer of material.
ex: two-ply toilet paper
The designer critic's staff would come in with, for example, loads of three-ply cashmere. The students weren't even selecting their own fabrics.

s.def: A strand that, twisted together with other strands, makes up rope or yarn.
Clipping of plywood.
ex: The compartment ceiling panels are of plastic material backed with ply or hardboard panels.

s.def: In two-player sequential games, a "half-turn" or a move made by one of the players.
ex: He proposed to build Deep Purple, a super-computer capable of 24-ply look-ahead for chess.

s.def: A condition, a state.
To bend; to fold; to mould; (figuratively) to adapt, to modify; to change (a person's) mind, to cause (a person) to submit.
To bend, to flex; to be bent by something, to give way or yield (to a force, etc.).
To work at (something) diligently.
ex: He plied his trade as carpenter for forty-three years.

s.def: To wield or use (a tool, a weapon, etc.) steadily or vigorously.
ex: He plied his ax with bloody results.
[T]his abuse is as outrageous as are the acts of any Ku-Klux that ever plied the lash or sounded a whistle, […]

s.def: To press upon; to urge persistently.
ex: to ply someone with questions or solicitations

ety: Etymology tree English ply Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *h₁weydʰh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-us Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)wéydʰ(h₁)us Proto-Germanic *widuz Proto-West Germanic *widu Old English widu Old English wudu Middle English wode English wood English plywood From ply (“sheet”) + wood.

s.def: Construction material supplied in sheets, and made of three or more layers of wood veneer glued together, laid up with alternating layers having their grain perpendicular to each other.
ex: After the hurricane there was a severe regional shortage of plywood, especially exterior plywood.

s.def: A specific grade or type of this construction material.
ex: We stock exterior plywoods, interior plywoods, and furniture plywoods.

s.def: To fit or block up with plywood.
Initialism of pissing myself laughing (used to indicate great amusement).
Abbreviation of mean sea level pressure (derived from the notation P_(MSL)).

ety: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “I blow, breathe”). Doublet of neume.

s.def: A neume.
ex: With swaying arms they wail in pneuma over the recreant Bloom.

s.def: The spirit or soul.
ex: But bound to reach out and beyond this flesh. / Become Pneuma

s.def: One of three levels of a human being, the spirit, along with the body and soul.

ety: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breath”).

s.def: Of, relating to, or resembling air or other gases
Of or relating to pneumatics
Powered by, or filled with, compressed air
ex: a pneumatic instrument or engine

s.def: Having cavities filled with air
ex: pneumatic cells or bones

s.def: Spiritual; of or relating to the pneuma
well-rounded; full-breasted; bouncy
ex: Her almost pneumatic bust tightened itself, and she was quite prepared to say uncharitable things, as she saw Felicia enter.
"Every one says I'm awfully pneumatic," said Lenina reflectively, patting her own legs.
This short but pneumatic woman had killed six men and yet for some reason he wasn't afraid.

s.def: A vehicle, such as a bicycle, whose wheels are fitted with pneumatic tyres.
In the gnostic theologian Valentinus' triadic grouping of man, the highest type; a person focused on spiritual reality (the other two being hylic and psychic).

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *plew- Proto-Indo-European *-mṓ Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō Ancient Greek πλεύμων (pleúmōn) ▲ Ancient Greek πνέω (pnéō)influ. ▲ Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma)influ. Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn)bor. English pneumo- From Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”).

s.def: Relating to the lungs.

ety: From pneumo- + -coccus.

s.def: A gram-positive bacterium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, that causes pneumonia and other infectious diseases

ety: Alteration of pneumonoconiosis, after pneumo- (“lung”). Compare French pneumoconiose. By surface analysis, pneumo- + coniosis (“disease caused by the inhalation of dust”).

s.def: A disease of the lungs caused by inhalation of particulate matter.

ety: From pneumo- + gastric.

s.def: Of or pertaining to the lungs and the stomach
vagus (attributive)

The pneumogastric nerve; one of the tenth pair of cranial nerves which are distributed to the pharynx, esophagus, larynx, lungs, heart, stomach, liver, and spleen, and, in fishes and many amphibia, to the branchial apparatus and also to the sides of the body.

ety: From pneumology + -ical.

s.def: Relating to pulmonology.

ety: From New Latin pneumologia, from Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -logia (“-logy”). By surface analysis, pneumo- + -logy.

s.def: The study of the respiratory system and organs.

ety: From Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía, “lung disease”), from πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -ία (-ía).

s.def: Inflammation of the lungs caused by viruses, bacteria or other infectious microorganisms.
ex: He had always been remarkably immune from such little ailments, and had only once in his life been ill, of a vicious pneumonia long ago at school.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *plew- Proto-Indo-European *-mṓ Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō Ancient Greek πλεύμων (pleúmōn) ▲ Ancient Greek πνέω (pnéō)influ. ▲ Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma)influ. Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn)bor. English pneumo- Ancient Greek θώρᾱξ (thṓrāx)bor. Latin thoraxder. English thorax English pneumothorax From pneumo- + thorax.

s.def: Presence of air inside the pleural cavity, usually caused by injury either to the lung or the chest wall.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Πνύξ (Pnúx); since ancient times it has been claimed the word is derived from πυκνός (puknós, “close-packed; dense; thick”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *puḱ- (“to press together”), but the Oxford English Dictionary considers this a folk etymology with no evidence supporting it.

s.def: A hill in Athens west of the Acropolis with a stone platform and steps set into its side, which was used as the meeting place of the democratic assembly in Ancient Greece.

ety: From Italian Po, from Latin Padus.

s.def: The longest river in Italy, which flows 652 kilometers eastward to the Adriatic Sea near Venice.
A large plain that occupies most of northern Italy south of the Alps, surrounding the river Po.

ety: From Middle English pochen (“to poach (eggs)”), from Old French pocher "to put (egg yolks) in pockets" (i.e. in bags formed by the whites), from Old French poche (“pocket”).

s.def: To cook (something) in simmering or very hot liquid (usually water; sometimes wine, broth, or otherwise).
To be cooked in such manner.
The act of cooking in simmering liquid.
ex: Peaches are so perfect they need very little to make them extra special—just a quick poach in basil-scented rosé wine and a few adoring strawberries.

s.def: To trespass on another's property to take fish or game.
To take game or fish illegally.
To take anything illegally or unfairly.
To intrude; to interfere; to get involved inappropriately, without welcome.
ex: to poach in foreign academic disciplines

s.def: To entice (an employee or customer) to switch from a competing company to one's own.
ex: What's going on here? Are you trying to poach my teamaker?

s.def: To make soft or muddy by trampling.
ex: Cattle coming to drink had punched and poached the river bank into a mess of mud.
the poach'd filth that floods the middle street

s.def: To become soft or muddy by being trampled on.
ex: Chalky and clay lands […] chap in summer, and poach in winter.

s.def: An egg that has been cooked by gently breaking it into simmering or very hot water.

ety: Etymology tree English poach Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English poacher From poach + -er.

s.def: A person who trespasses in order to take game illegally, one who poaches; a person who illegally takes animals or plants from the wild.
A vessel with shallow cuplike compartments in which eggs are cooked over boiling water.
An attacker with good movement inside the penalty box.
ex: Cubarsí’s shot bounces awkwardly in front of him but there’s not a lot of power behind it. Merino, a veritable poacher these days, is there first.

ex: If you want to have a go right now, then Famitracker will let you compose songs for the NES and it'll run on a Windows-operated potato.

s.def: To hit very hard; to pummel.
ex: Bradshaw doesn't find much humour in it though, and beats the tar out of Dustin, potatoing him with every blow.

s.def: To hit with a thrown or fired potato.
The rhythmic sound produced by a V-twin engine—a distinctive deep, throaty exhaust note.

der: all that and a bag of potato chips

s.def: A thin slice of potato that has been deep-fried until it is brittle and crispy, and which is eaten when cool; they are typically packaged and sold as a snack.
ex: Edward, give me another of those delicious olives. / What's that? Potato crisps? No, I can't endure them.

s.def: A utensil used to mash potatoes.
A type of stick hand grenade resembling such a utensil.
ex: ‘A hand-grenade. One of those potato-mashers. It just blew the whole side of my foot off.’

s.def: A salad made from chopped boiled potatoes and a variety of other ingredients in a dressing.
A widely diffused vegetable substance found in the extracted material of potatoes used in cooking.

ety: From pot + belly.

s.def: A large, protruding, or swollen abdomen; a paunch.
Ellipsis of potbelly stove.
Ellipsis of Vietnamese pot-bellied pig.

ety: From pot + boy.

s.def: A boy or man employed in a public house to collect empty pots or glasses.
ex: (“Hoo-roa,” ejaculates a pot-boy in a parenthesis, “put the kye-bosh on her, Mary.”)

s.def: A boy employed in a plant nursery to tap clay pots with a stick for their ringing sound, indicating whether the plant required watering.
ex: GC&HTJ 1985 volume 198 page 17

s.def: A boy employed as waiter to serve (pots of) drinks, as in a tavern.
ex: I put on my kitchen potboy disguise and rode down to B-1 in an elevator that smelled like chicken soup, barbecue sauce, and Jack Daniel's.

ety: Borrowed from Latin potentia. Doublet of Potenza.

s.def: Power, authority.
ex: I would to heauen I had your potencie, And you were Isabell: should it then be thus? No: I would tell what 'twere to be a Iudge, and what a prisoner.
Beset on either hand by potencies greater than himself, he becomes the battle-ground of immortals.
The doctor is the modern master of the mythological realm, the knower of all the secret ways and words of potency.

s.def: The ability or capacity to perform something
ex: Pliny the Elder states that, to increase sexual potency, the right testis of an ass should be worn in a bracelet.

s.def: Concentration; strength
Potentiality, ability, capacity.
Cardinality.

ety: From Middle English potent, borrowed from Latin potens, potentis (“powerful, strong, potent”), present participle of posse (“to be able”), from potis (“able, powerful, originally a lord, master”).

s.def: Powerful; possessing power; effective.

s.def: Able to procreate.
Able to differentiate.
A prince; a potentate.
ex: Cry, havock , kings! back to the stained field, You equal potents

s.def: A staff or crutch.
A heraldic fur formed by a regular tessellation of blue and white T shapes.

ety: From Middle English potentat, from Old French, from Late Latin potentātus (“rule, political power”), from Latin potēns (“powerful, strong”), the active present participle of possum (“to be able”).

s.def: A powerful leader; a monarch; a ruler.
A powerful polity or institution.
A self-important person.
Someone acting in an important role.
ex: "Those foreigners," thought the female potentate of the Sun, "won't know what to order; but I'll show them what a good supper is."

s.def: Regnant, powerful, dominant.

s.def: A currently unrealized ability (with the most common adposition being to).
ex: Even from a young age it was clear that she had the potential to become a great musician.
Comrades, our own fleet doesn't know our full potential. They will do everything possible to test us, but they will only test their own embarrassment.

s.def: The gravitational potential: the radial (irrotational, static) component of a gravitational field, also known as the Newtonian potential or the gravitoelectric field.

The work (energy) required to move a reference particle from a reference location to a specified location in the presence of a force field, for example to bring a unit positive electric charge from an infinite distance to a specified point against an electric field.
A verbal construction or form stating something is possible or probable.
Existing in possibility, not in actuality.
ex: The heroic man,—and is not every man, God be thanked, a potential hero?—has to do so, in all times and circumstances.

s.def: Being potent; endowed with energy adequate to a result
irrotational

s.def: irrotational (see potential flow on Wikipedia)
ex: The non-viscous flow of the vacuum should be potential (irrotational).
