the synergistic effect of two drugs given simultaneously

ety: Borrowed from translingual Potentilla, from Latin potentilla, from potēns (“strong”) + -illa (dimintuive suffix).

s.def: Any of many shrubs and herbs of the genus Potentilla; the cinquefoils.
ex: Potentilla, for instance, used to drive out the demon of fever, was also good against witches.

ety: First sense appears c. 1957 in the writings of Jack Gelber. Third sense appears c. 1639.

s.def: A person who smokes cannabis frequently, or to excess.
ex: That pothead Shane has a nasty bong.

s.def: An electric motor's terminal connection or wiring box.
A stupid individual; a fool.

ety: Origin uncertain. Compare Dutch peuteren (“to rummage, poke”), and English potter, pudder.

s.def: A commotion, a tempest.
ex: Let the great gods, / That keep this dreadful pother o’er our heads, / Find out their enemies now.
(name of the article) Flight Of Hess Causes Pother Among Germans

s.def: To make a bustle or stir; to be fussy.
To puzzle or perplex.

ety: From pot + herb.

s.def: Any plant whose leaves, stems or flowers may be used as a culinary herb.
ex: It is laid out in sections covering aromatics, potherbs, oils, resins, pitch, [...] vinegar and wine.

ety: From dialectal pot (“pit, hollow, cavity”) + hole. The "cave" senses, attested since at least 1809 (as pot-hole), may be from Middle English pot, potte (“a deep hole for a mine, or from peat-digging”), of uncertain origin; perhaps related to English pit, pote, or pot. Compare Scots pott, patt (“a pit dug in the ground; coalpit”).

s.def: A shallow pit or other edged depression in a road's surface, especially when caused by erosion, weather or traffic.
ex: I was so tired that potholes, fumes and noise aside, I slept regardless, my head rag-dolling from side to side.

s.def: A pit formed in the bed of a turbulent stream.
A vertical cave system, often found in limestone.
A pit resulting from unauthorized excavation by treasure-hunters or vandals.
A shallow hole dug for the purpose of prospecting for opal or gold.
A hyperlink with text displayed on a page that is different from the title of the page to which the text links; a piped link.
A hole or recess on the top of a stove into which a pot may be placed.

ety: From pot + hook.

s.def: An S-shaped iron hook used to suspend a cooking pot over a fire.
A crooked stroke in writing; a scrawl.

ety: Borrowed from Georgian ფოთი (poti).

s.def: A port city in the region of Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti, Georgia, located on the eastern Black Sea coast; built near the site of the ancient Greek colony of Phasis.

ety: From Middle English pocioun, borrowed from Old French pocion, from Latin pōtiō (“a drinking”), pōtiōnis, from pōtāre (“to drink”). Displaced native Old English drenċ whence Modern English drench. Doublet of poison.

s.def: A small portion or dose of a liquid which is medicinal, poisonous, or magical.
ex: He hoped to win the princess's heart by mixing the love potion the witch gave him into her drink.
Everything changed when I found this potion that gives me a huge speed boost whenever I drink it.

s.def: To drug (someone).

ety: The noun is borrowed from Chinook Jargon potlatch, pátlač (“to give; gift; gift-giving ceremony, potlatch”), from Nootka Jargon pa'chatle, pa'chēētle, pah-chilt (“to give, give me”), from Nootka p̕ačiƛ (“to give a gift during a potlatch ceremony”). Sense 1 of the verb (“to give; especially, to give a gift during a potlatch ceremony”) is borrowed from Chinook Jargon potlatch, pátlač (see above); sense 2 (“to carry out or take part in a potlatch ceremony”) is derived from the noun.

s.def: A ceremony amongst certain indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest in which gifts are bestowed upon guests and personal property is destroyed in a show of generosity and wealth.
ex: That night there was a grand wedding and a potlach; so that for two days to follow there was no fishing done by the village.

s.def: A communal meal to which guests bring dishes to share; a potluck.
To give; especially, to give as a gift during a potlatch ceremony.
ex: He was a Chilkaht chief, and it being New Year's day, he had been to General Davis's house and "potlatched" (treated) to a bottle of whiskey.
I came to see if you can potlatch any old sword, and hi-yu buttons [plenty buttons].

s.def: To carry out or take part in a potlatch ceremony.
ex: Natives did not get their wheels into the water until the [salmon] run was nearly over; were all potlaching until the latter part of July.

ety: From pot + luck. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, sense 3 (“a shared meal consisting of whatever guests have brought”) is unlikely to have been influenced by potlatch.

s.def: A meal, especially one offered to a guest, consisting of whatever food is available.
ex: Here are some leftover beans and meat; we can make a good potluck stew from them.
Me, to pot-luck, may any friend invite: / The treat, I can return, is my delight.

s.def: Whatever is available in a particular situation.
A shared meal consisting of whatever guests have brought (sometimes without prior arrangement); a potlatch; also, a dish of food brought to such a meal.

s.def: The last draft or portion of an alcoholic beverage in a pot or other drinking vessel.
To take part in a potluck, where each participant brings a meal to be shared by all.

ety: From French pot-pourri (“stew, potpourri”), a calque of Spanish olla podrida (“stew”, literally “rotten pot”). Doublet of olla podrida.

A mixture of dried fragrant plant material, often in a decorative bowl, used to scent a room.
A ragout or stew of meat and vegetables.
A collection of various things; an assortment, mixed bag or motley.

s.def: An anthology of miscellaneous prose.

ety: From Middle English pot-sherd, pot-schord, pot scherd, pot scarth, from Middle English pot, pote, potte (“a container, pot, vessel; especially an earthenware vessel”) (from late Old English pot, pott (“a pot”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *budn- (“a type of vessel”)) + Middle English sherd (“piece of fired clay or broken earthenware; potsherd”) (from Old English sceard (“a shard, sherd”), from Proto-Germanic *skardą (“a nick, notch”)); equivalent to pot + sherd (“shard”).

ety: From Middle English pottage, from Anglo-Norman and Old French potage, equivalent to pot + -age.

ety: From pot + -ed. Adjective meaning "prepared in advance" by analogy with potted meat (canned meat), first used in a published work by L. ety: From Old French poterie, from potier (“potter”), from the root of pot, equivalent to pot + -ery. First attested in the 13th century.

ety: From Middle English potell, potel, from Old French potel, diminutive of pot; see more at pot.

ety: From pot (“chamberpot”) + -y (diminutive suffix).

ety: From Middle English pult, a variant of pulet, polet, from Old French poulet (“young fowl”), diminutive of poule (“hen”), from Latin pulla. For the development of the stressed vowel, see poultry. Doublet of pullet.

s.def: A young bird, a chick; now especially, a young game bird (turkey, partridge, grouse etc.).

To treat with a poultice.

ety: From Middle English pound, from Old English pund (“a pound, weight”), from Proto-West Germanic *pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą (“pound, weight”), an early borrowing from Latin pondō (“by weight”), ablative form of pondus (“weight”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull, stretch”). ety: The basic unit of currency in medieval England was the silver penny or sterling, weighing ¹⁄₂₄₀ of a tower pound. 240 of these coins made a "pound of sterlings". This term (shortened to "pound sterling" in later usage) continued to be used for a sum of 240 pence even after the sterling had ceased to circulate. The modern pound sterling is equivalent to 100 new pence.

a precipitous mountain
a precipitous decline

s.def: Headlong
ex: a precipitous fall

s.def: Hasty; rash; quick; sudden
ex: precipitous attempts
[…]humans have been responsible for a precipitous decline of elephants, from perhaps 300,000 in the early 1970s to some 10,000 today.

s.def: Alternative spelling of précis.
Alternative form of précis.

ety: From Middle French précis, from Latin praecīsus, perfect passive participle of praecīdere, from prae- (“before, in front”) + caedere (“cut; strike”), cognate with hit. Related to incise. Doublet of précis.

s.def: Both exact and accurate.
ex: precise definition
highly precise
precise calculation

s.def: Consistent, clustered close together, agreeing with each other (this does not mean that they cluster near the true, correct, or accurate value).
Adhering too much to rules; prim or punctilious.
To make or render precise; to specify.
ex: This proposal for a new basic regulation is justified because there is a need to precise the objectives of the CFP.

ety: From Middle French precision. Equivalent to precise + -ion.

s.def: The state of being precise or exact; especially, both exact and accurate.
ex: Near-synonyms: exactitude, exactness; accuracy

s.def: The ability of a measurement to be reproduced consistently.
ex: Near-synonyms: repeatability; reproducibility

s.def: The number of significant digits to which a value may be measured reliably.
A bidding system that makes use of many artificial bids to describe a hand quite precisely.
Used for exact or precise measurement.
ex: precision instruments

s.def: Made, or characterized by accuracy.
ex: But there was nothing he could do about Villa's second when Agbonlahor crossed from the left and Bent finished with a precision volley.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- Proto-Indo-European *-éyti Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- Proto-Indo-European *-né- Proto-Indo-European *ḱl̥néyti Proto-Hellenic *klíňňō Ancient Greek κλῑ́νω (klī́nō) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-ā́ Ancient Greek -ᾱ (-ā) Ancien…

s.def: Describing the period of a disease before any symptoms appear
Describing a test or trial of a new pharmaceutical on animals (or in vitro) rather than on humans

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae- Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w-der. Proto-Italic *klaudō Latin claudō Latin praeclūderelbor. English preclude Learned borrowing from Latin praeclūdere.

s.def: To remove the possibility of; to rule out; to prevent or exclude; to render impossible.
ex: It has been raining for days, but that doesn’t preclude the skies clearing by this afternoon!
"Now, own the truth,—are you not very sorry that my having been in the opposition precludes your going to the most brilliant fête of the season?"

ety: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”). Doublet of apricot.

s.def: Characterized by exceptionally early development or maturity.
ex: The precocious plant was already blooming flowers by day 4.
She's precocious and she knows just / What it takes to make a pro blush
Both groups, also, have already evolved precocious (intracapsular) spore germination.

s.def: Exhibiting advanced skills and aptitudes at an abnormally early age.
ex: The precocious child began reading the newspaper at age four.
Mary: Even though the sound of it is something quite atrocious / If you say it loud enough you'll always sound precocious.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French precognition or its source, Latin praecognitio, from praecognōscō (“to know beforehand”). Doublet of Germanic-based foreknowledge and Greek-based prognosis. Equivalent to pre- + cognition.

s.def: Knowledge of the future; understanding of something in advance, especially as a form of supernatural or extrasensory perception.
The practice of taking a factual statement from a witness before a trial.

ety: From precompile + -er.

s.def: A program or algorithm that precompiles.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English conceive English preconceive From pre- + conceive.

s.def: To conceive, or form an opinion of, beforehand; to have a preconception

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English condition English precondition From pre- + condition.

s.def: A condition that requires satisfaction before taking a course of action.
ex: A marriage licence is a precondition for a wedding.

s.def: A medical illness, ailment, or adverse condition that exists before an insurance policy takes effect.
To condition in advance
ex: The hearts were preconditioned by either ischemia or bradykinin or adenosine.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English cook English precook From pre- + cook.

s.def: to partially or completely cook in advance

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English cum English precum From pre- (“before”) + cum (“ejaculate”).

s.def: Cowper's fluid; pre-ejaculate.
ex: Bert made precum like some kind of instant coffee; it was always available.
However, in some men precum will contain sperm so adequate protection should be used to prevent pregnancy.

ety: Inherited from Middle English precursour, from Middle French precurseur or its etymon Latin praecursor (“forerunner”). By surface analysis, precurse + -or.

s.def: That which precurses: a forerunner, predecessor, or indicator of approaching events.
One of the compounds that participates in the chemical reaction that produces another compound.
Caused by the following symbol.

ety: From Latin praedor + -acious.

s.def: Alternative spelling of predaceous.
ex: ‘Behold the predacious lion that butchered our flock!’

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English date English predate From pre- + date.

s.def: To designate a date earlier than the actual one; to move a date, appointment, event, or period of time to an earlier point (contrast "postdate".)
To exist or to occur before something else; to antedate.
ex: The Chinese use of Pascal's Triangle predates its discovery by Blaise Pascal.
"The Tees Valley has ageing diesel trains that predate any form of emission control.

s.def: A publication, such as a newspaper or magazine, that is issued with a printed date later than the date of issue.
To prey upon something.

ety: Borrowed from Latin praedātiō, praedātiōnis, from praedor (“pillage, plunder”), from praeda (“plunder, spoils”).

s.def: The preying of one animal on others.
The action of attacking or plundering.

ety: Borrowed from Latin praedātor, from praedor (“loot, pillage”), from praeda (“booty, spoils, prey”).

s.def: Any animal or other organism that hunts and kills other nonplant organisms (their prey), primarily for food.
ex: So if you're the only thing worth eating in the middle of the ocean, the predator that grabs you will probably have gotten there by a Levy walk.

s.def: Someone who attacks and plunders for gain.
A sexual predator.

ety: Borrowed from Latin praedātōrius, equivalent to predator + -y.

s.def: Of, or relating to a predator.
ex: And while there are plenty of benches, there's little shelter from the wind (or predatory seagulls the size of dogs) out on the platforms.

s.def: Living by preying on other living animals.
Exploiting or victimizing others for personal gain.
ex: predatory lending
predatory inclusion

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English decease English predecease From pre- + decease.

s.def: The death of one person or thing before another.
To die sooner than.
ex: Husbands usually predecease their wives.
Frederick, Prince of Wales, predeceased his father and never became king.
Two brothers and a sister predeceased him. Bergoglio is survived by a sister, María Elena.

ety: From Middle English predecessour, from Old French predecesseor (“forebear”), from Late Latin praedēcessor, from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + Latin dēcessor (“retiring officer”), from Latin dēcēdō (“to retire, to die”) (English decease).

s.def: One who precedes; one who has preceded another in any state, position, office, etc.; one whom another follows or comes after, in any office or position.
A model or type of machinery or device which precedes the current (or later) one. Usually used to describe an earlier, outdated model.
ex: The steam engine was the predecessor of diesel and electric locomotives.

s.def: A vertex having a directed path to another vertex

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English define English predefine From pre- + define.

s.def: To define in advance.

ety: From predestine + -arian.

s.def: Of or relating to predestination.
ex: But it is wrong to stress only the predestinarian aspect of protestantism […].

s.def: One who believes in predestination.

ety: From Middle English predestinate, from Latin praedestinātus, past participle of praedestināre. By surface analysis, pre- + destinate.

s.def: To predestine.
ex: Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son.

s.def: Predestined, preordained.
ex: God keep your ladyship still in that mind; so some gentleman or other shall 'scape a predestinate scratched face.
It’s said there’s one predestinate / To be his mortal foe; / But that man is yet unborn, / And long may it be so.
There once was a man who said, “Damn! It is borne in upon me I am An engine that moves In predestinate grooves, I’m not even a bus, I’m a tram.”

ety: From Middle English predestinacion, from Old French predestination, from Late Latin praedēstinātiō. By surface analysis, predestine + -ation. Displaced native Old English foreteohhung.

s.def: The doctrine that everything has been foreordained by God or by fate.
The doctrine that certain people have been elected for salvation, and sometimes also that others are destined for reprobation.
Destiny or fate.

ety: From Latin praedēterminō; equivalent to pre- + determine.

s.def: To determine or decide in advance.
To doom by previous decree; to foredoom.
Capable of being predicated or affirmed of something; affirmable; attributable.
That may be used in the predicate of a sentence, especially following a form of the verb "to be".
Anything affirmable of another; especially, a general attribute or notion as affirmable of, or applicable to, many individuals.
One of the five most general relations of attributes involved in logical arrangements, namely, genus, species, difference, property, and accident.

ety: From Middle English predicament, from Old French predicament, from Late Latin praedicāmentum (“that which is predicated, a predicament, category”).

s.def: A definite class, state or condition.
An unfortunate or trying position or condition.
That which is predicated; a category.

ety: From Middle English predicat(e), from Old French predicat (French prédicat), from Medieval Latin praedicātum (“thing said of a subject, predicate”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of praedicātus, the perfect passive participle praedicō (“to proclaim”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix); see also Etymology 2 below. The adjective was derived from the noun by metanalysis, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: The part of the sentence (or clause) which states a property that a subject has or is characterized by.

A term of a statement, where the statement may be true or false depending on whether the thing referred to by the values of the statement's variables has the property signified by that (predicative) term.
ex: A propositional variable may be treated as a nullary predicate.
A predicate is either valid, satisfiable, or unsatisfiable.

s.def: An operator, expression, or function that returns either true or false.
ex: Predicates are usually found in a query's WHERE or HAVING clauses, though they can be located elsewhere (e.g. in CASE expressions).

s.def: Of or related to the predicate of a sentence or clause.
Predicated, stated.
Relating to or being any of a series of criminal acts upon which prosecution for racketeering may be predicated.
To announce, assert, or proclaim publicly.
To assume or suppose; to infer.
To base (on); to assert on the grounds of.
ex: The law is what constitutes both desire and the lack on which it is predicated.

s.def: To make a term (or expression) the predicate of a statement.

ety: Etymology tree English predicate Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English predicative From predicate + -ive.

s.def: Modifying a noun from within a predicate.
ex: in predicative position

s.def: An element of the predicate of a sentence which complements the subject or object by means of the verb. Predicatives may be nominal or adjectival.
In some languages, a special part of speech used as a predicate and denoting a state of being.

ety: Compare Latin praedicatorius (“praising”).

s.def: affirmative; making a clear assertion or statement of praise, especially one with religious or moral implications.
ex: Hex's sermon clearly shows a lack of predicatory features, although, according to the colophon, the preacher himself wrote it.

s.def: Forming an ontologically neutral predicate; implying no new information or qualities.

ety: Early 17th century, from Latin praedicō (“to mention beforehand”) (perfect passive participle praedictus), from prae- (“before”) + dīcō (“to say”). Equivalent to Germanic forespeak, foretell, and foresay.

s.def: to state, or make something known in advance
To make a prediction: to forecast, foretell, or estimate a future event on the basis of knowledge and reasoning; to prophesy a future event on the basis of mystical knowledge or power.
ex: Professor Trelawney kept predicting Harry’s death, which he found extremely annoying.

s.def: To imply.
ex: It is interesting to see how clearly theory predicts the difference between the ascending and descending curves of a dynamo.
For both men and women, greater symmetry predicted a larger number of past sex partners.

s.def: To make predictions.
ex: The devil can both predict and make predictors.

s.def: To direct a ranged weapon against a target by means of a predictor.
ex: They're predicting us now; looks like a barrage.

s.def: A prediction.
ex: Or say with Princes if it shall go well, / By oft predict that I in heaven find.

ety: Etymology tree English predict Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English predictable From predict + -able.

s.def: Able to be predicted.
ex: a predictable mathematical pattern
a boring film with a predictable ending
Despite the predictable squalling on some of the Twilight fanblogs, the two leads are impeccably cast.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English digest English predigest From pre- + digest.

s.def: To digest food in advance of eating it
ex: Spiders predigest their food by injecting enzymes into their victims.

s.def: To preprocess in order to deliver the most important parts in a simplified form.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedīlēctiō.

s.def: A condition of favoring or liking; a tendency towards; proclivity; predisposition.
ex: But for him the first rule of judging was to set aside personal predilection and vote the law and the facts.
... youth’s predilection for revolt.
Wilson doesn’t see any inconsistency between his socialism and his predilection for the high life.

ety: Either a back-formation from predisposition or borrowed from Middle French predisposer.

s.def: To make someone inclined to something in advance; to influence.
To make someone susceptible to something (such as a disease).

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English disposition English predisposition From pre- + disposition.

s.def: The state of being predisposed or susceptible to something, especially to a behavior or a health condition.

ety: Etymology tree Latin praegnāns Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānusder. English -ane English pre(gnane) Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Hellenic *dwi- Ancient Greek δῐ- (dĭ-)bor. Latin di-bor. English di- French -ènebor. English -ene English d(ie)ne Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- Proto-Indo-European *(s)kert- Proto-Indo-European *(s)kort-ek-sder. Latin cortexder. English cortico- Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- Proto-Hellenic *kʰolā́…

s.def: A glucocorticoid C₂₁H₂₆O₅ that is a dehydrogenated analog of cortisone, used to relieve rheumatic and allergic conditions and to treat leukemia.

ety: From Middle French prédominant, ultimately from Medieval Latin praedominans. By surface analysis, pre- + dominant.

s.def: Common or widespread; prevalent.
Significant or important; dominant.
A subdominant.

ety: From Latin praedominātus, past participle of praedominor. By surface analysis, pre- + dominate.

s.def: To dominate, have control, or succeed by superior numbers or size.
ex: These qualities tend to predominate among conservatives but they are present among liberals too.

s.def: To be prominent; to loom large; to be the chief component of a whole.
ex: All in her mind was confusion; still the paramount sense that predominated over all others, was the bitter conviction of his unworthiness.
Thus, even though a total of four lags of inflation enters the right hand side, forward looking behavior still predominates.

s.def: To dominate or hold power over, especially through numerical advantage; to outweigh.
Predominant.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French preeminent and its source, Latin praeēminēns, present participle of praeēmineō (“to stand out, excel”), from prae- (“pre-”) + ēmineō.

s.def: Exceeding others in quality or rank; of outstanding excellence, extremely notable or important.

ety: Back-formation from preemption.

s.def: To appropriate first.
ex: He preempted that hill to be its king.

s.def: To displace or take the place of (by having higher precedence, etc).
ex: Floppy disks were preempted by CDs.
A German move from the west had preempted them. By nightfall the whole Sidi Rezegh Ridge was in German occupation.

s.def: To prevent or beat to the punch, to forestall an expected occurrence by acting first.
ex: By his statement, the Secretary-General had effectively preempted the usual frustrating debates over questions of fact and law.
In fact, before Jane said anything at all, Claudia preempted her and began to speak very rapidly.
He always preempted his enemies by being the first to greet them and inquiring about their well-being.

s.def: To secure (land, etc.) by the right of preemption (purchasing before others, e.g. land because one already occupies it).
To make a preemptive bid at bridge.
A preemptive bid.
A guaranteed publication deal contingent upon the work being immediately taken off the market and offered to nobody else.

ety: From Middle English pren, from Old English prēon, from Proto-Germanic *preunaz (compare Icelandic prjónn (“pin, knitting-needle”), Danish pryne (“needle, eel-spear”)), of uncertain origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *brewn- (“protrusion, tip, edge”) (compare Lithuanian briaunà (“edge”), Albanian brez (“belt, girdle”)). Cognate with German Pfriem. The verb is from Middle English prenen, from pren (“a preen”), akin to German pfriemen.

s.def: A forked tool used by clothiers for dressing cloth.
A pin.
ex: She never seemed to want for siller; the house was as bright as a new preen, the yaird better delved than the manse garden; […]

s.def: A bodkin; brooch.
To pin; fasten.
To groom; to trim or dress the feathers with the beak.
To spend time making oneself attractive and admiring one's appearance, e.g. in front of a mirror.
To show off, posture, or smarm.
ex: His preening self-satisfaction, chest thrown forward as he settles into a chair in his mansion...
He preened under her compliments.
“Six look like dyin', and five dead,” preened the killer.

s.def: To flatter.
ex: New York nurtured and preened the most sophisticated audiences in the nation.

s.def: To comb; to make orderly.
ex: My two roommates are engineers who preen the diesels.
Preen the deer hair rearward around the hook shank, and take 3 tight thread wraps to secure it.
Now Prossiden's finger was brandished, and preened the air in front of Onascam's face with florid implications.

s.def: To trim up, as trees.
ex: Adjusting his spectacles on the bridge of his nose, he gently preened the bush with his pruners.
I ignored him and looked around, wondering who preened the conical fir trees on each ledge of the building.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English exist English preexist From pre- + exist.

s.def: To exist before something else.
ex: The new device utilized technologies that preexisted.

ety: A clipping.

s.def: Prefabricated.
A prefabricated building.
ex: Having donned our PPE, we walk through the site to the prefab that controls access to the tunnel.

s.def: A prefabricated section of a building.
A single-storey prefabricated home built in many British cities immediately after World War II, intended to have a short life, but in a few cases still in use.
A reusable object in a video game world.
To prefabricate.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English fabricate English prefabricate From pre- + fabricate.

s.def: To manufacture (a building, etc.) in standard components that can be fitted together on site.

ety: Late 14th century, from Middle English preface, prefas, from Old French preface (from which derives the modern French préface), from Medieval Latin prefātia, for classical Latin praefātiō (“a saying beforehand”), from praefor (“to speak beforehand”), from prae- (“beforehand”) + for (“to speak”).

s.def: A beginning or introductory portion that comes before the main text of a document or book, typically serving to contextualize or explain the writing of the book and sometimes to acknowledge others' contributions; especially, such a discussion written by the work's own author.
ex: Holonyms: front matter, prelims
The book included a brief preface explaining the author's motivations for writing.

s.def: An introduction, or series of preliminary remarks.
ex: This superficial tale / Is but a preface of her worthy praise.
Heav'ns high behest no preface needs.
And now, without any further preface, we proceed to our next chapter.

s.def: A variable prayer forming the prelude or introduction to the Eucharistic Prayer or canon of the Mass, following the Sursum corda dialogue and leading into the Sanctus.
ex: Meronyms: protocol, embolism, eschatocol

s.def: A title or epithet.
To introduce or make a comment before (the main point); to premise.
ex: Let me preface this by saying that I don't know him that well.

s.def: To give a preface to.
ex: to preface a book

ety: From Medieval Latin *praefator + -ory (“agent”), from Medieval Latin prefatia (whence preface), for classical Latin praefatio (“a saying beforehand”) – see preface for details. Note that this is borrowed from Latin, not derived in English from preface, as in occasional misspelling *prefecatory.

s.def: Serving as a preface or prelude; introductory, preliminary.

ety: From Middle English prefect and prefecte, from Old French prefect (Mod. French préfet), from Latin praefectus (“one placed in charge, overseer, director, prefect”), from praeficere (“to place in charge”).

s.def: An official of Ancient Rome who controlled or superintended a particular command, charge, department, etc.
The head of a department in France.
The head of a county in Albania or Romania.
The head of a prefecture in Japan.
A school pupil in a position of power over other pupils.
A commander.
A head of a dicastery of the Roman Curia of the Roman Catholic Church.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French préfecture, from Latin praefectūra. Equivalent to prefect + -ure. As an East Asian administrative division, a calque of Chinese 府 (fǔ) and 郡 (jùn), also used to describe 縣 /县 (xian, “county”) and 州 (zhou, “province”) in some eras.

s.def: The office or position of a prefect.
The jurisdiction of a prefect; the region administered by a prefect, especially as a translation of certain French, Chinese, and Japanese administrative divisions.

ety: From Middle English preferren, from Anglo-Norman preferer, from Latin praeferō. Displaced native Old English foresettan and foreberan. Doublet of prelate. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as collate and confer among others.

s.def: To be in the habit of choosing something rather than something else; to favor; to like better.
ex: I prefer tea to coffee.
I'd prefer it if you didn't do it.
I'd prefer to stay home rather than drive/driving in the blizzard.

s.def: To advance, promote (someone or something).
ex: Tiberius preferred many to honours in his time, because they were famous whoremasters and sturdy drinkers[…].

s.def: To present or submit (something) to an authority (now usually in "to prefer charges").
To put forward for acceptance; to introduce, recommend (to).
ex: one Master David Hume, who making some use of his purse, gave him Letters to his friends in Scotland to preferre him to King Iames.

ety: From prefer + -able, probably after Middle French preferable. Compare preference, preferential, etc.

s.def: Better than some other option; preferred.

ety: Etymology tree English preferable Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder. Proto-Germanic *-līkaz Proto-Germanic *-ê Proto-Germanic *-līkê Proto-West Germanic *-līkē Old English -līċe Middle English -ly English -ly English preferably From preferable + -ly.

s.def: In preference; by choice; in a preferable manner.
ex: The nondegerming system grinds corn, preferably white dent corn, into meal with little, if any, separation of germ.
He felt having a Micronesian navigator meant he needed a pureblooded Polynesian, preferably a Hawaiian, as captain.

s.def: To exceed in weight or influence; hence, to predominate.
ex: Train journeys were not long in terms of distance, and having regard to these factors, the tank engine inevitably preponderated.

ety: From Middle English preposicioun, from Old French preposicion, from Latin praepositio, praepositionem, from praepono (“to place before”), equivalent to pre- + position. Compare French préposition. So called because it is placed before the word with which it is phrased, as in a bridge of iron, he comes from town, it is good for food, he escaped by running.

s.def: An adposition.

Any of a class of non-inflecting words and multiword terms typically employed to connect a following noun or a pronoun, in an adjectival or adverbial sense, with some other word: a particle used with a noun or pronoun (in English always in the objective case) to make a phrase limiting some other wo…
ex: I love this girl. “On which I can get my hands” — even in her darkest moment, she cannot bring herself to end a sentence with a preposition.

s.def: A proposition; an exposition; a discourse.
ex: […] he made a longe preposicion & oracion cōcernynge yͤ allegiaūce which he exortyd his lordes to owe

s.def: Alternative spelling of pre-position.
ex: It is important to preposition the material before turning on the machine.

s.def: A phrase containing both a preposition and its object or complement and which may be used as an adjunct or a modifier.

ety: From Latin praepositivus, past participle of praepono (“to place before, to place ahead of”).

s.def: Put before; prefixed.
ex: a prepositive adjective
a prepositive cone
a prepositive object

s.def: A prepositive word.

ety: From pre- (prefix meaning ‘before, earlier in time’) + possess. Cognates * Late Latin prepossessus (“seized beforehand”)

s.def: Chiefly followed by by or with: to preoccupy (someone) in an emotional or mental way, so as to preclude other things.
To cause (someone) to have a previous inclination against, for, or to something; to bias or prejudice; specifically, to induce in (someone) a favourable opinion beforehand, or at the outset.
To cause (someone) to think a certain way.
To occupy or possess (something) beforehand.
Chiefly followed by of or with: to cause (oneself) to obtain possession of something beforehand, or ahead of someone else.
ex: to prepossess oneself of land

ety: From prepossess + -ing. Attested in 1610s with the meaning of "getting possession of (ground or land) beforehand". The meaning "to possess (a person) beforehand with a feeling, notion, etc." developed in 1630s, acquiring by the 40s of the same century the meaning of "to cause (someone) to have a favorable opinion of something, preoccupy the mind or heart of".

s.def: Tending to invite favor; attracting confidence, favor, esteem, or love; attractive
ex: In repose the faces of the men were intelligent and dignified, those of the women ofttimes prepossessing.
He was a frank, prepossessing fellow, but I saw that he could add nothing to his original account.

s.def: Causing prejudice.
present participle and gerund of prepossess

ety: From Latin praeposterus (“with the hinder part before, reversed, inverted, perverted”), from prae (“before”) + posterus (“coming after”).

s.def: Absurd, or contrary to common sense.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae- Proto-Indo-European *pótis Proto-Italic *potis Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Italic *-ējō Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ēō Proto-Italic *potēō Proto-Italic *potēnts Latin potēns Latin praepotensbor. English prepotent Borrowed from Latin praepoten…

s.def: Very powerful; superior in force, influence, or authority; predominant.
ex: To ordre his subiectes after true iustice / As a prepotent prince
[…] Jeff’s eyes were dry, though his face was discharged of all its prepotent impudence.
[…] the exigencies of awareness are that we focus on certain dimensions of the objects before us, make certain ways of seeing them prepotent.

s.def: Characterized by prepotency.
ex: […] the mother strain, if not prepotent in the sense of science, seems to me to have outweighed that of any other relative of whom we have record.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English processor English preprocessor From pre- + processor.

s.def: program that processes its input data to produce output that is used as input to another program

ety: From Middle English prepuce, prepuse, from Old French prepuce (“foreskin”), from Latin praepūtium (“prepuce, foreskin”), a combination of prae- (“fore-”) + Old Latin pūtos (“penis”).

s.def: The foreskin, or retractable fold of tissue covering the glans penis.
ex: Jehovah, collector of prepuces, is no more.
But there are a fair number of halfway Jews – you know, those who want God without having to have their prepuces torn off to get him.

s.def: The clitoral hood.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English requisite English prerequisite From pre- + requisite.

s.def: Required as a prior condition of something else; necessary or indispensable.
ex: The prerequisite warm-up to the match was ignored.
A good command of Spanish is prerequisite for enrolling in this course.

s.def: A course or topic that must be completed before another course or topic can be started.
ex: Algebra is typically a prerequisite for physics.

s.def: Something that is required as necessary or indispensable, or as a prior condition of something else.
ex: A degree is a prerequisite for entry into this profession.
If you examine the prerequisites list, you will notice it does not include bootstrapper packages for the Office 2003 PIAs.

ety: From Anglo-Norman prerogative (noun), from Latin praerogātīva (“previous verdict; claim, privilege”), noun use of the feminine singular of praerogātīvus (“having first vote; privileged”).

s.def: A right, especially when due to one's position or role.
ex: The best thing about being a woman Is the prerogative to have a little fun and...
If you want to wear your hair a certain way, that's your prerogative. You don't have to check with all your friends to make sure it's okay.
If you choose another approach — that's your prerogative. But the problem is that parents often don't realize they're making the choice […]

s.def: A property, attribute or ability which gives one a superiority or advantage over others; an inherent advantage or privilege; a talent.
Characterized by lawless state actions, as in a prerogative state.
Having a hereditary or official right or privilege.

ety: From Middle English presage, from Latin praesāgium.

s.def: A warning of a future event; an omen.
An intuition of a future event; a presentiment.
ex: Glad was I when I reached the other bank. / Now for a better country. Vain presage!

s.def: To predict or foretell something.
To make a prediction.
To have a presentiment of; to feel beforehand; to foreknow.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English sale English presale From pre- + sale.

s.def: The sale of something privately, before it is available to the public
The sale of a property before it is built

ety: From New Latin presbyōpia, from Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old man”), and New Latin -ōpia (“vision problem”), from Ancient Greek ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”). By surface analysis, presby- + -opia.

s.def: Inability of the eye, due to ageing, to focus on nearby objects.

ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Doublet of prester and priest.

s.def: An elder, priest, pastor, or minister in various Christian churches.
An elder of the Presbyterian church.
An elder of the congregation in early Christianity.

ety: From Late Latin presbyterium + -an. By surface analysis, presbyter + -ian or presbytery + -an.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a presbyter, or to ecclesiastical government by presbyters; relating to those who uphold church government by presbyters; also, to the doctrine, discipline, and worship of a communion so governed.

ety: From Middle English presbetory, presbytory (“part of church reserved for clergy”), from Late Latin presbyterium (“group of presbyters, part of church reserved for clergy”), from Ancient Greek πρεσβῠτέρῐον (presbŭtérĭon, “group of presbyters”), from πρεσβῠ́τερος (presbŭ́teros, “elder, priest”) + -ῐον (-ĭon). By surface analysis, presbyter + -y. Doublet of presbyterium.

s.def: The home of a Roman Catholic parish priest.
ex: Near-synonyms: curatage, parsonage, vicarage

s.def: A section of a church reserved for the clergy, containing the altar.
ex: Near-synonym: chancel (broadly synonymous)

s.def: Presbyters collectively; the body of presbyters of a congregation.
ex: Meronym: presbyter

s.def: The district (jurisdiction) of those presbyters.
ex: Near-synonyms: diocese, parish

s.def: A body of elders in the early Christian church.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae-lbor. Middle English pre- English pre- English school English preschool From pre- + school.

s.def: Of or relating to the years of early childhood before attendance at primary school.
A nursery school.
ex: What could you do with the transumer trend in your agency? What about a coffee cart where parents pick up their children from preschool or classes?

s.def: A school including nursery and kindergarten. It is succeeded by elementary school.
To provide nursery school education for.
To undergo nursery school education.

ety: Inherited from Middle English prescience, from Old French prescience, from Latin praescientia.

s.def: Knowledge of events before they take place.
ex: God's certain prescience of the volitions of moral agents

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin praesciēns (“foreknowing; foretelling, predicting”), present participle of) Latin praesciō (“to foreknow”), from prae- (prefix meaning ‘before; in front’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before; in front”)) + sciō (“to know, understand; to have knowledge of”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect; to split”)). The word is cognate with Middle French prescient (modern French prescient (“prescient”)), Italian presciente (“prescient”).…

s.def: Exhibiting or possessing prescience: having knowledge of, or seemingly able to correctly predict, events before they take place.
ex: Benignant Heaven, præscient and kind, / Made man for toil, and left sweet Sleep behind, / To nerve the arm which labour had unstrung— […]
The kind sorrowful blue eyes looked at me for a moment with the prescient sadness of a coming and a long farewell.
Members opposite seem to be prescient; they seem to know what I am going to say before I have said it.

ety: From Latin praescindō (“to cut off in front”), from prae- (“before”) + scindō (“split, divide”).

s.def: To abstract (from); to dismiss from consideration.
ex: But one cannot prescind from humanity. There can be no renewal of our relationship with nature without a renewal of humanity itself.

s.def: To pay exclusive attention to.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i? Proto-Italic *prai Proto-Italic *prai- Latin prae- Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-? Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreybʰ- Proto-Indo-European *(s)kréybʰeti Proto-Italic *skreiβō Latin scrībō Latin praescrībōbor. English prescribe Borrowed from Latin praescrībere, from prae- (“before, in front”) and scrībere (“to write”).

s.def: To order (a drug or medical device) for use by a particular patient (under licensed authority).
ex: The doctor prescribed aspirin.

s.def: To specify by writing as a required procedure or ritual; to lay down authoritatively as a guide, direction, or rule of action.
ex: The property meets the criteria prescribed by the regulations.
Prescribe not us our duties.

s.def: To develop or assert a right; to make a claim (by prescription).
ex: Most probable that one presentation and 40 years possession thereafter, is sufficient to prescribe a right of patronage.

s.def: To become invalidated or unenforceable by prescription, to lapse

ety: Latin praescriptum: compare Old French prescript.

s.def: Something prescribed; a rule, regulation or dictate.
ex: By his prescript a sanctuary is framed Of cedar

s.def: A medical prescription.
Directed; prescribed.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French prescripcion, from Latin praescriptio (“preface; pretext; something written ahead of time”), from prae- (“pre-, before”) + scribere (“to write”) + -tio (“-tion, forming nouns”). Equivalent to prescribe + -tion.

s.def: A written order from an authorized medical practitioner for provision of a medicine or other treatment, such as (ophthalmology) the specific lenses needed for a pair of glasses.
ex: The surgeon had written thousands of prescriptions for pain killers without proper examinations before the police raided the clinic.

s.def: The medicine or treatment provided by such an order.
ex: I need you to pick up gramma's prescriptions on your way home.

s.def: Any plan of treatment or handling; the treatment or handling thus provided.
ex: Early to bed and early to rise is a prescription for a long, healthy, and terrible life.
Change is the universal prescription for a wounded spirit. "It will do you so much good," is the constant remark.
...looking at him I saw that I had been wrong in my prescription, if not in my diagnosis, and that the whisky was working against us.

s.def: Synonym of enactment, the act of establishing a law, regulation, etc., particularly in writing; an instance of this.
ex: A statute that cannot find justification for its prescription in one or more of these principles violates international law.

s.def: The act of establishing or formalizing ideal norms for language use, as opposed to describing the actual norms of such use; an instance of this.
An established time period within which a right must be exercised and after which it is null and permanently unenforceable.
An established time period after which a person who has uninterruptedly, peacefully, and publicly used another's property acquires full ownership of it.
Synonym of self-restraint, limiting of one's actions especially according to a moral code or social conventions.
ex: There is an air of prescription about him which is always agreeable to Sir Leicester; he receives it as a kind of tribute.

ety: From Latin praescriptivus (“relating to a legal exception”), from praescript- (“directed in writing”), from the verb praescribere.

s.def: Of or pertaining to prescribing or enjoining, especially an action or behavior based on a norm or standard.

ety: Through Old French presence, from Latin praesentia (“a being present”), from praesentem. Displaced native Old English andweardnes.

s.def: The part of space within one's immediate vicinity.
ex: Bob never said anything about it in my presence.

s.def: The fact or condition of being present, or of being within sight or call, or at hand.
ex: Any painter can benefit from the presence of a live model from which to draw.

s.def: A quality of poise and effectiveness that enables a performer to achieve a close relationship with their audience.
A quality that sets an individual out from others; a quality that makes them noticed and/or admired even if they are not speaking or performing.
ex: Despite being less than five foot, she filled up the theatre with her stage presence.
Perrin Ferris succeeds in his equally demanding task of maintaining some semblance of presence while sharing the stage with a chronic upstager.

s.def: Something (as a spirit) felt or believed to be present.
ex: I'm convinced that there was a presence in that building that I can't explain, which led to my heroic actions.

s.def: A company's business activity in a particular market.
An assembly of great persons.
The state of being closely focused on the here and now, not distracted by irrelevant thoughts.
Synonym of room tone.
Ellipsis of presence chamber.

ety: From Middle English present, from Old French present, from Latin praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“to be present”), from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + esse (“to be”). Displaced Old English andweard (“present, current”).

s.def: Relating to now, for the time being; current.
ex: The barbaric practice continues to the present day.
The present manager has been here longer than the last one.
up to the present day

s.def: The current moment or period of time.
To bring (someone) into the presence of (a person); to introduce formally.
ex: to present an envoy to the king

s.def: Located in the immediate vicinity.
ex: Only half of all present members were present at the meeting.
Is there a doctor present?
Several people were present when the event took place.

s.def: Having an immediate effect (of a medicine, poison etc.); fast-acting.
Not delayed; immediate; instant.
ex: Sign me a present pardon for my brother,
An ambassador[…]desires a present audience.

s.def: Ready; quick in emergency.
ex: a present wit

s.def: Favorably attentive; propitious.
ex: to find a god so present to my prayer

s.def: Relating to something a person is referring to in the very context, with a deictic use similar to the demonstrative adjective this.
ex: Near-synonyms: this (determiner), this (pronoun), current
in the present study; the present article; the present results

s.def: Attentive; alert; focused.
ex: Sorry, I was distracted just now, I'll try to be more present from now on.

s.def: A tense that describes an ongoing action in the present. In English it is formed by use of a form of be with a present participle.
A perfect tense that expresses action in the past (usually completed) with consequences in the present time.
A grammatical tense whose principal function is to locate a situation or event in the present time.
In existence now; current or contemporary.
ex: Antlers and horns have been the insignia of devils and black magicians from time immemorial, and are worn by present-day witch doctors.
The new bridge (6) gives headroom of 13ft at high tide, sufficient for present-day river traffic.
Ch'üan Ch'i was the scion of a great family of Feng-yang in Shang-lo [in present-day Shensi province].

ety: From Middle French presentable, from Old French, as if present + -able.

s.def: In good enough shape to be shown or offered to other people; tidy; attractive.
ex: Before we go out, let me just go to the washroom and make myself presentable.

s.def: Acceptable; worth considering.
Capable of being presented to a church living.

ety: From Old French presentation (French présentation), from Latin praesentātiōnem, accusative singular of praesentātiō (“representation, exhibition”). Morphologically present + -ation.

s.def: The act of presenting, or something presented.
ex: Prayers are sometimes a presentation of mere desires.

s.def: A lecture or speech given in front of an audience.
The outward appearance or representation of a person or thing to the human mind.
A dramatic performance.
An award given to someone on a special occasion.
Money given as a wedding gift.
A slideshow created on a computer.
The symptoms, signs, and other possible indications of disease, trauma, etc., that are exhibited by a patient who has sought, or has otherwise come to, the attention of a physician.
ex: The presentation of the thirty-four-year-old male in the emergency room was slight fever, dilated pupils, and marked disorientation.

s.def: The position of the foetus in the uterus at birth.
Gender presentation; gender expression.

ety: The adjective is derived from Late Latin praesentativus (“that presents for consideration”) + English -ive (suffix signifying belonging or relating to, of the nature of, serving to, or tending to, forming adjectives). Praesentativus is from Latin praesentātus (“presented, exhibited, or shown”) + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives); while praesentātus is the perfect passive participle of praesentō (“to present, exhibit, or show”), from praesēns (“at hand, present; existing; immediate; prompt; prop…

s.def: Presenting, or able to represent, an idea in the mind.
ex: Now the face is a traditional metonym for divine presence in Jewish theology and, in its human form, the presentative image of God.

s.def: Of a benefice, or the advowsons, tithes, etc., associated with a benefice: that a patron has the right to present.
Serving to present something, or draw it to the attention of the interlocutor.
Of or pertaining to a presentation (“an image formed in the mind after an object is perceived”).
Synonym of representative (“representing another, or representing a larger group”).
Of or pertaining to an act of presenting or giving an object to someone.
A construct that serves to present something, or draw it to the attention of the interlocutor.

ety: From present + -ee; second sense likely a blend of present + absentee.

s.def: A person who is presented (e.g. to a benefice), or to whom an award is given.
One who is present at work, especially if too sick to be productive, or working beyond the expected hours.

ety: Etymology tree English presend English -t English present Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English presenter From present + -er.

s.def: Someone who presents a broadcast programme; a compere or master of ceremonies.
Someone who presents a thing or person to someone else.
A small handheld device used to remotely control a computerised slide show.
A conceptual layer in GUI-based software that assumes the functionality of the "middleman".

ety: From French pressentiment, from Middle French, equivalent to pre- + sentiment.

s.def: A premonition; a feeling that something, often of undesirable nature, is going to happen.
ex: A man, my good Sir, has seldom an offer of kindness to make to a woman, but she has a presentiment of it some moments before.
Oh, those women! They nurse and cuddle their presentiments, and make darlings of their ugliest thoughts, as they do of their deformed children.
This unfortunate accident has upset me. I have a horrible presentiment that something of the kind may happen to me.

ety: From present + -ive.

s.def: Denoting a conception or notion; depicting a tangible object.
ex: presentive words

s.def: Introducing or asserting the existence or occurrence of something in the present.
ex: How greatly the word "will" is felt to have lost presentive power in the last three centuries.

s.def: A grammatical construct that introduces or asserts the existence or occurrence of something in the present.

ety: From Middle English presently; equivalent to present + -ly.

s.def: Immediately, at once; quickly.
ex: Polonius: My lord, the queen would speak with you, and presently.
And presently the fig tree withered away.

s.def: Before long; soon.
ex: Presently all was quiet again.
‘I shall presently be getting a call to tell me of that.’

s.def: At present; now; currently.
ex: The towns and forts you presently have.

s.def: With actual presence; in actuality.

ety: From Anglo-Norman presentment, presentement, Middle French presentement, corresponding to present + -ment.

s.def: A statement made on oath by a jury.
ex: In 1771, a grand jury presentment in Georgia revealed that "Slaves are permitted to rent houses …."

s.def: The notice taken by a grand jury of any offence from their own knowledge or observation, without any bill of indictment laid before them.
ex: the presentment of a nuisance, a libel, etc.

s.def: A formal complaint submitted to a bishop or archdeacon.
The act of presenting something for acceptance; now specifically, presenting something (e.g. a bill or cheque) for payment.
An artistic representation; a picture.
Presentation of a performance, as of a play or work of music.
The aspect or form in which something presents itself; appearance.
The official notice (formerly required to be given in court) of the surrender of a copyhold estate.
ex: As to the presentment: that, by the general custom of manors, is to be made at the next court baron immediately after the surrender

ety: From Old French preservacion, from Medieval Latin preservatio. Morphologically preserve + -ation.

s.def: The act of preserving; care to preserve; act of keeping from destruction, decay or any ill.
ex: The eyes of the Lord are upon them that love him, his is ther mighty protection, a preservation from stumbling, and a help from falling.
Further, the Society pleads for the preservation of Sutton's Charity.
Preservation of two railway routes between Belfast and Derry could no longer be justified and one of them must go.

s.def: The state of being preserved, how something has survived.
ex: The canoe is of pure black oak, and is in excellent preservation.

ety: From Old French preservatif, from Medieval Latin praeservativus.

s.def: Any agent, natural or artificial, that acts to preserve, especially when added to food.
ex: Salt, sugar, and acid all act as preservatives when making pickles.

s.def: Tending to preserve.
ex: The curators took preservative actions to maintain the ancient collection.

ety: From Middle English preserven, from Old French preserver, from Medieval Latin prēservāre (“keep, preserve”), from Late Latin praeservāre (“guard beforehand”), from prae (“before”, adverb) + servāre (“maintain, keep”). Displaced native Old English nerian.

s.def: A sweet spread made of any of a variety of fruits.
A reservation, a nature preserve.
An exclusive area of activity.
ex: Kids regard their tree houses as their own preserve.

s.def: To protect; to keep from harm or injury.
ex: Let's pray that we'd be preserved from danger.
Every people has the right to preserve its identity and culture.

s.def: To maintain throughout; to keep intact.
ex: to preserve appearances; to preserve silence
I preserved a composed manner throughout the interrogation.
Better men than you, men who could believe and obey, twisted the entrails of iron and preserved the legend of fire.

s.def: To save from decay by the use of some preservative substance, such as sugar or salt; to season and prepare (fruits, meat, etc.) for storage.
ex: to preserve peaches or grapes

s.def: past participle of preshrink

ety: From Old French presider, from Latin praesidēre (“preside”), from pre- (“before”) + sedere (“to sit”). Displaced Old English foresittan, which might have been a calque of the Latin.

s.def: To act as president or chairperson.
To exercise authority or control.
To be a featured solo performer.
ex: I’ll preside at the organ.

ety: From Medieval Latin praesidentia. By surface analysis, president + -cy.

s.def: The office or role of president.
ex: After many years as a party leader, she finally ascended to the presidency.
The American people gave me the priceless privilege of serving them in the Presidency.

s.def: The bureaucratic organization and governmental initiatives devolving directly from the president.
ex: Because of the president's lame duck status, the presidency was often hampered by congressional actions.

s.def: The time during which one is president; a president's term of office.
ex: In France, a presidency lasts for five years.
Ernest was a historian specializing in the presidency of Herbert Hoover.

s.def: A supreme local council made up of three persons; (usually capitalized; also First Presidency) the highest authority.
One of the three original provinces of British India.
The role of ordained clergy in the celebration of the Eucharist in some denominations.

ety: From Old French president, from Latin praesidēns (“presiding over; president, leader”) (accusative: praesidentem). The Latin word is the substantivized present active participle of the verb praesideō (“preside over”). The verb is composed from prae (“before”) and sedeō (“sit”). The original meaning of the verb is 'to sit before' in the sense of presiding at a meeting. A secondary meaning of the verb is 'to command, to govern'. So praesidēns means 'the presiding one on a meeting' or 'governor, c…

s.def: The head of state of a republic, sometimes also the head of government as well, particularly (US politics) the head of the executive branch of the federal government of the United States of America.
ex: The vast majority of presidents have been male.
[…] to change the pattern of the last 220 years of only voting for a white male president, and elect a woman president […]

s.def: A person presiding over a corporation, usually an executive overseeing daily operations under a chief executive officer but sometimes a separate position held by a CEO.
A person presiding over a meeting.
A person presiding over a dinner or similar informal conversation.
Occupying the first rank or chief place; having the highest authority; presiding.
ex: His angels president / In every province.

s.def: To act as president; to do presidential duties.
Obsolete form of precedent.

ety: Etymology tree English president Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisder. Old French -ialder. Middle English -ial English -ial English presidential From president + -ial.

s.def: Pertaining to a president or presidency.
Presiding or watching over.
With the bearing or composure that befits a president; stately, dignified.

ety: From Middle English price (“price, prize, value, excellence”), borrowed from Old French pris, preis, from Latin pretium (“worth, price, money spent, wages, reward”); compare praise, precious, appraise, appreciate, depreciate, etc.

ety: From Middle English prykkyl, prykyl, from Old English pricel, pricels, pricle (“a prickle, sharp point, bit”), from a conflation of Proto-West Germanic *prikislī and *prikil (“prickle”). ety: From Middle English prime, from Old French prime and its etymon, Latin prīmus (“first”), from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“beyond, before”). s.def: First in time, order, or sequence.
ex: Both the English and French governments established prime meridians in their capitals.

s.def: Having exactly two integral factors: itself and unity (1 in the case of integers).

First in importance, degree, or rank.

Early; blooming; being in the first stage.
