ex: This is a list of all prime ministers since Churchill.
Yesterday we had a visit from the Prime Minister / prime minister.

s.def: Any natural number (including 1) that is divisible only by itself and 1.
Any natural number greater than 1 that cannot be formed by multiplying two smaller natural numbers.

ety: From Middle English primer, primere, from Medieval Latin primarius and primarium (“prayer book”) possibly via Anglo-Norman primer (“prayer book”), from prima (“prime the liturgical hour and office”) + -arius and -arium (suffix forming related objects). Its use for schoolbooks derived from the late medieval and early modern use of such prayer books to teach reading.

s.def: A children's book intended to teach literacy: how to read, write, and spell.
A substance used to prime wood, metal, etc. in preparation for painting.

A prayer or devotional book intended for laity, initially an abridgment of the breviary and manual including the hours of the Virgin Mary, 15 gradual and 7 penitential psalms, the litany, the placebo and dirige forming the office of the dead, and the commendations.
Any of various similar works issued in England for private prayer in accordance with the Book of Common Prayer.
An introductory text on any subject, particularly basic concepts.
An elementary school class; an elementary school student.
Any substance or device, such as priming wire or blasting cap, used to ignite gunpowder or other explosive.
A person who primes explosives.
A layer of such a substance.
A layer of makeup that goes beneath the foundation; undermakeup.

ety: From Latin primaevus (“in the first or earliest period of life”) + -al, from primus (“first”) + aevum (“time, age”); see prime and age.

s.def: Belonging to the first ages.
ex: a primeval galaxy

s.def: Primary; original.
ex: But if life has a happiness over which the primeval curse has passed and harmed not, it is the early and long enduring affection of blood and habit.

s.def: Primitive.
A forest unaffected by humans, typically containing large live trees, large dead trees, and large logs.
A substance used as a primer.
A form of seed planting preparation in which the seeds are presoaked in a nanoparticle solution.
A harmful condition in which water is carried over from the boiler of a steam locomotive.
ex: There have been failures, of course, and especially delays due to bad steaming, and, more often, priming.
Priming may easily be detected by the motion of the water in the glass water gauge, or by the "flutter" of the gauge cocks when opened.

s.def: The powder or other combustible used to communicate fire to a charge of gunpowder, as in a firearm.
The first contact that an antigen-specific T helper cell precursors have with an antigen.
A cognitive process in which media information increases temporarily the accessibility of knowledge units in the memory of an individual.
The effect that a nutrient has on the rate of organic matter decomposition
The process of flushing the tubing with IV fluid to remove air before connecting it to a patient.
The implicit memory effect in which exposure to a stimulus influences response to a subsequent stimulus.
A form of positive priming that induces a tendency to repeat or more easily process a sentence that is similar in structure to one previously presented.

ety: From New Latin prīmiparus, from prīmus (“first”) + pariō (“to give birth”).

s.def: Pregnant or giving birth for the first time.
ex: [The linea nigra] may generally be regarded, especially in a primiparous female, as a certain sign of pregnancy[…]

s.def: Having borne only one child.

ety: From Middle English primitif, from Old French primitif, from Latin prīmitīvus (“first or earliest of its kind”), from prīmus (“first”); see prime. Doublet of primitivo.

s.def: A member of a primitive society.
An original or primary word; a word not derived from another, as opposed to derivative.
Primitive or primeval nature; the innate, instinctive element within a person; the deep, instinctive, precultural layer of human nature.
Natural or premodern environment or conditions; life lacking modern technology and society.
Any of the simplest elements (instructions, statements, etc.) available in a programming language.
ex: A write-what-where primitive allows the attacker to write arbitrary data wherever they want in the memory

s.def: A basic geometric shape from which more complex shapes can be constructed.
A simple-minded person.
A data type that is built into the programming language, as opposed to more complex structures.
A function whose derivative is a given function; an antiderivative.
Occurring in or characteristic of an early stage of development or evolution.
The Irish language as attested from the fourth to the seventh centuries C.E. and written in the Ogham alphabet, the predecessor of Old Irish.

ety: From Latin primus (“first”) + -o- + genitor (Latin genitor). Compare progenitor.

s.def: An initial ancestor.

ety: From French, from Late Latin primogenitura, from Latin primus (“first”) + genitura (“birth”) (from genitus, past participle of gignere).

s.def: The state of being the firstborn of the children of the same parents.
The principle that the eldest child has an exclusive right of inheritance.
An instance of such a right of inheritance, established by custom or law.

ety: From the Latin prīmōrdiālis (“of the beginning”). Compare primordium and -al.

s.def: First, earliest or original.
ex: the primordial facts of our intelligent nature
As an archetypal image of primordial unity, the cosmic egg suggests that there is unity and fragmentation, eternity and time.

s.def: Characteristic of the earliest stage of the development of an organism, or relating to a primordium.
ex: a primordial leaf; a primordial cell

s.def: Primeval.

Of an element or isotope: occurring primordially (on Earth) (i.e. inherited from when the Earth was formed); because it is stable, or radioactive but so long-lived that some is left over from when the Earth was formed. For example, primordial radioisotopes (T = half-life in years) include uranium-2…
A first principle or element.
A primordial condition or state.
The state of the Earth's oceans at a very early time in the planet's history, during the early development of multicellular organisms.
A collection of ideas or objects that become refined over time.
ex: While the number of ideas floating in this primordial soup is quite large , only a few ever receive serious consideration.

ety: Blend of prime + factorial. Coined by American engineer and mathematician Harvey Dubner.

s.def: product of primes
Any number belonging to the integer sequence whose nth element is the product of the first n primes.

A unary operation, denoted by the postfix symbol # and defined on the nonnegative integers, which maps 0 to 1, 1 to 1, and each subsequent number to the product of all primes less than or equal to it; the value mapped to by said operation for a given input.
ex: The primorial of 6 is #92;textstyle 6#92;#35;#61;2#92;times 3#92;times 5#61;30.

ety: 16th century, a variant of prim.

s.def: To spend time improving one's appearance, often in front of a mirror.
ex: "Then I promise I'll let you take your bath and primp all day for your date."

s.def: To dress in an affected manner.

ety: From Middle English primerose, from Old French primerose, from Medieval Latin prima (“first”) + rosa (“rose”). The designation may derive from the fact that certain species of primroses are among the earliest flowers to bloom in the spring season.

s.def: A flowering plant of the genus Primula.
ex: A mile or so further on is the intermediate station of Ryhall, smothered with primroses in the season, and at all times a veritable flower garden.
Here is spring were celandine, marsh marigold, wind-flower, primrose, cowslip and dog's violet.

s.def: A plant of the family Primulaceae.
A plant of the genus Oenothera, better known as an evening primrose.
A flower of a primrose plant.
A light yellow colour.
Of a light yellow colour.
ex: Passenger saloons are tastefully furnished with wood veneer and partitions, mottled grey Vyanide walls, pale primrose ceilings and grey floor.

s.def: To pick primroses.
ex: We went primrosing on Sunday and returned with a full basket.

s.def: portable kerosene stove
A type of portable stove that uses pressurized kerosene as fuel, used by campers and the like.
Any portable stove marketed under the Primus trademark that may use also other fuels, particularly butane or propane gas ("camping gas").
Alternative spelling of preen.
Alternative spelling of preen.

ety: From Middle English prince, from Anglo-Norman prince, from Latin prī̆nceps (“first head”), from prīmus (“first”) + capiō (“seize, take”). Cognate with Old English fruma (“prince, ruler”). Doublet of princeps and principe. Displaced English atheling (“prince”), from Middle English, from Old English æþeling (“prince”). Displaced also Middle English kinebarn (from cynebearn, literally “kinbairn”, i.e. “royal child”), alder < ealdor (“elder, leader, chief, prince, king”), and drighten < dryhten (“l…

s.def: The (male) ruler or head of a principality.
ex: He is the prince who never grew up – a one-time playboy and son of the Hollywood star Grace Kelly and Prince Rainier of Monaco.

s.def: son or male-line grandson of a reigning monarch
A (male) ruler, a sovereign; a king, monarch.
A female monarch.
ex: Queen Elizabeth, a prince admirable above her sex.

s.def: Someone who is preeminent in their field; a great person.
ex: He is a prince among men.

s.def: A male member of a royal family other than the ruler; especially (in the United Kingdom) the son or grandson of the monarch.
A non-royal high title of nobility, especially in France and the Holy Roman Empire.
ex: Prince Louis de Broglie won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physics.

s.def: A type of court card used in tarot cards, the equivalent of the jack.
The mushroom Agaricus augustus.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the genus Rohana.

ety: Calque of French Roi Charmant (“Charming King”).

s.def: A fictional heroic prince in various fairy-tales.
A heterosexual woman's prototypical ideal romantic partner, especially but not necessarily if he embodies common characteristics of the fictional princes, such as being courageous or chivalrous.
ex: She's still unmarried because she is waiting for her Prince Charming... and he may not exist.
She did not listen. She was free in her prison of passion. Her prince, Prince Charming, was with her.
There's always love for sale / A grown up fairy tale / Prince charming always smiles / Behind a silver spoon

s.def: A royal title given to the male heir apparent to the reigning monarch of the United Kingdom.

ety: From Middle English princely, pryncely, equivalent to prince + -ly (adjectival suffix). Compare Dutch prinselijk.

s.def: Relating to a prince.
ex: princely birth or character
She so bewitched the whole princely race that six different princes, although each was married to a young wife, remained childless.

s.def: Similar or comparable to a prince.
Befitting a prince.
ex: a princely sum
No expense was spared in making it a princely residence.

s.def: In the manner of a royal prince's conduct.
ex: […] my appetite was not princely gote, […]
Has the princely generous Dr. Townsend turned traitor to the old folks?
Harmeet was a 6 feet tall sardar, good sense of humor as all sardars do. He was also very princely dressed.

ety: From Middle English princesse, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman princesse, Old French princesse. By surface analysis, prince + -ess.

s.def: A female member of a royal family other than a queen, especially a daughter or granddaughter of a monarch.
ex: She did not cry long, however, for she was as brave as could be expected of a princess of her age.

s.def: A female ruler or monarch; a queen.
A woman or girl who excels in a given field or class.
ex: Michael Jackson was the king of pop. Britney Spears was the pop princess. Until they weren't.

s.def: The wife of a prince; the female ruler of a principality.
ex: Princess Grace was the Princess of Monaco.

s.def: A young girl; used as a term of endearment.
A young girl or woman (or less commonly a man) who is vain, spoiled, or selfish; a prima donna.
ex: Jonathan, if you hear this, you're a beautiful princess, but you're also a big, fat dork.

s.def: A tinted crystal marble used in children's games.
A type of court card in the Tarot pack, coming between the 10 and the prince (Jack).
A female lemur.
A Bulgarian open-faced baked sandwich prepared with ground meat.

ety: From princess + Elisabeth + island. Calque of Dutch Prinses Elisabetheiland. Named after Belgian princess Elisabeth of Brabant.

s.def: An island of the North Sea, Belgium.

ety: Borrowed from French princesse.

s.def: Being or relating to a princesse dress.
Archaic spelling of princess.
ex: But gently could his passion entertaine, / Though she Love's princesse, he a lowly swaine.

ety: From Middle English principal, from Old French principal, from Latin prīncipālis.

s.def: The chief administrator of a school.
ex: The important administrative figure to the teacher is the school principal.

s.def: Primary; most important; first level in importance.
ex: Smith is the principal architect of this design.
The principal cause of the failure was poor planning.
For many years, Oslo had no railway communication with Bergen and Stavanger, the principal seaports on the south-west coast.

s.def: Of or relating to a prince; princely.
ex: But walkt at will, and wandred to and fro, / In the pride of his freedome principall.

s.def: Chosen or assumed among a branch of possible values of a multi-valued function so that the function is single-valued.
ex: Two is the principal square root of 4. Both −2 and +2 are square roots of 4.

s.def: The money originally invested or loaned, on which basis interest and returns are calculated.
ex: A portion of your mortgage payment goes to reduce the principal, and the rest covers interest.
In March 1902, I find in the statement of liabilities and assets £711 put down as arrears of interest, but there is no entry of arrears of principal.
Coordinate term: interest

s.def: The chief executive and chief academic officer of a university or college.
ex: Coordinate term: bursar

s.def: A legal person that authorizes another (the agent) to act on their behalf; or on whose behalf an agent or gestor in a negotiorum gestio acts.
ex: When an attorney represents a client, the client is the principal who permits the attorney, the client′s agent, to act on the client′s behalf.
My principal sells metal shims.

s.def: The primary participant in a crime.
ex: The accessories may be prosecuted, tried and punished, though the principal has not been prosecuted or has been acquitted.

s.def: Either party in a duel.
A partner or owner of a business.

ety: From Middle English principalte, principalite, from Anglo-Norman principalté, Middle French principalté, from Late Latin prīncipālitās, from Latin prīncipālis (“principal”) + -tās. Equivalent to principal + -ity.

s.def: A region or sovereign nation headed by a prince or princess.
ex: At this time Russia consisted of a dozen or so principalities, which were frequently at war with one another.

s.def: A spiritual being, specifically in Christian angelology, the third lowest level of angels, ranked above archangels and below powers.
The state of being a prince or ruler; sovereignty, absolute authority.
The state of being principal; pre-eminence.
Former official name of Albania: a country and former principality in Southeastern Europe, existing from 1914 to 1925.
Official name of Andorra: a microstate in Southern Europe.

ety: From Middle English principle, from Old French principe, from Latin prīncipium (“beginning, foundation”), from prīnceps (“first”). By surface analysis, prīmus (“first”) + -ceps (“catcher”); the former ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”); see also prince.

s.def: A fundamental assumption, fundamental law or guiding belief.
ex: We need some sort of principles to reason from.

s.def: Moral rule or aspect.
ex: I don't doubt your principles.
You are clearly a person of principle.
It's the principle of the thing; I won't do business with someone I can't trust.

s.def: A rule or law of nature, or the basic idea on how the laws of nature are applied.
ex: Bernoulli's principle
The Pauli Exclusion Principle prevents two fermions from occupying the same state.
The principle of the internal combustion engine

s.def: A rule used to choose among solutions to a problem.
ex: The principle of least privilege holds that a process should only receive the permissions it needs.

s.def: A fundamental essence, particularly one producing a given quality.
ex: Many believe that life is the result of some vital principle.

s.def: A source, or origin; that from which anything proceeds; fundamental substance or energy; primordial substance; ultimate element, or cause.
ex: The soul of man is an active principle.

s.def: An original faculty or endowment.
ex: those active principles whose direct and ultimate object is the communication either of enjoyment or suffering

s.def: Misspelling of principal.
A beginning.
ex: Doubting sad end of principle unsound.

s.def: To equip with principles; to establish, or fix, in certain principles; to impress with any tenet or rule of conduct.
ex: Let an enthusiast be principled that he or his teacher is inspired.

ety: From Middle English prinken (“to wink, signal with the eye”), from prinke, prinche (“a wink, twinkling of the eye, momentary gesture”), from Old English princ (“a wink”). More at pry.

s.def: to give a wink; to wink.
The act of adjusting one's dress or appearance; the act of sprucing oneself up.
ex: “Is my sash right; and does my hair look very bad?” said Meg, as she turned from the glass in Mrs. Gardiner’s dressing-room, after a prolonged prink.

s.def: To look, gaze.
To dress finely, primp, preen, spruce up.
ex: […] by the Mass: You’ll make excellent Wives, Cuckold your Husbands immoderately: You mind nothing but prinking your selves up.

s.def: To strut, put on pompous airs, be pretentious.
To improve; to make stylish.
To pre-drink.

ety: From Middle English *printen, prenten, preenten, an apheretic form of emprinten, enprinten (“to impress; imprint”) (see imprint). Compare Dutch prenten (“to imprint”), Middle Low German prenten (“to print; write”), Danish prente (“to print”), Swedish prenta (“to write German letters”). Compare also Late Old French printer, preindre (“to press”), from Latin premere (“to press”).

s.def: To produce one or more copies of a text or image on a surface, especially by machine.
ex: Print the draft double-spaced so we can mark changes between the lines.

s.def: Of, relating to, or writing for printed publications.
ex: a print edition of a book

s.def: To produce a microchip (an integrated circuit) in a process resembling the printing of an image.
ex: The circuitry is printed onto the semiconductor surface.

s.def: To write very clearly, especially, to write without connecting the letters as in cursive.
ex: Print your name here and sign below.
I'm only in grade 2, so I only know how to print.

s.def: To publish in a book, newspaper, etc.
ex: How could they print an unfounded rumour like that?
From the moment he prints, he must expect to hear no more truth.

s.def: To stamp or impress (something) with coloured figures or patterns.
ex: to print calico

s.def: To fix or impress, as a stamp, mark, character, idea, etc., into or upon something.
ex: A look will print a thought that never may remove.
Upon his breastplate he beholds a dint, / Which in that field young Edward's sword did print.
some footsteps printed in the clay

s.def: To stamp something in or upon; to make an impression or mark upon by pressure, or as by pressure.
ex: Forth on his fiery steed betimes he rode, / That scarcely prints the turf on which he trod.

s.def: To inadequately conceal a weapon such that its outline or imprint is visible on the person wearing it.
To display a string on the terminal.
ex: However, when you print the string you can see only 11 characters (c, a, r, ', s,, w, h, e, e, l).
On the RHS side we write the current date to the variable date and print it to the terminal window, followed by the string "Chris coming home...." .

s.def: written or published
Put down on paper by a printing press or a computer printer.
ex: The parliament levied a tax on all printed matter.
All printed personal information must be shredded before it leaves this building.

s.def: Written to a data file.
ex: The output of this sample program is simply some printed lines such as "Hello, World; my name is [Name]."

s.def: Written on paper by hand in noncursive script.
ex: The signature was illegible, but the printed name beneath it clearly said "William Wilson."
Capitals, or 'printed handwriting' as one sees them called, are just as idiomorphic as a cursive form.

s.def: Ellipsis of 3D printed
ex: Then we take these various printed and machined components and build the assembly.

s.def: A flat board that holds chips and other electronic components in layers that interconnect by means of copper pathways, often called traces.

ety: From print + -er.

s.def: The operator of a printing press or the owner of a printing business; (metonymic) any printing business.
ex: Never one to waste an opportunity, he says now: "The low points? You can read about them in my forthcoming book! It's at the printers now.

s.def: A device, usually attached to a computer, used to print text or images onto paper; an analogous device capable of producing three-dimensional objects.
ex: By the use of these keys in conjunction with the other keys, the operator has perfect control over the receiving printer at the distant station.

s.def: One who makes prints.

ety: From printer + friendly.

s.def: Of a document or layout, suitable for printing, without any extraneous formatting, images, etc.
ex: On the flip side, your main navigation bar and the related links should be removed from the printer-friendly version.

ety: By surface analysis, print + -ing.

s.def: The process or business of producing printed material by means of inked type and a printing press or similar technology.
ex: In those days, printing was big business in this city. Giant web-fed presses churned out countless tons of printed matter annually.

s.def: Synonym of printed matter.
ex: They delivered a huge batch of printing yesterday, so you can expect an invoice shortly.

s.def: Synonym of print run (“all the copies of a publication that have been printed in one batch”).
ex: She owns a copy of the first printing, which is a favorite among book collectors because some of the typos in it seem like Freudian slips.

s.def: Handwritten characters that are not joined up.
present participle and gerund of print.

ety: From the expansive sense of house to refer to any building, particularly those like shops or workshops where people work together for a common purpose. Originally used in reference to printing workshops supplying or included within a bookshop; later used more expansively to refer to any institution or company involved in printing.

s.def: An institution or commercial company chiefly devoted to printing.
ex: Meronym: imprint (subsidiary printing house or brand name)

s.def: The building where printing occurs.
A place to make personal copies.
Synonym of printing house (“an institutional or commercial publisher”).
A mechanical device used for printing text or images repeatedly.

ety: Deverbal from print out.

s.def: Something printed on paper, usually a copy generated by a printer (machine).
ex: During the meeting, Trump brandished printouts of what he said were reports about White South Africans being killed.

ety: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin prior (“earlier, former, previous, prior; in front; (figurative) better, superior”), from Proto-Italic *priōs (“earlier, previous”, literally “more before”), ultimately from *pri (“before”) (from Proto-Indo-European *pró (“leading to, toward”) and its etymon *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + *-jōs (suffix forming comparative adjectives). Doublet of before, fore, and former. The adverb and noun are derived from the adjective.

s.def: Coming before in order or time; earlier, former, previous.
ex: His prior residence was smaller than his current one.
I had no prior knowledge you were coming.
Lady Marney, duly warned of the impending catastrophe, was experiencing all the advantages of prior information.

s.def: Chiefly in prior probability: of the probability of an event: determined without knowledge of the occurrence of other events that bear on it, before additional data is collected.
More important or significant.
Chiefly followed by to: in advance, before, previously.
ex: The doctor had known three months prior.

s.def: A prior probability distribution, that is, one determined without knowledge of the occurrence of other events that bear on it, before additional data is collected.
A previous arrest or criminal conviction on someone's criminal record.
ex: And a little later we get the routine report on his prints from Washington, and he's got a prior back in Indiana, attempted hold-up six years ago.

s.def: A high-ranking member of a religious house or religious order.
A chief magistrate of the Republic of Florence (1115–1569) in what is now Italy.
The elected head of a guild of craftsmen or merchants in some countries in Europe and South America.
A person who is the earliest or most prominent in a field; the chief.

ety: From priority + -ize. First attested in 1967 as U.S. government jargon, becoming more widespread through the 1970s and ’80s, but still denounced as officialese by purists into the 1990s.

s.def: To arrange or list a group of things in order of priority or importance.
To value, do, or choose something first, or before other things.
ex: When I don't have time to buy everything at the store, I prioritize fresh fruit and vegetables over foods like rice or noodles.
Loretta's already designing the next smelter. She has some improvements in mind. The new one will prioritize silicon extraction and—
Skinimalism prioritizes skin health and lets your natural beauty shine through.

s.def: To rank something as having high priority.
with priority, having priority

ety: From Old French priorite, from Latin priōritās. Surface analysis: prior + -ity.

s.def: An item's relative importance.
ex: He set his e-mail message's priority to high.

s.def: A goal of a person or an organisation.
ex: She needs to get her priorities straight and stop playing games.

s.def: The quality of being earlier or coming first compared to another thing; the state of being prior.
ex: In bankruptcy law, a business' debt to its employees has priority over its debt to a landlord, so the employees must be paid first.

s.def: A superior claim to use by virtue of being validly published at an earlier date.
Precedence; superior rank.
ex: Follow Cominius. We must follow you. / Right worthy you priority.
Who has priority, one's mother or one's wife? Question: To whom should a married man should give much preference, either his mother or wife?

s.def: Right of way; The right to pass (an intersection) before other road users.

ety: From Anglo-Norman priorie.

s.def: A monastery or convent governed by a prior or prioress.

s.def: type of polyhedron
transparent block used to reflect or refract light
A polyhedron with parallel ends of the same polygonal shape and size, the other faces being parallelogram-shaped sides.
ex: The beams, that thro' the Oriel shine, / Make prisms in every carven glass, […]

s.def: A retroreflector (“device which reflects light back to its source with minimal scattering”) which is usually attached to a surveying pole as a target for a total station which emits a light beam at the device and calculates how long it takes to be reflected back in order to measure distance.
A perspective that colours one's perception.
ex: I had surveyed the landscape through the prism of poetry, which tinged every object with the hues of the rainbow.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek πρῑ́ω (prī́ō) Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Hellenic *-mə Ancient Greek -μᾰ (-mă) Ancient Greek πρίσματος (prísmatos) Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -ique Middle French -ique French -ique French prismatiquebor. English prismatic Borrowed from French prismatique. Equivalent to prism + -atic.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a prism; having the form of a prism; containing one or more prisms.
Separated or distributed by, or as if by, a transparent prism; formed by a prism; varied or brilliant in color.
Colors visible when white light is split in a prism.
Colours visible when white light is split in a prisma.

ety: From Middle English prisoun, prison, from Old English prisūn, a borrowing from Old French prison, from Latin prehensiōnem, accusative singular of prehensiō, from the verb prehendō. Doublet of prehension.

s.def: A place or institution where people are held against their will, in the US especially for long-term confinement, as of those convicted of serious crimes or otherwise considered undesirable by the government.
ex: The cold stone walls of the prison had stood for over a century.

s.def: Confinement in prison (sense 1).
ex: Prison was a harrowing experience for him.

s.def: Any restrictive environment, such as a harsh academy or home.
ex: The academy was a prison for many of its students because of its strict teachers.

s.def: To imprison.
The room to which a prisoner is confined in a prison.

ety: From Middle English prisoner, from Old French prisonier (compare Medieval Latin prisōnārius), equivalent to prison + -er.

s.def: A person incarcerated in a prison, while on trial or serving a sentence.
ex: Two other prisoners were staying in the same cell as him.

s.def: Any person held against their will.
A person who is or feels confined or trapped by a situation or a set of circumstances.
ex: I am no longer a prisoner to fear, for I am a child of God.
I'm a prisoner of your love.
You're not a hit and run driver, no no, racing away. You just picked up a hitcher, a prisoner of the white lines on the freeway

ety: Defined by Peter Benenson in his article "The Forgotten Prisoners" in 1961.

ex: My pronouns are she/her. What are your pronouns?

ety: Borrowed from Spanish pronunciamento. Doublet of pronouncement.

ety: From Middle English pronunciacioun, from Middle French prononciation, pronunciation, from Latin prōnūntiātiō, noun of action from perfect passive participle prōnūntiātus, from verb prōnūntiāre (“proclaim”), from prō- (“for”) + nūntiāre (“announce”). Doublet of pronuntiatio.

ety: From Middle English proof, from Old French prove, from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from Latin probō (“to prove”); see prove; compare also the doublet probe.

s.def: An effort, process, or operation designed to establish or discover a fact or truth; an act of testing; a test; a trial.
ex: I need proof of your unconditional love. Lend me some dough.
France I more praise and love; you are, my lord, Yourself for horsemanship much famed; and there You shall have many proofs to shew your skill.

s.def: The degree of evidence which convinces the mind of any truth or fact, and produces belief; a test by facts or arguments which induce, or tend to induce, certainty of the judgment; conclusive evidence; demonstration.
ex: I'll have some proof.
Faith, faith is an island in the setting sun But proof, yes Proof is the bottom line for everyone

s.def: The quality or state of having been proved or tried; firmness or hardness which resists impression, or does not yield to force; impenetrability of physical bodies.
Experience of something.
ex: But the chaste damzell, that had never priefe / Of such malengine and fine forgerye, / Did easely beleeve her strong extremitye.

s.def: Firmness of mind; stability not to be shaken.
A proof sheet; a trial impression, as from type, taken for correction or examination.
ex: And these men scour the printed proof for error, blunder, and misspelling.

s.def: A process for testing the accuracy of an operation performed. Compare prove, transitive verb, 5.

A sequence of statements consisting of axioms, assumptions, statements already demonstrated in another proof, and statements that logically follow from previous statements in the sequence, and which concludes with a statement that is the object of the proof.

I want to thank Sherri and Dee Humphreys, Mark Randolph and Paul Gonzalez for their proofreads and input.
To Veronique Kaemerer and her eng. 101 students, Michael Horanburg and Brady Meador for their proofreads.

ety: From proof + reader.

ety: From Middle English proppe (“a prop, support, support for a vine or plant”), from Middle Dutch proppe (“support, support for a vine, stopper for a bottle”). Compare Middle Low German proppe (“plug, stopper”), German Pfropfen (“plug”), Danish prop (“plug, stopper”).

An object placed against or under another, to support it; anything that supports.

ety: First attested in 1535; from Latin prōpāgātus, perfect passive participle of prōpāgō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

ex: I can discern your nature and see that even without any arguments (logoi) from me it will propel you to what you say you are drawn towards,

A steamboat thus propelled; a screw steamer.
A spinnerbait.

ety: From Middle English propertee, properte, propirte, proprete, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French propreté, proprieté (“propriety, fitness, property”), from Latin proprietās (“a peculiarity, one's peculiar nature or quality, right or fact of possession, property”), from proprius (“special, particular, one's own”). ety: From Latin prophylacticus, from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, “prophylactic”).

ex: The securities laws are a prophylactic against stock fraud.

s.def: Serving to prevent or protect against an undesired effect, especially disease or pregnancy.

ex: The role of statins in prophylaxis for cardiovascular disease is well supported by the medical literature.

s.def: Action that works to prevent some bad outcome.
ex: The central bankers viewed these moves as prophylaxis against inflation.

s.def: An aromatic glue-like substance produced by honeybees from tree resin, waxes, and their own secretions, used in the construction of their hives.

Making proposals; proposing.

s.def: A quantity of something that is part of the whole amount or number.
Harmonious relation of parts to each other or to the whole.
Proper or equal share.
ex: Let the women[…]do the same things in their proportions and capacities.

s.def: The relation of one part to another or to the whole with respect to magnitude, quantity, or degree.
ex: the proportion of the parts of a building, or of the body

Size.

ex: “Wiktionary is a good dictionary” is a proposition.

s.def: An assertion so formulated that it can be considered true or false.
An assertion which is provably true, but not important enough to be called a theorem.
A statement of religious doctrine; an article of faith; a creed.
ex: the propositions of Wyclif and Huss

s.def: The part of a poem in which the author states the subject or matter of it.

s.def: To put forward; to offer for discussion or debate.
ex: Today I'll expound at length the theory that I propounded last year.

ex: ‘I can see from your records you were prescribed propranolol for your headaches.’

ety: From French propriétaire, from Latin proprietārius. By surface analysis, propriety + -ary. Compare with the Latin proprietas (“property”) and proprius (“ownership”).

ex: proprietary rights

s.def: Owning something; having ownership.
ex: the proprietary class

s.def: Created or manufactured exclusively by the owner or licensee of intellectual property rights, as with a patent or trade secret.
ex: The continuous profitability of the company is based on its many proprietary products.

s.def: Nonstandard and controlled by one particular organization.
ex: a proprietary extension to the HTML standard for Web page structure

s.def: Privately owned.
ex: a proprietary lake; a proprietary chapel

s.def: Possessive, jealous, or territorial.
A proprietor or owner.
A body of proprietors, taken collectively.
The rights of a proprietor.
A monk who had reserved goods and belongings to himself, notwithstanding his renunciation of all at the time of profession.

ety: Probably from proprietary + -or.

s.def: An owner.
ex: Here the proprietor has had the good sense of holding on to the good old fashion of giving his customers their moneyworth of good wines and liquors.

s.def: A sole owner of an unincorporated business, also called a sole proprietor.
One of the owners of an unincorporated business, a partner.
One or more persons to whom a colonial territory is assigned, like a fief, including its administration.

ety: From late Middle English proprietee, propretee, propriete (“ownership”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman propreté, Middle French proprieté, from Latin proprietās. By surface analysis, prop(e)r + -iety. Doublet of property.

s.def: The particular character or essence of someone or something; individuality.
A characteristic; an attribute.
A piece of land owned by someone; someone's property.
More generally, something owned by someone; a possession.
The fact of possessing something; ownership.
Correct language or pronunciation.
Suitability, fitness; the quality of being appropriate.
ex: I find such a pleasure, sir, in obeying your commands, that I take care to observe them without ever debating their propriety.
Now, if we may, with propriety, refer to the people one question, why may we not, with equal propriety, refer another?

s.def: Correctness in behaviour and morals; good manners, seemliness.
ex: Elinor then ventured to doubt the propriety of her receiving such a present from a man so little, or at least so lately known to her.

s.def: exophthalmos

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsio, propulsionis, from the past participle of Latin propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).

s.def: The process of propelling, driving, or pushing, typically forward or onward; a propulsive force or impulse.
That which propels.
ex: However, nuclear propulsion provides a very high specific impulse and consistent, long duration energy source.
This propulsion provides an initial velocity for the vehicle in a short time span.
Solar-electric propulsion accelerates a spacecraft by means of a low-thrust ion jet.

ety: From Latin propylaeum, from Ancient Greek προπύλαιον (propúlaion), from προ- (pro-, “before”, “in front of”) + πύλη (púlē, “gate”).

ety: Borrowed from Latin propylon, from Ancient Greek πρόπῠλον (própŭlon).

s.def: Alternative spelling of propylaeum.

ety: American English derivation from pro rata, from Latin pro (“according to”) + ratus (“calculated”).

s.def: To divide proportionately, especially by day; to divide pro rata.

ety: From Old French proroger, proroguer, from Latin prōrogō (“prolong, defer”).

s.def: To suspend (a parliamentary session) or to discontinue the meetings of (an assembly, parliament etc.) without formally ending the session.
To defer.
To prolong or extend.
ex: Mirth[…]prorogues life, whets the wit, makes the body young, lively, and fit for any manner of employment.
The King settled to prorogue Parliament until the Christmas holidays, and to do nothing else for the present.

ety: From Latin prō (“for, on behalf of”) and contrā (“against”).

ety: From Middle English proscriben, from Latin prōscrībō (“to proclaim, forbid, banish”).

s.def: To denounce.
ex: The word ‘ain't’ is proscribed by many authorities.

s.def: To banish or exclude.
ex: Many Roman citizens were proscribed for taking part in rebellions.

ety: From Middle English proscripcion, from Latin prōscrīptiō, from prōscrībō (originally "publish in writing"), from prō- and scrībō (“write”).

s.def: A prohibition.
Decree of condemnation toward one or more persons, especially in the Roman antiquity.

s.def: The act of proscribing, or its result.
A decree or law that prohibits.

ety: From Middle English prose, from Old French prose, from Latin prōsa (“straightforward”) from the term prōsa ōrātiō (“a straightforward speech – i.e. without the ornaments of verse”). further etymology and related terms The term prōsa (“straightforward”), a colloquial form of prorsa (“straight forwards”), the feminine form prorsus (“straight forwards”), from Old Latin prōvorsus (“moving straight ahead”), from pro- (“forward”) + vorsus (“turned”), form of vertō (“to turn”). Compare verse.

s.def: Language, particularly written language, not intended as poetry.

s.def: Language which evinces little imagination or animation; dull and commonplace discourse.
A hymn with no regular meter, sometimes introduced into the Mass.
To write or repeat in a dull, tedious, or prosy way.

ety: Borrowed from Latin prōsecūtus, perfect participle of prōsequor. Doublet of pursue, from Old French. Compare also persecute.

s.def: To start criminal proceedings against.
ex: to prosecute a man for trespass, or for a riot

s.def: To charge, try.

ex: to prosecute a right or a claim in a court of law

s.def: To pursue something to the end.
ex: to prosecute a scheme, hope, or an investigation

ety: Equivalent to prosecute + -ion, from Middle French prosecution, from Late Latin prōsecutio, from Latin prōsequor (“follow, pursue”), from pro- (“onward”) + sequor (“follow”) (English sequel). Compare persecution, and see more at prosecute.

s.def: The act of prosecuting a scheme or endeavor.

ex: Backed by public outrage, the prosecution requested the death penalty to be imposed on the murderer.

ety: First use appears c. 1542, from Medieval Latin prosecutor, from prōsequor (English prosecute). By surface analysis, prosecute + -or.

A prosecuting attorney.

s.def: A person, as a complainant, victim, or chief witness, who institutes prosecution in a criminal proceeding.
ex: The prosecutor got the witness to admit he was lying.

ety: From Old French proselite, from Late Latin proselytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”) (from πρός (prós, “to, towards”) and the stem -ηλυ- of ἐλήλυθα (elḗlutha), perfect of ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “come”)), translation of Hebrew גר (ger) in the Septuagint translation of the Torah (e.g., Exodus 12:49); also used in Matthew 23:15, Acts 2:10, Acts 6:5.

s.def: One who has converted to a religion or doctrine, especially a gentile converted to Judaism.
ex: You are my doctor, my saviour, my omnipotent judge, my priest, my god, the surgeon of my soul. And I am your proselyte to sanity.

s.def: To proselytize.

ety: From Middle English prospecte, from Latin prōspectus (“view, sight, prospect; panorama”), from prōspiciō (“to look forward”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns), from pro (“before, forward”) + speciō, spiciō (“to look, to see”). The authority assumed by a state over another state deemed inferior or dependent, whereby the former protects the latter from invasion and shares in the management of its affairs but the protected state retains its nominal sovereignty.
ex: Egypt became a British protectorate in 1914.

s.def: An autonomous state under protectorate.
The office or position of protector (sense 5).
A former protectorate of Nazi Germany, established in 1939 and covering present-day Czech Republic.

s.def: A food supplement created to provide a greater share of protein than natural nutrition.

ex: We held a protest in front of City Hall.
All this has led to an explosion of protest across China, including among a middle class that has discovered nimbyism.

ex: How dare you, I protest!

s.def: To affirm (something).
ex: I protest my innocence.
I do protest and declare …

s.def: To object to.
To publicly demonstrate against.
ex: They protested the demolition of the school.

s.def: To call as a witness in affirming or denying, or to prove an affirmation; to appeal to.
ex: Fiercely [they] opposed / My journey strange, with clamorous uproar / Protesting fate supreme.

s.def: to make a solemn written declaration, in due form, on behalf of the holder, against all parties liable for any loss or damage to be sustained by non-acceptance or non-payment of (a bill or note). This should be made by a notary public, whose seal it is the usual practice to affix.
To publish; to make known.
The noting by a notary public of an unpaid or unaccepted bill.

ety: From the genus name.

Credence table.

A registrar or chief clerk in various courts of law, especially (US) in a county court, (Australia) in certain state Supreme Courts, (Canada) in Federal Court.

Any of the eukaryotic, usually unicellular organisms—including protozoans, slime molds and some algae—historically grouped into the kingdom Protista (or Protoctista), now distributed over several clades; any eukaryote that is not a plant, animal or fungus.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French protocolle, protocole (“document, record”), from Late Latin protocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).

ex: An exception is Jabber, which is designed based on an open protocol called the extensible messaging and presence protocol (XMPP).

s.def: The minutes, or official record, of a negotiation or transaction; especially a document drawn up officially which forms the legal basis for subsequent agreements based on it.

ex: The terms of this protocol formed the basis for the Treaty of London signed by the British, French and Russian governments on 6 July 1827.

s.def: An amendment to an official treaty.

An accepted code of conduct; acceptable behaviour in a given situation or group.

A fever, following childbirth or abortion, due to infection of the uterus.
ex: It was the rise of penicillin, not improved hygiene, that finally conquered puerperal fever.

ety: Borrowed from Latin puerperium (“childbed, childbirth”), from puerpera (“woman in labor or childbed”) + -ium (nominal suffix), from puerperus (“parturient, bringing forth children”), from puer (“child, boy”) + pariō (“to bring forth, bear”) + -us (adjectival suffix).

s.def: The period of time lasting around a month immediately following childbirth, when the mother’s uterus shrinks back to its prepartum state.
ex: As exciting causes, psychic traumata, exposure to cold, the puerperium, excesses, have been brought forward.

ety: From Spanish Puerto Galera.

s.def: A municipality of Oriental Mindoro, Philippines.

ety: From Puerto Rico + -an.

s.def: A person from Puerto Rico.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Puerto Rico (literally “Rich Port”). In US English, the name is commonly pronounced and was formerly spelled Porto Rico; many other Spanish Puerto placenames were formerly also anglicized to Porto.

s.def: A self-governing commonwealth and dependent territory of the United States in the Caribbean.
ex: He also added, “I love Puerto Rico and vacation there. I made fun of everyone… watch the whole set.”

s.def: The island comprising most of that territory.
ex: The indigenous Taíno name for the island of Puerto Rico was 'Borikén', which literally means "Homeland of the People".

ety: From Middle English puff, puf, from Old English pyf (“a blast of wind, puff”), from Proto-West Germanic *puf(f)- (“to blow, puff”), of imitative origin. Cognate with Dutch puf (“puff, wind, fart”), Middle Low German puf, pof (“puff”).

s.def: A sharp exhalation of a small amount of breath through the mouth.
The ability to breathe easily while exerting oneself.
A small quantity of gas or smoke in the air.
ex: puff of smoke

s.def: A sudden but small gust of wind, smoke, etc.
ex: to every puff of wind a slave
"The wind we had was only an early puff! You'll see we shall have our full allowance!"

s.def: An act of inhaling smoke from a cigarette, cigar or pipe.
The drug cannabis.
A flamboyant or alluring statement of praise.
ex: […] though I care not one straw for the personal puffs of which I myself am so often the subject […]
[…] we critics were not his fellow-guests, but simply deadheads whose business it was to "dress the house" and write puffs.

s.def: A portion of fabric gathered up so as to be left full in the middle.
ex: a sleeve with a puff at the shoulder

s.def: A light cake filled with cream, cream cheese, etc.
A puffball.
ex: Bozzacchio, an acorne. Also a puffe or mushrump full of dust.

s.def: A light, flaky pastry that is made of alternating buttery and floury dough layers by repeatedly folding the rolled pastry into many layers.
To become proud. (Often written as puffed up with pride.)
To inflate with air.
ex: We puffed up the balloons.

s.def: To fluff up, such as an animal raising its fur or feathers to appear larger or conserve body heat.
ex: Small birds puff up while sleeping to keep warm.
The angry cat hissed and puffed up its fur.

s.def: To swell due to injury or illness.
ex: My hand puffed up where the cat had scratched me.

s.def: To trump up.

ety: From puff + ball.

s.def: Any of various fungi, usually globose, that produce a cloud of brown dust-like spores from their mature fruiting bodies, especially in family Lycoperdaceae.
Any of various mushrooms with globose fruiting bodies.
A dandelion flower that has gone to seed, a dandelion clock.
Something lacking substance.
ex: Scads of souls thought the record was yet another puffball from ex-Beatle Paul.

ety: Etymology tree English puff Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English puffer From puff + -er. The cellular automata definition is a clipping of puffer train.

s.def: Someone or something that puffs.
Any of several poisonous fish, of the family Tetraodontidae, which have the ability to inflate their bodies when in danger.
A manually-operated inhaler.
ex: For years he'd made relatively light of it, referring to the little inhaler he had to use as his ‘puffer’.

s.def: A train; a locomotive, usually one that is steam-powered.
A Clyde puffer, a kind of small ship.
A car left idling to warm up, emitting steam from the rear.
An insulated puffy jacket, such as a down jacket.
A person who gives exaggerated praise to a product, literary work, etc.
One who is employed by the owner or seller of goods sold at auction to bid up the price; a by-bidder.
ex: Cicero in his Offices declares his opinion , that a vendor ought not to appoint a puffer to raise the price

s.def: An alchemist; so named from their constant attendance to the bellows of their furnaces.

ety: From Middle English poffin, poffoun, puffon, equivalent to puff + -ing, or perhaps ultimately from Middle Cornish (compare Breton poc'han (“puffin”)).

s.def: The Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica) or (by extension) any of the other various small seabirds of the genera Fratercula and Lunda that are black and white with a brightly-coloured beak.
The young of the Manx shearwater (Puffinus puffinus), especially eaten as food.
Any of various African and Asian pierid butterflies of the genus Appias. Some species of this genus are also known as albatrosses.
A puffball.

ety: From puff + -y.

s.def: Swollen or inflated in shape, as if filled with air; pillow-like.
Coming or exhaling in puffs.
ex: puffy breath
A puffy fat man in a tracksuit came jogging around the corner.

s.def: Speaking or writing in an exaggeratedly eloquent and self-important manner.
Having inflated cheeks.

ety: Origin unknown, possibly related to West Flemish pugge (“(adjective) small; (noun) short person; pet name derived from the first name Pugge”); though it is uncertain whether sense 1 (“senses relating to someone or something small”) and sense 2 (“senses relating to people”) are derived from the same source. Etymology 1 sense 1.8 (“small demon”) was probably influenced by, though not a variant of, puck.

s.def: Senses relating to someone or something small.
ex: Dear, delicate Madam, I am your little Paraquit, your Sparrovv, your Shock, your Pugg, your Squirrel.

s.def: Senses relating to people.
ex: In the vigor of his age he married Gargamelle, daughter to the King of the Parpaillons, a jolly pug, and well mouthed wench.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of PuG (“a group of players who are unknown to each other, grouped together to work toward a short-term goal such as completing a dungeon or a raid”).
The footprint or pawprint of an animal; a pugmark.
To track (an animal) by following pawprints; also (by extension) to track (a person) by following footprints.
Clipping of pugilist (“one who fights with their fists, especially a professional prize fighter; a boxer”).
To hit or punch (someone or something); also, to poke (someone or something).

To fill or stop up (a space) with pug (noun etymology 5, noun sense 1), clay, sawdust, or other material by tamping; (specifically) to fill in (the space between joists of a floor, a partition, etc.) with some material to deaden sound, make fireproof, etc.
To mix and work (wet clay) until flexible, soft, and free from air pockets and suitable for making bricks, pottery, etc.
ex: to pug clay ready for shaping

s.def: Of cattle, etc.: to trample (the ground, a place, etc.) until it becomes muddy and soft; to poach.

ety: From Latin pugil (“boxer”) + -ist, related to pugnus (“fist”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”). Compare contemporary pugilism (“boxing”) (1791).

s.def: One who fights with their fists, especially a professional prize fighter; a boxer.
ex: I laugh and hoot at ye, ye cricket-players, ye pugilists, ye deaf Burkes and blind Bendigoes!

s.def: One who engages in rhetorical attacks, for himself or on behalf of another.
ex: Mr. Patel has a long record as a fierce pugilist for Mr. Trump, pushing some of the pro-Trump orbit’s most dubious theories[.]
President Nixon tried to make leaders of communist bloc countries believe he was a volatile, irrational pugilist.

ety: From the stem of Latin pugnāx + -ous, from pugnō (“to fight”), from pugnus (“fist”). By surface analysis, Latin pugn- + -acious.

s.def: Naturally aggressive or hostile; combative; belligerent; bellicose.
ex: As he made the demand he spat out a mouthful of blood and teeth and shoved his pugnacious face close to Oofty-Oofty.
In the face of bad news Churchill normally became even more pugnacious, always wanting to respond to defeat by going on the attack.

ety: From Latin pugnacitas (whence -acity).

s.def: The act or characteristic of being aggressive or combative.
ex: His sister is out front, cleaning her gun with that intimidating pugnacity that has most of the men in town keeping well clear of her.

s.def: Younger; junior.
Insignificant, petty; ineffectual.
Inferior in rank, as designation of any justice, judge etc. other than the most senior.
ex: the puisne barons of the Court of Exchequer

s.def: Coming later in time; subsequent, secondary.
ex: a puisne date to eternity

s.def: A person of puisne rank.

ety: From Middle English puissaunt, from Middle French puissant, poissant, Anglo-Norman puissant, Old French pussant, et al., present participle of pooir (“to be able”), ultimately from Latin posse (“be able”).

s.def: Powerful, mighty, having authority.
ex: Awake remembrance of these valiant dead, / And with your puissant arm renew their feats.
I cried in a loud voice, "Long live the most puissant king of Lilliput!"
How comes all this, if there be not something puissant in whaling?

ety: Probably imitative; or, alternatively related to Proto-Germanic *pukaną (“to spit, puff”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). If so, then related to German pfauchen, fauchen (“to hiss, spit”), Dutch spugen (“to spit, spit up”), German spucken (“to spit, puke, throw up”), and Old English spīwan (“to vomit, spit”). More at spew. Attested as early as 1581, first mention is the derivative pukishness (“the tendency to be sick frequently”). In 1600, "to spit up, regurgitate", recorded…

s.def: A person from Missouri.
ex: "Pukes" and "suckers" had badly mauled the Saints, the first pummeling them from Missouri and the second from Illinois.

s.def: vomit.
A drug that induces vomiting.
ex: "at 8 a.m. took a puke of vinum antimoniale; which operated very kindly; was very weak the remainder of the day."

s.def: A worthless, despicable person.
To vomit; to throw up; to eject from the stomach.
ex: Unfortunately, he could not hold it long enough till the end of the ride, so he puked on the bus seat.
At first the infant, Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms

s.def: To sell securities or investments at a loss, often under duress or pressure, in order to satisfy liquidity or margin requirements, or out of a desire to exit a deteriorating market.
A fine grade of woolen cloth.
ex: Puke-stocking caddis garter

s.def: A very dark, dull, brownish-red color.

ety: From Hindi पक्का (pakkā, “certain, sure”), Punjabi ਪੱਕਾ (pakkā, “mature, ripe; cooked; strong, substantial; genuine, sound, true, valid”) and Urdu پکا (pakkā, “mature, ripe; cooked; strong, substantial; genuine, sound, true, valid”), from Sanskrit पक्व (pakva, “baked, cooked, roasted”), from पचति (pacati, “to bake, cook, roast”).

s.def: Genuine or authentic; hence of behaviour: correct, socially acceptable or proper.
ex: Maha Rajah said it was necessary to witness it to make it pukka; and they said so too, and then signed it.
But let's assume it's a real pukka rare bird.

s.def: Constructed as a permanent building, with high-quality materials (especially fired clay bricks and tiles as opposed to unfired mud and thatch).
ex: The kutcha house made of mud, bamboo, and thatch and its modern replacement the pukka house, constructed of fired bricks, cement, and steel.

s.def: Superior or of high quality; first-class; excellent.
ex: Mind you, it was a pukka, respectable opium-house, and not one of those stifling, sweltering chandoo-khanas, that you can find all over the City.

ety: From Middle English pulcritude, from Latin pulchritūdō, from pulcher (“beautiful”).

s.def: Physical beauty.
ex: Do you know why a woman of such pulchritude is married to me? 'Cause I make a comfortable living.

ety: From French piauler, a variant of French piailler (“to chirp, cheep”). Compare Italian pigolare (“to cheep as a chicken”).

s.def: A plaintive melancholy whine.
To whimper or whine.
ex: Although the elderly man felt mounting pain from his illness, he never complained or puled.
... rain-drops over the puling baby she carried in her arms;[…]

s.def: To pipe or chirp.
To fall in a continuous, light dribble.
ex: ... looked at the puling sky, face upturned to a mirr of rain.

s.def: A Serbian cheese made from donkey milk.

ety: Verb from Middle English pullen, from Old English pullian (“to pull, draw, tug, pluck off”), of uncertain ultimate origin. Related to West Frisian pûlje (“to shell, husk”), Middle Dutch pullen (“to drink”), Middle Dutch polen (“to peel, strip”), Low German pulen (“to pick, pluck, pull, tear, strip off husks”), Icelandic púla (“to work hard, beat”). Noun from Middle English pul, pull, pulle, from the verb pullen (“to pull”).

s.def: To apply a force to (an object) so that it comes toward the person or thing applying the force.
ex: When I give the signal, pull the rope.
Pull your belt tight before starting off, will you?
He put forth his hand […] and pulled her in.

s.def: To gather with the hand, or by drawing toward oneself; to pluck or pick (flowers, fruit, etc.).
ex: to pull fruit from a tree
pull a finch

s.def: To attract or net; to pull in.
ex: Television, a favored source of news and information, pulls the largest share of advertising monies.

s.def: To persuade (someone) to have sex with one.
ex: I pulled at the club last night.
He's pulled that bird over there.
Grab your coat, love, you've pulled.

s.def: To interest (someone) in dating or pursuing one (whether or not this has led to sex).
ex: Wow, Joyce pulls, actually.

s.def: To remove or withdraw (something), especially from public circulation or availability.
ex: Each day, they pulled the old bread and set out fresh loaves.
The book was due to be released today, but it was pulled at the last minute over legal concerns.

s.def: To retrieve or look up for use.
ex: I'll have to pull a part number for that.
This computer file is incorrect. Can we pull the old version from your backups?
They'll go through their computer system and pull a report of all your order fulfillment records for the time period you specify.

s.def: To obtain (a permit) from a regulatory authority.
ex: It's the contractor's responsibility to pull the necessary permits before starting work.

s.def: To do or perform, especially something seen as negative by the speaker.
ex: He regularly pulls 12-hour days, sometimes 14.
You'll be sent home if you pull another stunt like that.
What are you trying to pull?

s.def: To copy or emulate the actions or behaviour associated with the person or thing mentioned (with a and the name of a person, place, event, etc.).
ex: He pulled an Elvis and got really fat.
They're trying to pull a Watergate on us.

der: it's not the whistle that pulls the tra…

s.def: To carry out a trick or act of deception; to behave contrary to expectations.
ex: This isn't worth anything like what you paid them. I think they pulled a fast one on you.
The man known as Chainsaw Al pulled a fast one last week, buying three companies when everyone assumed he would be selling his own.
7. Claimants are pulling a fast one. No. Less than 1% of the welfare budget is lost to fraud.

s.def: To stay awake throughout the night, usually when working or studying.
ex: Near-synonyms: burn the midnight oil, elucubrate
OK, let's order some pizzas and get comfortable, because we're gonna be pulling an all-nighter to get this emergency help put together.

s.def: To demolish or destroy (a building etc.).
ex: Bawd. But shall all our houses of resort in the Suburbs be puld downe?

s.def: To make (something) lower (especially of clothes).
To cause to fall to the floor
To fabricate (a factual-sounding claim) from no factual basis or evidence.
ex: Don says his community is 95% Caucasian, but I think he pulled that figure out of his ass.

s.def: To come to a stop, and turn off the road (i.e. onto the roadside or hard shoulder).
ex: Can you pull over just after the post office? My house is next door.

s.def: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see pull, over.
To command or force someone to drive their vehicle to the side of the road or curb and come to a stop.
ex: The cops pulled me over for speeding.

ety: The phrase from Scotland originally meant to make a fool of someone, often by cheating him. One theory is that it is derived from tripping someone by yanking or pulling his leg in order to make him stumble and look foolish.

s.def: To tease someone; to lead someone on; to goad someone into overreacting.
ex: I hadn't pulled Mrs. Barstow's leg for any of that stuff, she had just handed it to me on a platter, and that wasn't my fault.
No, I'm just pulling your leg, it's crucifixion really.

s.def: To extract money from someone (by taking out a loan or by swindling).
ex: The verb 'to-pull-his-leg' means to extract from his pocket all the lucre it will yield.

der: pull the other one, it's got bells on

ety: Deverbal from pull up.

s.def: An exercise done for strengthening the arms and back in which one lifts one's own weight while hanging from a bar. Palms may be facing in any direction.
Pork barbecued for a long time at a low heat, making it tender enough to be pulled apart.

ety: From Middle English polet, pulet, from Anglo-Norman pullet, Old French poulet (“young chicken”); polette (“young hen”), from poule (“hen”), from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of pullus. Doublet of poult. Compare also Middle English pulle. By surface analysis, pull(us) + -et.

s.def: A young hen, especially one less than a year old.
ex: They died not because the Pullets would not feed: but because the Devil foresaw their death, he contrived that abstinence in them.
The dinner-hour being arrived, Black George carried her up a pullet, the squire himself [...] attending the door.
The writer complained that a fox had been the night before and killed three more of his pullets […].

s.def: A spineless person; a coward.
A girl or young woman.

ety: From Middle English puly, poley, from Old French poulie, polie (“a pulley, windlass”), from Medieval Latin polidia, plural mistaken for the feminine of neuter polidium, from Ancient Greek πολίδιον (polídion, “little pivot”), diminutive of πόλος (pólos, “pivot, hinge, axis”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to turn”). Associated with pull (verb) by folk etymology.

s.def: One of the simple machines; a sheave, a wheel with a grooved rim, in which a pulled rope or chain lifts an object (more useful when two or more pulleys are used together, as in a block and tackle arrangement, such that a small force moving through a greater distance can exert a larger force through…
ex: These pulleys […] placed collaterally.

s.def: Annular ligament of the finger.
To raise or lift by means of a pulley.

ety: Deverbal from pull out.

s.def: A withdrawal, especially of armed forces.
The change of the flight of an aircraft from a dive to level or climbing flight.
An object, such as a newspaper supplement, that can be pulled out from something else.
Synonym of liftout (“quotation given special visual treatment”).
An area by the side of a road where vehicles may temporarily stop in safety. Typical pullouts allow drivers and passengers to safely exit the vehicle but rarely have additional amenities.
The ending of a period of surfing by navigating the surfboard into or over the back of a wave.
ex: Here's a pretty strange pullout. An "El Rollo." When Corky does something strange, everyone for 50 yards knows all about it.
Most pullouts, then and today, are done by simply angling or pivoting the board up and over the wave crest.
[…] Machado, who turns what might seem like a handicap, that lankiness, to rubbery advantage in his sinuous carving and slackly cool pullouts.

s.def: The coitus interruptus method of birth control.

ety: Deverbal from pull over.

s.def: A sweater that must be put on by pulling it over the head; a sweater without buttons or a zipper in front.
An exercise performed lying on the back in which the arms are extended behind the head and exertion lifts the weight above the head.
An exercise in which the gymnast pulls up from a hang lifting the legs up and over the bar thus rolling into a support position.
An instance of a vehicle being pulled over.
ex: I followed my training in the academy regarding vehicle pullovers.

ety: Borrowed from Latin pullulātus, perfect passive participle of pullulō (“sprout forth”), from pullulus (“a young animal, a sprout”), diminutive of pullus.

s.def: To multiply rapidly.
To germinate.
To teem with; to be filled (with).
ex: I must say the whole of Oxford has become most peculiar suddenly. Last night it was pullulating with women.

ety: Borrowed from Latin pulmōnārius (“of the lungs”), from pulmō (“lung”) + -ārius, from Proto-Indo-European *pléu-mon-. Cognate with Greek πλεμόνι (plemóni), French poumon, Lithuanian plaučiai, Polish płuco and Russian пла́вать (plávatʹ, “to swim”).

s.def: Pertaining to, having, or affecting the lungs.
ex: Wiener-Kronish's case showed plexogenic pulmonary angiopathy and positive immunofluorescent staining for IgG, C₃ and C1q in the lung (1981). […]

s.def: A small air sac in the lungs, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.
The part of blood circulation which carries oxygen-depleted blood away from the heart, to the lungs, and returns oxygenated blood back to the heart.
The most common form of active tuberculosis (TB) infecting the lungs, generally caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pulmōnicus, from pulmō (“lung”).

s.def: Of, pertaining to, or produced by the lungs.
Produced by pushing air from or into the lungs.
a medicine for treating a lung disease.
a person affected by a lung disease.
