Latin -logialbor. French -logiebor. English -logy English pulmonology From Latin pulmō + English -logy.

s.def: The branch of medicine dealing with diseases of the lungs and respiratory tract.

ety: From Middle English pulpe, from Latin pulpa.

s.def: A soft, moist, shapeless mass or matter.
A magazine or book containing lurid subject matter and characteristically printed on rough, unfinished paper.
To make or be made into pulp.
To beat to a pulp.
To deprive of pulp; to separate the pulp from.
Of or pertaining to pulp magazines; in the style of a pulp magazine or the material printed within such a publication.

ety: From Middle English pulpit, from Old French pulpite and Latin pulpitum (“platform”). Doublet of pulpitum and polypus. Piecewise doublet of polypod.

s.def: A raised platform in a church, sometimes enclosed, where the minister or preacher stands when giving the sermon; also, the lectern on such a platform.
ex: [H]is `Amens' were ejected at the pulpit with the severity of a reprimand.

s.def: Activity associated with or usually performed from a church pulpit; preaching, sermons, religious teaching.
The preaching profession, office, or role in general; the pastorate, the priesthood, the ministry.
Preachers collectively; clergy; the priesthood.
Bully pulpit.
The railing at the bow of a boat, which sometimes extends past the deck; also called bow pulpit. The railing at the stern is sometimes called the stern pulpit or the pushpit.
A bow platform for harpooning.
A plane's cockpit.
ex: In the slang of the Royal Air Force man, the cockpit of his plane is the ‘pulpit’ or ‘office’, the glass covering over it the ‘greenhouse’.

s.def: Any lectern, podium, dais, or platform for an orator or public speaker.
An individual or particular preaching position or role; a pastorate.
ex: He seems like too timid a man to fill the pulpit at such a large church.

ety: From pulp + wood.

s.def: Wood, usually softwood, used for pulping to make paper.

ety: From pulp + -y.

s.def: Having the characteristics of pulp.
ex: the pulpy texture of overripe fruit

s.def: Having the characteristics of pulp fiction; thus, having a garish focus on sex and violence.
ex: a pulpy TV thriller
In a sly bit of casting, Tony Goldwyn — a star of the pulpy TV series “Scandal” — shows up as one of the leaders of the Christmas Adventurers Club..

ety: Blend of pulsating + (radio) star, patterned after quasar. Coined by British astronomers Antony Hewish and Jocelyn Bell in 1968, and first used in print in The Daily Telegraph. By surface analysis, pulse + -ar

s.def: A rotating neutron star that emits radio pulses periodically.

ety: Perhaps formed within English as a back-formation from pulsation (attested from the early 15th century, in Middle English). A figurative derivation from New Latin pulsō, pulsātum (“(of an organ) to pulse, to emit a pulse”, intransitive) is also possible, itself a back-formation of New Latin pulsātiō (“pulsation”, 14th century), or derived from classical Latin pulsō (“to strike repeatedly”, transitive) with semantic influence from classical pulsus (“a pulse”). Ultimately from Latin pellō (“to st…

s.def: To expand and contract rhythmically; to throb or to beat, exhibit a pulse.
To quiver, vibrate, or flash; as to the beat of music.
ex: The party pulsated with revellers.

s.def: To pulse, to be full of life, energy: to bustle, thrive, flourish.
To produce a recurring increase and decrease of some quantity.

ety: From Late Middle English pulse, Middle English pous, pouse (“regular beat of arteries, pulse; heartbeat; place on the body where a pulse is detectable; beat (of a musical instrument); energy, vitality”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman puls, pous, pus, and Middle French pouls, poulz, pous [and other forms], Old French pous, pulz (“regular beat of arteries; place on the body where a pulse is detectable”) (modern French pouls), and from their etymon Latin pulsus (“beat, impulse, pulse, stroke…

s.def: A normally regular beat felt when arteries near the skin (for example, at the neck or wrist) are depressed, caused by the heart pumping blood through them; the qualitative nature of this beat.
ex: Her pulse was thready and weak.

s.def: The rate of this beat as an indication of a person's health.
ex: Her pulse was 110 at 8 a.m.

s.def: A beat or throb; also, a repeated sequence of such beats or throbs.
ex: I roved at random through the town, / [...] / And caught once more the distant shout, / The measured pulse of racing oars / Among the willows; [...]

s.def: The focus of energy or vigour of an activity, place, or thing; also, the feeling of bustle, busyness, or energy in a place; the heartbeat.
ex: You can really feel the pulse of the city in this district.

s.def: An (increased) amount of a substance (such as a drug or an isotopic label) given over a short time.
A setting on a food processor which causes it to work in a series of short bursts rather than continuously, in order to break up ingredients without liquidizing them; also, a use of this setting.
The beat or tactus of a piece of music or verse; also, a repeated sequence of such beats.
A brief burst of electromagnetic energy, such as light, radio waves, etc.
Synonym of autosoliton (“a stable solitary localized structure that arises in nonlinear spatially extended dissipative systems due to mechanisms of self-organization”).
A brief increase in the strength of an electrical signal; an impulse.

ety: From pulse + -meter.

s.def: A sphygmograph.
Any of various devices designed to monitor someone's pulse.
A vacuum pump or hydrotrope.
American and Oxford British spelling of pulverise.

ety: Compare Latin pulvereus, from pulvis, pulveris (“dust, powder”). By surface analysis, pulver + -ous.

s.def: Resembling or consisting of dust or powder.

ety: From Latin pulverulentus, from pulvis (“dust”). By surface analysis, pulver + -ule + -ent.

s.def: Consisting of, covered with, or disintegrating into a fine powder; powdery; dusty.
ex: The first pulverulent snows told that Christmas was at hand.

ety: From Latin pulvillus (“a little cushion”).

s.def: One of the tiny cushions or pads on the feet of certain insects.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Quechuan *puma Quechua pumabor. Spanish pumabor. English puma Borrowed from Spanish puma, borrowed from Quechua puma, from Proto-Quechuan *puma.

s.def: A mountain lion or cougar (Puma concolor).
Any feline belonging to the genus Puma.
A woman in her 20s or 30s who seeks relationships with younger men; a younger cougar.

ety: From Anglo-Norman and Old French pomis (“pumice stone”), from Latin pūmex (“pumice stone”). Doublet of pounce.

s.def: A light, porous type of pyroclastic igneous rock, formed during explosive volcanic eruptions when liquid lava is ejected into water or air as a froth containing masses of gas bubbles, which are frozen into the rock as the lava solidifies.
To abrade or roughen with pumice.
A piece of pumice.
ex: in the midst a little riuer plaide / Emongst the pumy stones, which seemd to plaine / With gentle murmure, that his course they did restraine.

s.def: Pumice (the substance).

ety: From Middle English pumpe, possibly from Middle Dutch pompe (“pipe, water conduit”) or Middle Low German pumpe (“pump”), probably ultimately imitative. Compare Dutch pompen, German pumpen, and Danish pompe; also Spanish bomba (“pump”).

s.def: A device for moving or compressing a liquid or gas.
ex: This pump can deliver 100 gallons of water per minute.

s.def: An instance of the action of a pump; one stroke of a pump; any action similar to pumping.
ex: It takes thirty pumps to get 10 litres; he did 50 pumps of the weights.

s.def: A device for dispensing liquid or gas to be sold, particularly fuel; a gas pump.
ex: This pump is out of order, but you can gas up at the next one.

s.def: A swelling of the muscles caused by increased blood flow following high intensity weightlifting.
ex: Want a skin-stretching pump? Up the volume by using high-rep sets. A great pump is better than coming.

s.def: A ride on a bicycle given to a passenger, usually on the handlebars or fender.
ex: She gave the other girl a pump on her new bike.

s.def: The heart.
The vagina.
To use a pump; to move (water or other liquid) by means of a pump.
ex: I've been pumping for over a minute but the water isn't coming through.
I've pumped over 1000 gallons of water in the last ten minutes.
With each beat, your heart's left ventricle pumps blood into your arteries, which are all different sizes.

s.def: To inject or pour (something) into someone or something in a manner similar to a pump.
To put (a person or part of the body) under a stream of water from a pump, as a punishment or as a form of medical treatment; to force a pump of water upon or on someone.
ex: Pump him soundly, impudent Fellow.
‘So much the worse for him. I've had my eye on him for some time. He shall be prettily pumped upon.’

s.def: A form of financial fraud where the fraudster purchases stocks at a very low price, generates excitement about those stocks in order to create a temporary price increase, then sells the stocks before the price depreciates.
ex: The newest thing in finance had apparently fallen prey to one of the oldest investor hoaxes around – a classic pump-and-dump scheme.

s.def: one-night-stand
A situation where a woman uses a breast pump and then discards the milk, typically because she has had an infection, or has been drinking alcohol.
A situation where a person has sex with a partner on a single occasion, without immediate intention of further contact or pursuing a serious relationship.
ex: I am tired of the pump-and-dump lifestyle, so please help me stop acting like a slut.

ety: From Westphalian German Pumpernickel, from Pumper (“fart”) (or a related form, such as pumpern) and Nickel (“rascal”) (from the male name Nikolaus (“Nicholas”)), possibly originating as an insult for a person or for the bread itself by outsiders. A false folk etymology claims that this comes from the phrase pain pour Nicole ("bread for Nicole"), referring to Napoleon disliking the taste so much that he thought it was fit for his horse Nicole.

s.def: A German sourdough bread made from rye.
ex: There was a cut-crystal pitcher full of water, a basket of fruit, and a big loaf of pumpernickel for them to eat.

ety: Alteration of pompion, pumpion (“pumpkin”) with the diminutive -kin, from Middle French pompon, from Latin pepō (whence English pepo), from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). The first attestation is from 1647. The alternative theory that it may be from Massachusett pôhpukun (“grows forth round”) is false. The automotive sense is by fancied resemblance.

s.def: A domesticated plant, in species Cucurbita pepo, similar in growth pattern, foliage, flower, and fruit to the squash or melon.
ex: Nevertheless, the comprehensive comparative analysis of pumpkin viromes across various geographic regions by NGS remains deficient.

s.def: The round yellow or orange fruit of this plant.
Any of a number of cultivars from the genus Cucurbita; known in the US as winter squash.
A term of endearment for someone small and cute.
ex: You must be daddy’s little pumpkin.

s.def: The housing for a differential, built into an axle of a vehicle; the housing and its contents.
The typical color of the ripe fruit of the pumpkin plant.
An edible seed of a pumpkin or other cultivars of squash.

ety: From pumpkin + seed. The fish is so named for its small body that is shaped much like a pumpkin seed.

s.def: A North American sunfish; Lepomis gibbosus.
A type of small riverboat.
Alternative form of pumpkin seed (“the seed of a pumpkin”).
ex: The current menu includes curried goat, rack of lamb with a pumpkinseed crust, and braised short ribs.

ety: From pump + -man.

s.def: A man employed to operate a pump, as in a mine.

ety: From Middle English ponnen, ponen, punen, from Old English punian, pūnian (“to pound, beat, bray, bruise, crush, grind”), from Proto-Germanic *punōną (“to break to pieces, pulverize”). See pound. As a kind of word play, from the notion of “beating” the words into place.

s.def: To beat; strike with force; to ram; to pound, as in a mortar; reduce to powder, to pulverize.
To make or tell a pun; to make a play on words.
ex: We punned about the topic until all around us groaned.

s.def: A joke or type of wordplay in which similar definitions or sounds of two words or phrases, or different definitions of the same word, are deliberately confused.
ex: The pun is the lowest form of wit.

s.def: Alternative form of bun (“Korean unit of measure”).
A certain number of cowries, generally 80.
ex: Hackeries and carriages, loaded and empty, 8 annas. Sheep, goats, &c., 1 pun of cowries each.

ety: From Middle English punchen, partially from Old French ponchonner (“to punch”), from ponchon (“pointed tool”), from Latin punctio, from punctus, perfect passive participle of pungō (“I prick”); and partially from Middle English punchen, a syncopated variant of punischen ("to punish"; see punish). Also influenced by Middle English punchon ("a punch"; see puncheon). Compare also Middle English bunchen, bonchen (“to punch, deliver a blow, pound, beat”).

s.def: A hit or strike with one's fist.
To make holes in something (rail ticket, leather belt, etc) (see also the verb under Etymology 2).
ex: So I punched a hole in the roof, ah-ah, ah-ah Let the flood carry away all my pictures of you

s.def: To employ a punch to create a hole in or stamp or emboss a mark on something.
A beverage, generally containing a mixture of fruit juice and some other beverage, often alcoholic.
A blow from something other than the fist.
Power, strength, energy.
ex: The tornado is finally losing its punch.
Nixon inadvertently took most of the punch out of the Red Scare by trekking to Peking and Moscow.

s.def: Impact.
ex: Has your ad copy plenty of punch?

s.def: To strike with one's fist.
ex: If she punches me, I'm gonna break her nose.

s.def: To herd.
To operate (a device or system) by depressing a button, key, bar, or pedal, or by similar means.
ex: As night watchman he was required to punch a watchman's clock; the stations were scattered all over the place.

ety: From Middle English punchoun, from Anglo-Norman ponchon, pounceon et al., and Middle French ponçon, poinchon et al., from Old French ponchon, from Latin pūnctiōnem (“act of piercing”). Doublet of punction. Related to Middle High German punze (“chisel; burin, graver”), ponze (“puncheon, standardized cask”), German Punze (“puncheon, punch, counter”).

s.def: A figured stamp, die, or punch, used by goldsmiths, cutlers, etc.
A short, upright piece of timber in framing; a short post; an intermediate stud.
A piece of roughly dressed timber with one face finished flat (by either hewing or sawing).
A split log or heavy slab of timber with the face smoothed, used especially for flooring but also for log cabin walls, piers, or plank roads.
A walkway or short, low footbridge over wet ground constructed with such timbers, made by laying one or more planks or dressed timbers over sills set directly on the ground.
A short low bridge of similar construction.
A cask of a certain size; its volume used as a measure of capacity varying from 72 to 120 gallons.
ex: Then he went to the scullery, wetted his hands, scooped the last white dough out of the punchion, and dropped it in a baking-tin.

ety: From Punchinello.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Punchinello.
A small brown butterfly, Zemeros flegyas, family Riodinidae, of Asia.
A tough bag, usually cylindrical, filled with air, sand, or other material, often suspended so that it swings freely, which is punched or kicked when practising sports such as boxing or martial arts.
A person serving as an object of abuse.

ety: From Italian puntiglio, or Spanish puntillo, diminutive from Latin pūnctum (“point”).

s.def: A fine point in exactness of conduct, ceremony, etiquette or procedure.
ex: Covert gestures of kindness saved me from trouble, or explained the punctilio of some futile but unavoidable chore.

s.def: Strictness in observance of formalities.
ex: This rudeness and official punctilio, however, brought forth a storm of protest from my fellow voyagers.

ety: Etymology tree English punctilio Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Old French -usbor. Middle English -ous English -ous English punctilious From punctilio (“fine point in exactness of conduct”) + -ous.

s.def: Strictly attentive to detail; meticulous or fastidious, particularly to codes or conventions.
ex: With a punctilious slap of the gloves, the duel was now inevitable.
He was punctilious. According to those who worked with him, even his paperwork was the best they'd seen.

s.def: Precise or scrupulous; finicky or nitpicky.
ex: Of course, humans do not treat time in such a punctilious fashion.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis (“relating to a point”), from Late Latin pūnctus (“point”) + -ālis (adjective suffix).

s.def: prompt
Observing trivial points; punctilious.
Existing as a point or series of points.
Prompt; on time.
ex: Luis is never late; he's the most punctual person I know.

s.def: Expressing a momentary action that has no duration.
Periodic; occasional.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuātus, perfect passive participle of pūnctuō (“to mark with points”), from Medieval Latin pūnctus (“a point, dot”), from pungō (“to prick, punch”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of punch.

s.def: To add punctuation to.
ex: That occurrence of "its" needs to be punctuated as "it's".

s.def: To add or to interrupt at regular intervals.
ex: My father punctuated his tirade with thumps on the desk.
Most soldiers would testify that the everyday experience of war is long stretches of boredom punctuated by sudden, terrifying spells of disorder.

s.def: To emphasize; to stress.
Point-like; consisting of or marked with one or more points.
ex: Positive HPV 16 hybridization signal in two cervical carcinomas. A punctuate signal (a) and a punctuate and diffuse signal (b).
[…] with a punctuate wall calcification (arrow) along the right postcentral sulcus.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuātiō (“a marking with points, a writing, agreement”), from punctuō (“to mark with points, settle”). Morphologically, punctuate + -ion.

s.def: A set of symbols and marks which are used to clarify meaning in text by separating strings of words into clauses, phrases and sentences; examples include commas, hyphens, and stops (periods).
ex: Different languages have different rules for punctuation.

s.def: Nikud.
An act of punctuating.
Any of various symbols used in writing and printing to indicate pauses, divisions, etc., and to aid the reader in understanding what is written.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ-der. Proto-Italic *pungō Latin pungō Latin pūnctus Proto-Indo-European *-tew-? Proto-Indo-European *-r-eh₂? Latin -tūra Late Latin punctūrabor. English puncture Borrowed from Late Latin punctūra.

s.def: The act or an instance of puncturing.
A hole, cut, or tear created by a sharp object.
ex: There were two small punctures in his arm where the snake's fangs had pierced the skin.
The lion may perish by the puncture of an asp.

s.def: A hole in a vehicle's tyre, causing the tyre to deflate.
ex: On the way back we got a puncture, and we were stuck at the roadside for three hours until help arrived.
Dieter's car had suffered a puncture on the RN3 road between Paris and Meaux. A bent nail was stuck in the tire.

s.def: To pierce; to break through; to tear a hole.
ex: The needle punctured the balloon instantly.
The couple all bloody / Tongues punctured by each other's teeth / Died and didn't let go

s.def: To destroy the vitality or strength of.

ety: Etymology tree Sanskrit पण्डा (paṇḍā) Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-Iranian *-tás Sanskrit -इत (-ita) Sanskrit पण्डित (paṇḍita)bor. Hindi पंडित (paṇḍit)bor. Urdu پَنْڈِٹ (panḍiṭ)bor. English pundit Borrowed from Hindi पंडित (paṇḍit) / Urdu پنڈت (panḍit), from Sanskrit पण्डित (paṇḍita, “scholar, learned man, teacher, philosopher”). Doublet of pandit.

s.def: An expert in a particular field, especially as called upon to provide comment or opinion in the media; a commentator, a critic.
ex: This week we introduce Jenny Walker, who will be The Observer's expert pundit for the duration of the World Cup.

s.def: A learned person in India; someone with knowledge of Sanskrit, philosophy, religion and law; a Hindu scholar.
A native surveyor in British India, trained to carry out clandestine surveillance beyond British borders.
ex: At every hundredth pace the Pundit would automatically slip one bead. Each complete circuit of the rosary thus represented ten thousand paces.

ety: Etymology tree Sanskrit पण्डा (paṇḍā) Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-Iranian *-tás Sanskrit -इत (-ita) Sanskrit पण्डित (paṇḍita)bor. Hindi पंडित (paṇḍit)bor. Urdu پَنْڈِٹ (panḍiṭ)bor. English pundit English -ry English punditry From pundit + -ry.

s.def: The state of being a pundit.
The opinion or advice of a pundit.
The behaviour of a pundit.

ety: From pungent + -cy.

A foul odor.

ety: Borrowed from Latin pungens (stem pungent-), present participle of pungo (“to sting”). Doublet of poignant.

s.def: Having a strong odor that stings the nose; said especially of acidic or spicy substances.
ex: I accidentally dropped the bottle of ammonia and after few seconds, a very pungent stench could be detected.
I can almost smell the fir scent... resinous, pungent.

s.def: Having a strong taste that stings the tongue; said especially of hot (spicy) food, which has a strong and sharp or bitter taste.
Stinging; acerbic.
ex: The critic gave a pungent review.

s.def: Having a sharp and stiff point.

ety: From Latin Pūnicus, variant of Poenicus, from Poenus + -icus, from Ancient Greek Φοῖνιξ (Phoînix), from Mycenaean Greek 𐀡𐀛𐀑𐀍 (po-ni-ki-jo) under influence from φοινός (phoinós, “crimson red”) owing to its relation to Tyrian purple, apparently from or cognate with Egyptian fnḫw (“Asiatics, Semites”), f:n:x-w-V12:Z2. Equivalent to a modified Phoenician + -ic.

s.def: A native or inhabitant of ancient Carthage; a Carthaginian.
The language of Carthage.

ety: From Middle English punischen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French puniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of punir, from Latin puniō (“to inflict punishment upon”), from poena (“punishment, penalty”); see pain. Displaced Old English wītnian and (mostly, in this sense) wrecan.

s.def: To cause (a child, student, or someone else being looked after, or a suspect or criminal) to suffer for crime or misconduct, to administer disciplinary action, typically by an authority or a person in authority (for example: a parent, teacher, or police officer).
ex: If a prince violates the law, then he must be punished like an ordinary person.
The law needs to punish this behaviour as a deterrent to others.
His mother had punished him when he'd deserved it. She'd loved him, he was “all she had,” but she'd punished him, too.

s.def: To treat harshly and unfairly.
ex: Homer, moreover, gives the impression that the Sun punished Odysseus's men; but we are later told that the Sun cannot punish individual men […]
The rider who comes back on his horse in mid-air over a fence is punishing his horse severely.

s.def: To handle or beat severely; to maul.
To consume a large quantity of.
ex: A few moments later, we were all sitting around the veranda of the hunters' dining hall, punishing the gin, as usual.

rel: take the law into one's own hands

ety: From Middle English punishement, from Old French punissement, from punir (“to punish”). Equivalent to punish + -ment. Displaced native Old English wīte.

s.def: The act (action) or process of punishing, imposing and/or applying a sanction, typically by an authority or a person in authority (for example: a parent or teacher), especially when disappointed or dissatisfied with the behavior or actions of a child, student, or someone else being looked after.
ex: The naughty children were given a punishment by their teachers.

s.def: A penalty to punish wrongdoing, especially for crime.
ex: a light punishment
a harsh punishment

s.def: A suffering by pain or loss imposed as retribution.
Any harsh treatment or experience; rough handling.
ex: a vehicle that can take a lot of punishment

ety: From Middle French punitif, from Medieval Latin pūnitīvus, from pūniō (“to punish”).

s.def: Inflicting punishment; punishing.
ex: Beijing imposed punitive sanctions on Canada.
The jury awarded $10,000 in punitive damages.
The council took punitive measures against poachers.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep-der. Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hā́ps Proto-Iranian *Hā́fš Old Persian 𐎠𐎱𐎡𐎹𐎠 (a-p-i-y-a) Middle Persian ʾp̄ Classical Persian آب (āb) Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe Proto-Indo-Iranian *pánča Proto-Iranian *pánča Classical Persian پنج ▲ Sanskrit पञ्चनद (pañcanada)calq. Classical Persian پَنْجَاب (panjāb)bor. Punjabi ਪੰਜਾਬ /پنجاب (pañjāb)bor. English Punjab From Punjabi ਪੰਜਾਬ / پنجاب (pañjāb), from Classical Persian پَنْجَاب (panjāb, “[Land of] the Five Rivers”…

s.def: A geographical region of South Asia, divided (by the Radcliffe Line) between India and Pakistan. Pakistani Punjab includes the (West) Punjab Province and parts of the Islamabad Capital Territory; Indian Punjab includes (East) Punjab State and some other territories.
A state in northern India. Capital: Chandigarh. Largest city: Ludhiana.
A province in Pakistan. Capital: Lahore.

ety: Borrowed from Classical Persian پنجابی (panjābī), from پنجاب (panjāb) + ـی (-ī, adjectival suffix). Equivalent to Punjab + -i.

s.def: The main language spoken in the Punjab region, in eastern Pakistan and Northern India.

ety: Uncertain. Possibly from punk (“rotten wood dust used as tinder”), attested since 1678, to anything worthless (attested since 1869) and then to any undesirable person (since 1908). The relatively tame 21st century usage of punk (“prank”, verb) was popularized by the American television show Punk'd (2003).

s.def: One who engages in sexual intercourse
ex: My lord, she may be a punk; for many of them are neither maid, widow, nor wife.
[…] And made them fight, like mad or drunk, / For Dame Religion, as for punk...

s.def: A worthless person, particularly
ex: This fellow was just a punk... a nobody.

s.def: A worthless person
ex: He said the prisoner called them ‘punk’... He admitted that he shouted ‘punk’ to them.
There was nothing so special about the gang, punks are punks.

s.def: A group of associated musical, artistic and social movements emerging out of the counterculture in the 1970s:
ex: This emphasis on politics in the personal sphere might be a difference between punk now and punk fifteen years ago.
Despite this, Podemos's beginnings are still illuminating to understand punk's scope of influence adequately.

s.def: A follower of any of these movements, including:
ex: My girlfriend is a punk and she plays the drums.

s.def: Worthless, contemptible, particularly
ex: ... Donald Trump is also a coward. For all of his tough talk and bluster, the president of the United States is a punk ass bitch.

ex: You look very punk with your t-shirt, piercing, and chains.

ex: Ricky punked his new cell-mates.

s.def: To give up or concede; to act like a wimp.
ex: Jimmy was going to help me with the prank, but he punked (out) at the last minute.

s.def: To adapt or embellish in the style of the punk movement.
ex: Suzy, a pump young woman with sparkling brown eyes and punked hair tucked behind her ears, said blankly, "What?"

ety: See punk + rock. First attested in 1970 in reference to rockabilly; possibly coined in its current sense by American music critic Dave Marsh in the May 1971 issue of Creem, from earlier punk music.

s.def: A genre of rock music associated with short, loud, energetic songs played on electric guitars and drums and employing angry, offensive, and/or political lyrics.
ex: Punk rock died when the first kid said / "Punk's not dead, punk's not dead"

ety: Etymology tree English punk Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English punky From punk + -y.

Of or pertaining to the punk subculture.
ex: a punky hairstyle

s.def: Alternative spelling of punkie (“small two-winged fly or midge; lantern similar to a jack-o'-lantern”).
Alternative spelling of punkie (“pumpkinseed fish”).

ety: Etymology tree English pun Proto-West Germanic *-astrijā Old English -estre Middle English -estere English -ster English punster From pun + -ster.

s.def: A person who makes puns.
ex: Waglings and punsters — a vile race, / Who grin and jeer in any case!

ety: From Old English punt, from Latin pontō (“Gaulish flat-bottomed boat, pontoon”), from pons (“bridge”); readopted from Middle Low German punte (“ferry boat”) or Middle Dutch ponte (“ferry boat”) of the same origin.

s.def: A narrow shallow boat, square at both ends, traditionally propelled by a pole.
ex: Near-synonym: pontoon

s.def: To propel a punt or similar craft by means of a pole.
Of a fish, to walk along the seafloor using its fins as limbs.
To dropkick; to kick something a considerable distance.
ex: At the dump he emptied the station wagon quickly and only once punted a bag of refuse, exploding it like a pinata at a Mexican Christmas.
He even hated pets—I once saw him punt a cat.

s.def: To equivocate and delay or put off (answering a question, addressing an issue, etc).
To retreat from one's objective; to abandon an effort one still notionally supports.
To make the best choice from a set of non-ideal alternatives.
To eject; to kick out of a place.
ex: The user is punted from the channel, and must rejoin to gain access.

s.def: A kick made by a player who drops the ball and kicks it before it hits the ground.
A point in the game of faro.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pós Proto-Indo-European *-ti Proto-Indo-European *pósti Proto-Italic *posti Old Latin poste Latin post Proto-Indo-European *íh₂ Latin ea Latin posteā Vulgar Latin *postius Old French puis Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁tós Proto-Italic *gnātos Latin gnātus Latin nātus Old French né Old French puisné Middle French puisnébor. English puisne English puny PIE word *pós A respelling of puisne, from Anglo-Norman puis…

s.def: Of inferior significance, size, or strength; ineffective, small, weak.
ex: You puny earthlings are no match for Ming the Merciless!
a puny attempt at an apology
[W]e dart / O'er wave or field: yet breezes laugh to scorn // Our puny speed, […]

s.def: (Frequently) ill; poorly, sickly.
Alternative spelling of puisne.
ex: Many thought that he had altogether cut his own throat, and that he would have to take the first "puny" judgeship vacant.

A younger person; a junior.
Alternative spelling of puisne.
A new student at a school, university, the Inns of Court, etc.; a junior.

ety: Clipping of puppy.

s.def: A young dog, wolf, fox, seal, bat or shark, or the young of certain other animals.
ex: The dog has had that bed since he was just a pup.

s.def: A young, inexperienced person.
ex: The new teacher is a mere pup.

s.def: Any cute dog, regardless of age.
ex: My pup likes to run as fast as he can, yet cannot always stop in time!

s.def: A short semi-trailer used jointly with a dolly and another semi-trailer to create a twin trailer.
A new plant growing from a shoot that can be used for propagation.
A kind of small spotlight.
ex: Spots were also used for the foreground, usually the smaller type like a “pup,” which could be repositioned quickly for different setups.

s.def: An early edition of a periodical publication, intended for distribution to distant locations.
Someone who participates in pup play (the sexual practice of role-playing as a young dog).
ex: Mentorship, I learned from the Fog City pups, plays a huge role in their family business, where the pack hierarchy comes into play.

s.def: A small tributary or feeder stream in the US state of Alaska.
ex: [...] stream gravels of Bear Pup are auriferous for a distance of at least 2 miles above its mouth.
At last we reached the head of Young creek, and following a "pup" stream we worked out way over a third divide and down into the great Chitina valley.

s.def: To give birth to pups.

ety: Borrowed from New Latin, from a special use of Latin pūpa (“little girl; doll, puppet”). Doublet of pupe; compare also puppet, puppy.

s.def: An insect in the development stage between larva and adult.
ex: The public is the pupae of the purposely purblind […]

ety: From Middle English pupille, from Anglo-Norman pupille (“orphan”), from Latin pūpillus (“orphan, minor”), variant of pūpulus (“little boy”), from pūpus (“child, boy”).

s.def: A learner at a school under the supervision of a teacher.
ex: All of these different methods of teaching elementary reading were successful for some pupils, unsuccessful for others.
The bell which called the pupils to their lessons can still be seen on the roof.

s.def: One who studies under supervision of a renowned expert in their field.
ex: Plato was Socrates' pupil, and in turn Aristotle was Plato's pupil.

s.def: An orphan who is a minor and under the protection of the state.
The hole in the middle of the iris of the eye, through which light passes to be focused on the retina.
The central dark part of an ocellated spot.

ety: From pupil + -age.

s.def: The condition of being a pupil.
The period during which one is a pupil.
ex: A pupilage was normally two years, after three or four years as a premium apprentice.

ety: Borrowed from Latin pūpillāris, as if the form were *pūpillārius.

s.def: Of or pertaining to person below a certain legal age, or to a ward.
Of or pertaining to a student.
Of or pertaining to the pupil of the eye.
Producing young that are ready to pupate.

ety: From Middle English popet, probably from, though attested earlier than, Middle French poupette, diminutive of poupée (cf. also Medieval Latin *pupata), ultimately derived from Latin pupa (“doll, puppet; girl”). The nominal form first appears c. 1531, and the verbal form c. 1635. See also puppy.

s.def: Any small model of a person or animal able to be moved by strings or rods, or in the form of a glove.
A person, country, etc, controlled by another.
A poppet; a small image in the human form; a doll.
The upright support for the bearing of the spindle in a lathe.
To control or manipulate like a puppet.
A government which is formally independent, but de facto wholly controlled by a foreign power.

ety: Etymology tree English puppet Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -ārius Old French -ier Middle French -ierder. English -eer English puppeteer From puppet + -eer.

s.def: A person who uses a puppet.
Someone who is manipulative and thus able to get people to do what they want or to make events develop in the way they want in a puppet-like manner.

rel: the organ grinder, not the monkey

ety: From puppet + -ry.

s.def: The art of making, and performing with puppets
The action of a puppet, or a stilted or puppet-like dramatic performance
finery; affectation

ety: From earlier puppie (“a woman's pet dog”), of uncertain origin, but probably from Middle English *puppee, *poupee, from Old French poupée, popée (“a doll; puppet”). More at puppet. Mostly displaced native Middle English whelp (“puppy”), from Old English hwelp, whence Modern English whelp and whelpie.

s.def: A young dog, especially before sexual maturity (12–18 months).
A young rat.
A young seal.
A dog with a youthful appearance, or any dog.
A woman’s breast.
ex: Unclasp your bra and set those puppies free.

s.def: A (generic) thing; particularly something that is a nuisance; a sucker.
ex: I have another two dozen of these puppies to finish before I can go home.

s.def: A conceited and impertinent person, especially a young man.
ex: I found my place taken by an ill-bred, awkward puppy with a money bag under each arm.

s.def: To bring forth whelps or give birth to pups.

ety: The adjective is derived from Middle English purblind (“(adjective) completely blind; blind in one eye; near-sighted; (noun) near-sighted animal, specifically a hare”) [and other forms], possibly from pur, pure (“completely, entirely”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“to be clean; pure”); influenced by pur- (prefix meaning ‘completely; forward; in advance’)) + blind (“sightless, blind”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ- (“to blend, mix up; to make cloudy or opaque”)).…

s.def: Of a person: having impaired vision; partially blind; dim-sighted.
ex: [T]here were shown in to us an old, worn, purblind, ascetic-looking priest, […]

s.def: Of the eyes: unable to see well, especially due to old age; weak.
Of a person: lacking in discernment or understanding; dim-witted, unintelligent.
ex: A herd of palsied purblind idiots hugging their sterile profits close to their sunken chests in the face of my father’s displeasure.
The public is the pupae of the purposely purblind […]

s.def: Of a place: poorly illuminated; dark, dim.
Completely blind.
Having one eye blind.
Near-sighted, short-sighted; myopic.
ex: I am sorry to hear your complaints still of giddiness. I was in hopes you would have mended, like my purblind eyes, with old age.

s.def: Far-sighted, long-sighted; hypermetropic.
A person who has impaired vision or is partially blind.
ex: By the freak of Fortune we were like to like, three Kalendars and three purblinds, all blind of the left eye.

s.def: To cause (someone) to have impaired vision or become partially blind.
ex: Were he not, as has been said, purblinded by enchantment, you had but to bid him open his eyes and look.

ety: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (from Latin pro-) + chac(i)er (“to chase, pursue”). Compare Old French porchacier (“to follow, to chase”), which has given French pourchasser (“to chase without relent”).

s.def: The acquisition of title to, or property in, anything for a price; buying for money or its equivalent.
ex: They offer a free hamburger with the purchase of a drink.

s.def: That which is obtained for a price in money or its equivalent.
ex: He was pleased with his latest purchase.

s.def: A price paid for a house or estate, etc. equal to the amount of the rent or income during the stated number of years.
ex: Suppose a freehold house to be worth 20 years’ purchase […]

s.def: Any mechanical hold or advantage, applied to the raising or removing of heavy bodies, as by a lever, a tackle or capstan.
ex: It is hard to get purchase on a nail without a pry bar or hammer.

s.def: The apparatus, tackle or device by which such mechanical advantage is gained and (in nautical terminology) the ratio of such a device, like a pulley, or block and tackle.
Acquisition of lands or tenements by means other than descent or inheritance, namely, by one's own act or agreement.
ex: The difference […]between the acquisition of an estate by descent and by purchase

s.def: That which is obtained, got or acquired, in any manner, honestly or dishonestly; property; possession; acquisition.
The act or process of seeking and obtaining something (e.g. property, etc.)
The amount of hold one has from an individual foothold or ledge.
To buy, obtain by payment of a price in money or its equivalent.
ex: to purchase land, to purchase a house

s.def: The price at which something is actually purchased, especially from the point of view of the purchaser.
The amount of goods and services that can be bought with a unit of currency.
ex: The exchange rates do not always reflect true differences in the purchasing power of currencies.

s.def: The ability of a large collective or company to negotiate more favourable prices and terms than a smaller group or company.
ex: Large supermarkets usually have better purchasing power than small, local shops.

s.def: The amount of goods and services that can be bought by consumers.
ex: High interest rates are affecting the purchasing power of homeowners.

s.def: A theory of long-term equilibrium exchange rates based on relative price levels of two countries.

ety: Borrowed from Hindustani پردہ / पर्दा (pardā), and its etymon Classical Persian پرده (pardah, “curtain; screen; (archaic) veil”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Doublet of patka.

s.def: The situation or system of secluding women from the gaze of people, particularly men and strangers, in some Muslim and Hindu traditions, by using a curtain or screen, and/or wearing a face veil or attire covering most of the body.
A curtain, especially one used in some Hindu or Muslim traditions to conceal women from the gaze of people, particularly men and strangers.
ex: As she passed through the dining-room she heard, behind the purdah that cloaked the drawing-room door, her husband's voice, […]
"Come and see my wife a little then," said Hamidullah, and they spent twenty minutes behind the purdah.

s.def: A long veil or other attire covering most of the body, worn by women in some Muslim societies.
Keeping apart; isolation, seclusion; also, concealment, secrecy.
ex: The diagnosis of Kit's malady was soon verified, and Fleur went into purdah.

s.def: The period between the announcement of an election or referendum and its conclusion, during which civil servants refrain from making policy announcements or taking actions that could be seen as advantageous to certain candidates in the election.
A striped cotton cloth which is used to make curtains.

ety: From Middle English pure, pur, from Old French pur, from Latin pūrus (“clean, free from dirt or filth, unmixed, plain”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“to cleanse, purify”). Displaced native Middle English lutter (“pure, clear, sincere”) (from Old English hlūtor, hluttor), Middle English skere (“pure, sheer, clear”) (from Old English scǣre and Old Norse skǣr), Middle English schir (“clear, pure”) (from Old English scīr), Middle English smete, smeate (“pure, refined”) (from Old English smǣte;…

s.def: Free of flaws or imperfections; unsullied.
ex: Such was the origin of a friendship as warm and pure as any that ancient or modern history records.

s.def: Free of foreign material or pollutants.
ex: A guinea is pure gold if it has in it no alloy.
"Hetch Hetchy water is the purest, wholly unpolluted, and forever unpollutable."

s.def: Free of immoral behavior or qualities; clean.
Mere; that and that only.
ex: That idea is pure madness!

s.def: Done for its own sake instead of serving another branch of science.
Of a single, simple sound or tone; said of some vowels and the unaspirated consonants.
Without harmonics or overtones; not harsh or discordant.
Having no side effects.
ex: a pure method

s.def: A lot of.
ex: Well when ah's youngah, ah'd just light a candle rahn de dinna table play pure crazy 8s and spades vif my brotha til we lot dozed off...

s.def: to a great extent or degree; extremely; exceedingly.
ex: You’re pure busy.
I just get pure shy with the interview cats.

der: as pure as the driven snow

ety: From pure + bred.

s.def: Having genuine parents of the same breed, usually of an animal.
An animal which has genuine parents of the same breed.

ety: Borrowed from French purée.

s.def: A food that has been ground or crushed into a thick liquid or paste.
ex: Tomato sauce is generally a puree.

s.def: To crush or grind food into a puree.
ex: Puree the vegetables and add them to the stock.

s.def: Alternative form of puri (“type of unleavened bread”).

ety: From Old French porfiler, from Latin pro- + filum (“thread”). Doublet of profile.

s.def: An ornamental border on clothing, furniture or a violin; beading, stringing.
An ornamental border, edge, or line of a different tincture or material.
ex: Cross […] has its extremities ending in a flower of three leaves, or flower-de-luces, with a purfle, or line between them and the ends of the cross.

s.def: To decorate (wood, cloth etc.) with a purfle or ornamental border; to border.
ex: Remembering the exchange now, Dickie smiled that winning southern-boy smile. Then he went glum again. He thumped the purfled sound board.

s.def: To ornament with purfle.
ex: Crest; a dragon passant proper, wings elevated and purfled gules.

ety: From Middle English purgacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman purgacion, itself borrowed from Latin pūrgātiō; equivalent to purge + -ation.

s.def: The process or act of purging, such as by the use of a purgative.
ex: Seven or eight annual bloodings, and as many purgations — such was the common regimen the theory prescribed to ensure continuance of health[…].

s.def: The process or act of cleansing from sin or guilt.
Exoneration or the act undertaken to achieve exoneration.

ety: From Middle French purgatif.

s.def: purging
something, such as a substance or medicine, that purges; laxative

ety: From Middle English purgatorie, from Old French purgatore, purgatorie, from Latin purgātōrium (“cleansing”). Cognate to English purge.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Purgatory.
Any situation where suffering is endured, particularly as part of a process of redemption.
ex: the purgatory of lost love
[…] many Gods breedeth heathens miseries, many countries trauailers humors, many wiues mens purgatories, and many friends trustes ruine:
It might be […] that Ruth had worked her way through the deep purgatory of repentance up to something like purity again; God only knew!

s.def: Tending to cleanse; expiatory.
ex: This purgatory interval is not unfavourable to a faithless representative, who may be as good a canvasser as he was a bad governor.

s.def: An intermediate state after death in which some of those ultimately destined for Heaven must first undergo purification.

ety: From Middle English purgen, from Old French purgier, from Latin pūrgō (“to make pure, to cleanse”), from pūrus (“clean, pure”) + agō (“to make, to do”). The slang sense derived via the 2013 film The Purge.

s.def: An act or instance of purging.
To clean thoroughly; to rid of impurities; to cleanse; to clear of (something unwanted).
ex: After the process, the machine purges the chamber before venting it to remove toxic gases.

s.def: To remove by cleansing; to wash away.
To free from sin, guilt, or burden.
ex: We'll join our cares to purge away / Our country’s crimes.

s.def: To evacuate (the bowels or the stomach); to defecate or vomit.
To cause someone to purge; to operate (on somebody) using a cathartic or emetic, or in a similar manner.
To forcibly remove, for example, from political activity.
ex: Deng Xiaoping was purged twice during the Cultural Revolution, but managed to return to power after Mao's death.

s.def: To forcibly remove people by an organization.
ex: Cromwell had Colonel Pride purge Parliament of royalists who opposed Charles I's execution.

s.def: To clear of a charge, suspicion, or imputation.
To clarify; to clear the dregs from (liquor).

ety: From Old French purificacion, from Latin pūrificātiō.

s.def: The act or process of purifying; the removal of impurities.
ex: air purification
purification of water

s.def: A religious act or rite in which a defiled person is made clean or free from sin.
ex: purification of the soul

s.def: The pouring of wine into the chalice to rinse it after communion, the wine being then drunk by the priest.

ety: From Middle English purifien, purifyen, from Old French purifier, purifiier, from Latin pūrificō, pūrificāre, from pūrus (“pure; clean”).

s.def: To cleanse, or rid of impurities.
ex: The modern arts deviate from the standards set forth by the divine—art should be used to purify one’s heart and improve one’s morality.

s.def: To free from guilt or sin.
To become pure.

ety: Borrowed from German Purin.

s.def: Any of a class of organic heterocyclic compounds, composed of fused pyrimidine and imidazole rings, that constitute one of the two groups of organic nitrogenous bases (the other being the pyrimidines) and are components of nucleic acids.

ety: Borrowed from French puriste. By surface analysis, pur(e) + -ist.

s.def: Of or pertaining to purism.
ex: He was the first to play for money, a practice which got him ousted from the purist U.S. Lawn Tennis Association.

s.def: An advocate of purism.

ety: See Puritan.

s.def: A puritanical person.
Acting or behaving according to the Puritan morals (e.g. propagating modesty), especially with regard to pleasure, nudity and sex; ascetic.

ety: Probably from purity + -an, because they sought to purify Church of England worship of what they perceived as Roman Catholic aspects. The capitalised form preceded the lowercase form puritan.

s.def: A member of a particular Protestant religious sect advocating greater purity and piety.

ety: Etymology tree English Puritan Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English Puritanism From Puritan + -ism.

s.def: The beliefs and practices of the Puritans.

ety: From pure + -ity, from Old French purete, from Latin puritas.

s.def: The state or degree of being pure.
ex: The purity of the water was tested in a laboratory.
She admired the purity of the child’s laughter.
Gold is valued according to its level of purity.

ety: Unknown; apparently related to Scots and dialect pirl (“twist, ripple, whirl, spin”), and possibly to Older Scots pyrl ("thrust or poke at"). Compare Venetan pirlo, an embellishment where the woven threads are twisted together. May be unrelated to purfle, though the meanings are similar.

s.def: A particular stitch in knitting in which the working yarn is pulled through an existing stitch from front to back.
The edge of lace trimmed with loops.
An embroidered and puckered border; a hem or fringe, often of gold or silver twist; also, a pleat or fold, as of a band.
ex: A triumphant chariot made of carnation velvet, enriched with purl and pearl.

s.def: To decorate with fringe or embroidered edge
ex: Needlework purled with gold.

s.def: To use or create a purl stitch or stitches.
ex: Knit one, purl two.
Stockinette fabric is created by knitting the right-side rows and purling the wrong-side rows.

s.def: a heavy or headlong fall; an upset.
To upset, to spin, capsize, fall heavily, fall headlong.
ex: The huntsman was purled from his horse.

s.def: To flow with a murmuring sound in swirls and eddies.
ex: Swift o'er the rolling pebbles, down the hills, / Louder and louder purl the falling rills.
A little creek purled down from the mountain over stones[.]
[T]he road purled out ahead of us for miles, all prospect and promise, like the beginning of a long, good friendship.

s.def: To rise in circles, ripples, or undulations; to curl; to mantle.
ex: thin winding breath which purled up to the sky

s.def: A circle made by the motion of a fluid; an eddy; a ripple.

ety: From Middle English purlewe (“piece of land on the edge of a forest”), modification under the influence of Old French lieu (“place”) of porale, purale (“royal perambulation”), from Old French porale, from poraler (“to traverse”), from por- (“forth”) (from Latin prō-) + aler, aller (“to go”).

s.def: The ground on the edges of a forest, especially when partly subject to the same forest laws concerning game hunting etc.
The outskirts of any place; an adjacent district; the environs or neighborhood; milieu.
ex: Whether Lady Anne knew or suspected who it was that drew his steps from the purlieus of fashion he knew not, nor held himself bound to explain.
The mission occupied eight or ten ares of land, a barren purlieu that held a few goats and burros.
I wanted a beer, but coffee was undeniably easier to be had in the purlieus of the University, so we went into a cafe.

ety: Uncertain. Information on the etymology is scant at best. According to Websters it comes from 15th-century English. According to the Oxford Concise Dictionary, it is "Middle English, perhaps of French origin". Other sources reference Middle English or 15th-century English.

s.def: A longitudinal structural member bridging two or more rafters of a roof.
ex: The loft was broad and high, with splendid rough-cut oak purlins and three large Veluxes.

ety: From Middle English purloynen (“to remove”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman purloigner (“to put far away”), one of the variants of Old French porloignier. Doublet of prolong.

s.def: To take the property of another, often in breach of trust; to appropriate wrongfully; to steal.
ex: Had from his wakeful custody purloined / The guarded gold.
Probably my acquaintance, Mr Blank, therefore, would have been able, if he had so wished to do, to purloin the papers which he mentioned.
Or was this simply another item Mr. Stink had purloined during his career as a gentleman thief?

s.def: To commit theft; to thieve.
ex: The Apostle expressly forbiddeth servants to purloin (Titus 2:10).

ety: From Middle English purple, purpel, from Old English purpul (“purple”, adjective), taken from Old English purpure (“purple colour”, noun), from Latin purpura (“purple dye, shellfish”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra, “purple-fish”), perhaps of Semitic origin. Doublet of purpura and purpure. The sense of "imperial power" is from the wearing of the color purple by emperors and kings.

s.def: colour
colour
A colour between red and blue; violet, though often closer to magenta.
Any non-spectral colour on the line of purples on a colour chromaticity diagram or a colour wheel between violet and red.

Cloth, or a garment, dyed a purple colour; especially, a purple robe, worn as an emblem of rank or authority; specifically, the purple robe or mantle worn by Ancient Roman emperors as the emblem of imperial dignity.
ex: to put on the imperial purple

s.def: Imperial power.
ex: 1776-1788, Edward Gibbon, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire He was born in the purple.
The immediate successors of Augustus indulged in appalling cruelties towards senators and towards possible competitors for the purple.

s.def: Any of various species of mollusks from which Tyrian purple dye was obtained, especially the common dog whelk.
The purple haze cultivar of cannabis in the kush family, either pure or mixed with others, or by extension any variety of smoked marijuana.
ex: "Sure, some purple Owlsley."
She preferred to smoke some good purple, but getting high wasn't an option.

s.def: Purpura.
Earcockle, a disease of wheat.
A large, dark brown and white (female), or purple and white (male) butterfly, Apatura iris, of the family Nymphalidae.

Various species in the Porphyrio genus of the Rallidae family, including Porphyrio porphyrio, Porphyrio madagascariensis, Porphyrio poliocephalus, Porphyrio indicus, Porphyrio pulverulentus, and Porphyrio melanotus.

ety: Etymology tree English purple Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-isk Old English -isċ Middle English -isch English -ish English purplish From purple + -ish.

s.def: Somewhat purple in colour/color.

ety: From Middle English purporten, from Anglo-Norman purporter and Old French porporter (“convey, contain, carry”), from pur-, from Latin pro (“forth”) + Old French porter (“carry”), from Latin portō (“carry”).

s.def: To intend.
ex: He purported to become an international man of affairs.

s.def: To convey, imply, or profess (often falsely or inaccurately).
ex: He purports himself to be an international man of affairs.
The intermediate station seen here, Llanbister Road, is 5 hilly miles by road from the town it purports to serve.

s.def: Import, an intention or purpose.
ex: My practice, you say, refutes my doubts. But you mistake the purport of my question.
Lenin repeats this admonition several times, and its purport is clear.

s.def: A disguise; a covering.
ex: For she her sex under that strange purport / Did use to hide.

ety: From purport + -ed.

s.def: Supposed, or assumed to be.
Normally assumed to be.
Said or claimed by some individuals to be real or true or to have happened, although this may not be the case.

ety: Etymology tree English purported Middle English -ly English -ly English purportedly From purported + -ly.

s.def: As appears to be true or is stated or accepted to be (though might not be so).
ex: Near-synonyms: reportedly, reputedly, putatively, rumoredly, supposedly, allegedly, ostensibly, possibly, probably, likely, plausibly
In addition, none of the purportedly more common terms of these pairs appear to be especially frequent in modern Indian English.

ety: From Middle English purpos, from Old French purposer (“to propose”) (with conjugation altered based on poser), from Latin prō- (“forth”) + pōnere (“place, put”), hence Latin prōpōnō, prōpōnere. By surface analysis, pur- + pose (“halt, pause, put, place”).

s.def: The end for which something is done, is made or exists.
ex: What is the purpose of your visit?
The device can be used for both civilian and military purposes.

s.def: Function, role.
ex: The exceptionally small gate-leg table served the purpose of a tea table admirably.
As with all life forms, the sole purpose of a virus is to ensure reproduction in kind.
Is it the purpose of mosquitoes to ultimately provide calories to large birds of prey?

s.def: meaning for existing or doing something.
Resolution; determination.
ex: Perhaps you have heard that there was once some purpose of marriage between the Duc de Joyeuse and myself; it is of that which I have to tell.

s.def: The subject of discourse; the point at issue.
ex: But now, forasmuch as you have stopt up a few shards in these your last tedious commentaries, though very hardly and quite from the purpose, […]

s.def: To have or set as one's purpose or aim; resolve to accomplish; intend; plan.
ex: I purpose to write the history of England from the accession of King James the Second down to a time which is within the memory of men still living.

s.def: To have (an) intention, purpose, or design; to intend; to mean.
To discourse.

ety: From purpose + -ful.

s.def: Having purpose: having intention or meaning; intentional.
ex: […] spend purposeful time with my grandparents where we found out more about each other and had some interesting discussions.

s.def: Having a purpose in mind; resolute; determined, full of determination.

ety: Etymology tree Middle English purpos English purpose Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English purposive From purpose + -ive. Compare purpositive.

s.def: Serving a particular purpose; useful; adapted to a given purpose, especially through natural evolution.
Done or performed with a conscious purpose or intent.
ex: Most human activity is purposive.
Other ecclesiastics [...] were similarly accepting of a space for purposive and beneficent human action and betterment in a disenchanted world.

s.def: Pertaining to purpose, as reflected in behaviour or mental activity.
ex: Ursula could not believe the air in her nostrils. It seemed conscious, malevolent, purposive in its intense murderous coldness.
The question at once arises whether medieval thinkers really believed that what we now call inanimate objects were sentient and purposive.

s.def: Pertaining to or demonstrating purpose.
ex: The world was generally agreed to be a purposive one, responsive to the wishes of its Creator […].

s.def: Possessed of a firm purpose.
ex: I had a purposive air about me that night.

s.def: Of a clause or conjunction: expressing purpose.
A mood indicating a purpose of the course of activity expressed by the verb.
ex: This purposive was described by speakers as referring to the action which can be observed at the moment of speech; this is why it is termed ‘visual’.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin purpura. Doublet of purple and purpure.

s.def: The appearance of red or purple discolorations on the skin that do not blanch when pressure is applied, caused by subdermal bleeding.

ety: From Latin purpura (“purple”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra). The medical sense is from the English purpura (“the appearance of purple discolorations on the skin”). By surface analysis, purpura + -ic.

s.def: Pertaining to or affected with purpura (skin discoloration from blood inside it).
Purple or purplish (of spots which appear on the skin; regardless of their cause); Synonym of purpureal.
purple in colour; derived from or forming a substance which is purple; especially
purple in colour; derived from or forming a substance which is purple; especially:
ex: purpuric acid
a purpuric salt

der: papular purpuric gloves and socks syndr…

s.def: A red anthraquinone dye, extracted from madder, that is used as a biological stain
A protein of the lipocalin family
A brownish or deep red decorative glass used in ancient times

ety: Onomatopoeic.

s.def: To make a vibrating sound in its throat when contented or in certain other conditions.
ex: There was no one at home but a black cat, who was sitting quite content and purring on the hearth[.]

s.def: To say (something) in a throaty, seductive manner.
ex: "This is Cindy," she purred again, flashing a smile of perfect white teeth surrounded by full red lips.

s.def: To make a vibrating throaty sound, as from pleasure.
ex: He purred like a kitten when she massaged his neck.

s.def: To spend time enjoying and expressing pleasure (over something); to coo; to enthuse.
ex: No woman receiving her first mink would ever put it directly into storage. She would try it on and purr over it.

s.def: To make a low and consistent rumbling sound.
ex: Beverly passed the city limits sign with the Porsche's motor purring contentedly after its two hundred and fifty-mile romp.

s.def: The vibrating sound made by a cat in its throat when contented.
A throaty, seductive sound of pleasure made by a person.
ex: The trill of her purr echoed inside his mouth when he kissed her again. Clutching at his shirt, her fingers traveled the muscles in his back.

s.def: The low consistent rumble made by an engine at slow speed
Vibrating sound made by a cat.

ety: From pyro- + -logy.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥ Proto-Hellenic *pāwər Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr) Latin pyr English pyro- Ancient Greek λούω (loúō) Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Hellenic *-tis Ancient Greek -τῐς (-tĭs) Ancient Greek -σις (-sis) Ancient Greek λοῦσις (loûsis) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs)der. Latin -ītēslbor. French -iteder. English -ite English pyrolusite From pyro- + Ancient Greek λοῦσις (loûsis) + English -ite.

s.def: A dark coloured mineral, consisting of manganese dioxide (MnO₂), that is an important ore of manganese.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥ Proto-Hellenic *pāwər Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr) Latin pyr English pyro- Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁-der. Ancient Greek λύω (lúō) Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Hellenic *-tis Ancient Greek -τῐς (-tĭs) Ancient Greek -σις (-sis) Ancient Greek λῠ́σῐς (lŭ́sĭs)der. English -lysis English pyrolysis From pyro- + -lysis.

s.def: The decomposition of a material or compound by heat, in the absence of oxygen or other reagents.
ex: Techniques that have successfully identified ionic intermediates in solution have been applied to gas-phase pyrolyses.
Twenty years ago our real understanding of the mechanism of alkane pyrolyses was little better than rudimentary.

ety: From pyro- + -mania.

s.def: A compulsive disorder characterized by obsession with fire or uncontrollable urges to start fires.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥ Proto-Hellenic *pāwər Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr) Latin pyr English pyro- Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-tḗr Proto-Indo-European *-trom Proto-Hellenic *-tron Ancient Greek -τρον (-tron) Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron)lbor. French -mètrebor. English -meter English pyrometer From pyro- + -meter.

s.def: A thermometer designed to measure high temperatures.
An instrument for measuring the thermal expansion of solids.
A yellowish-green mineral, a mixed phosphate and chloride of lead with the chemical formula Pb₅(PO₄)₃Cl that is sometimes mined as an ore.

ety: From Latin pyrōpus, from Ancient Greek πυρωπός (purōpós, “fiery-eyed, fire-colored”), from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”); compare French pyrope.

s.def: A variety of garnet, of a poppy or blood-red color, frequently with a tinge of orange. It is used as a gemstone.
A soft, pale aluminosilicate mineral, somewhat resembling talc.

ety: From Ancient Greek πύρωσις (púrōsis, “burning”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + -σις (-sis, verbal noun suffix).

s.def: A burning sensation in the chest due to reflux of stomach contents in the esophagus.

ety: From pyro- + -stat.

s.def: A thermostat designed to operate at high temperatures.
An automatic draught-regulator for chimney-stacks, smoke-pipes, etc.

ety: From Latin pyrotechnica, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + τεχνικός (tekhnikós, “skillful, workmanlike”). Analyzable as pyro- + technic.

s.def: Of or relating to fireworks.
Of or relating to the use of fire in chemistry or metallurgy.
Resembling fireworks.
ex: [T]he Weston clan, whose dysfunctions are pyrotechnic in their scale and intensity.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥ Proto-Hellenic *pāwər Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr) Latin pyr English pyro- Ancient Greek τοξῐκός (toxĭkós) Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón)der. Latin toxicum English -in English toxin English pyrotoxin From pyro- + toxin.

s.def: Any of several pyrogenic bacterial toxins.
Any toxic agent produced by combustion.

ety: From French pyroxène, from pyro- + Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “stranger”).

s.def: Any of a group of crystalline minerals containing silicates of iron, magnesium and calcium.

ety: Etymology tree English pyroxene Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs)der. Latin -ītēslbor. French -iteder. English -ite English pyroxenite From pyroxene + -ite.

s.def: A heavy, dark igneous rock consisting mostly of pyroxene minerals with smaller amounts of olivine and hornblende.
Archaic form of pyroxylin.

ety: After Greek king Pyrrhus of Epirus, who suffered heavy losses while defeating the Romans.

s.def: A very costly victory, wherein the considerable losses outweigh the gain, so as to render the struggle not worth the cost.
ex: We now know that it [the Six-Day War] was a Pyrrhic victory.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek πυρρότης (purrhótēs) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs)der. Latin -ītēslbor. French -iteder. English -ite English pyrrhotite From Ancient Greek πυρρότης (purrhótēs) + English -ite.

s.def: A weakly magnetic ferrous sulfide mineral, FeS.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥ Proto-Hellenic *pāwər Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr) Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Hellenic *-rós Ancient Greek -ρός (-rós) Ancient Greek πῠρρός (pŭrrhós)der. German Pyrrolbor. English pyrrole From German Pyrrol, corresponding to Ancient Greek πυρρός (purrhós, “reddish, fiery”) + -ole.

s.def: Any of a class of aromatic heterocyclic compounds containing a ring of four carbon atoms and a nitrogen atom; especially the simplest one, C₄H₅N.

ety: From Ancient Greek Πῡθαγόρᾱς (Pūthagórās).

s.def: Ancient Greek mathematician and philosopher
A male given name from Ancient Greek of mostly historical use, and a transliteration from modern Greek.
Ellipsis of Pythagoras' theorem.

ety: Named after Pythagoras (from Ancient Greek Πυθαγόρας (Puthagóras)), the Greek mathematician and philosopher who by tradition is credited with the theorem’s discovery and proof.

s.def: A mathematical theorem which states that the square of the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of those of the two other sides.
ex: The Pythagorean theorem only applies to right triangles.

s.def: A generalization of the Pythagorean theorem for Euclidean triangles to Hilbert spaces.
Produced by filth.
ex: a pythogenic fever

ety: From Latin pȳthon, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn), the name of the mythological enormous serpent at Delphi slain by Apollo, probably from Πυθώ (Puthṓ), older name of Delphi.

s.def: Any of the family Pythonidae of nonvenomous constrictor snakes.
A penis.

ety: See Pythoness.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Pythoness.
A female soothsayer
A female python.
ex: On the fifteenth of January, it was discovered that the pythoness had excluded rather more than a hundred dirty-white, leathery-looking eggs.

ety: From python (“snake of the family Pythonidae”) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Python is derived from Latin Pȳthōn, from Ancient Greek Πῡ́θων (Pū́thōn, “Python, mythical serpent which lived at Delphi”), from Πῡθώ (Pūthṓ, “Pytho, ancient name of Delphi; Python, the mythical serpent”) (probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“deep; dark (?); unclear (?)”) or *puH- (“foul, rotten”)) + -ων (-ōn, suffix forming possessives).

s.def: Of or pertaining to, or resembling, a python (“large constricting snake of the family Pythonidae”); pythonlike.
ex: The blue glitter of Mr Kelly's eyes in the uttermost depths of their orbits became fixed, then veiled by the classical pythonic glaze.

s.def: Of or pertaining to an oracle or prophet, or to the telling of prophecies; oracular, prophetic.

Alternative letter-case form of Pythonic (“of or pertaining to, or resembling, the Python in Ancient Greek mythology, a serpent which lived at Delphi (regarded as the centre of the Earth) until it was killed by Apollo; (figurative) enormous; monstrous”).
Alternative letter-case form of Pythonic (“using the idioms of the Python programming language”).

ety: From py- + -uria.

s.def: The presence of pus in the urine.
ex: Pyuria may result from suppuration in any part of the urinary system, or from an abscess opening into the urinary tract.
The Sternheimer-Malbin stain is useful in diagnosis of pyelonephritis, and of even more help in differential diagnosis of the pyurias.

ety: The noun is derived from Late Middle English pix, pixe (“vessel for holding a host, pyx; hip bone socket, pyxis”) [and other forms], from Late Latin pyxis (“vessel for holding a host”), Latin pyxis (“small box for medicines or toiletries; box holding sample coins for testing; hip bone socket; sailor's compass”), from Koine Greek πυξίς (puxís), Ancient Greek πῠξῐ́ς (pŭxĭ́s, “box; box or tablet made of boxwood; cylinder”), from πῠ́ξος (pŭ́xos, “box tree; boxwood”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, suffix forming femin…

s.def: A small, usually round container used to hold the host (“consecrated bread or wafer of the Eucharist”), especially when bringing communion to the sick or others unable to attend Mass.
ex: [W]here am I to find such a sum? If I sell the very pyx and candlesticks on the altar at Jorvaulx, I shall scarce raise the half; […]

s.def: A (small) box; a casket, a coffret.
ex: [M]eantime some pyx to screen / The full-grown pest, some lid to shut upon / The goblin!

s.def: A box used in a mint as a place to deposit sample coins intended to have the fineness of their metal and their weight tested before the coins are issued to the public.
ex: The readers of the work will learn […] the proper methods of the survey of green-wax, and the trial of the pyx.

s.def: A compass used by sailors.
To place (the host) in a pyx.
ex: Than was yt boxed pyxed and tabernacled & so borne forth in processyon with torche lyght banner crosse candelstyck.

s.def: To enclose (something) in a box or other container; specifically, to place (a deceased person's body) in a coffin; to coffin, to encoffin.
ex: There pyxed in alabastrine cell, / All uncorrupt his shade shall dwell, / While waves his memory chime; […]

s.def: To deposit (sample coins) in a pyx; (by extension) to test (such coins) for the fineness of metal and weight before a mint issues them to the public.
ex: Among the incidental operations [in manufacturing coins] are […] "pyxing" the finished coin, or selecting specimens to be weighed and assayed; […]
Coins marked '2' were pyxed on 7 June 1603.

ety: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πυξίδιον (puxídion), diminutive of πῠξῐ́ς (pŭxĭ́s, “box”).

s.def: A seed capsule in the form of a box, the seeds being released when the top splits off.
ex: Key to Species of Cariniana Inflorescence predominantly terminal and subterminal; pyxidium without teeth at line of opercular dehiscence.
The pyxidium has the trigonoidly cylindrical or obconical form of that of Couratari, but it is much thicker, heavier, and more solid in substance.
A fruit of this kind is sometimes termed a pyxidium; that is, a little chest.

ety: From Latin pyxis (“small box”). Doublet of box, piseog, and pyx.

s.def: A small box.
A capsule in which the lid separates from the top of the fruit to release the seeds.
A nautical compass.
The box in which ashes are stored for Ash Wednesday.
acetabulum.
